posts.post_title: The autonomic nervous system is also known as
posts.post_content: The autonomic nervous system (ANS) is also known by which of the following names?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Visceral or vegetative nervous system

The ANS is also called the visceral, vegetative or involuntary nervous system.

Correct Option Explanation

It is widely distributed and controls involuntary visceral functions such as smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and secretory gland activity.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Somatic nervous system innervates skeletal muscle voluntarily at the neuromuscular junction, unlike the involuntary ANS.
  • Pyramidal nervous system refers to the corticospinal pathway controlling voluntary skeletal movement, not visceral function.
  • Peripheral motor nervous system is not the accepted synonym for the ANS in standard pharmacology texts.
Know More
  • ANS regulates respiration, blood pressure, heart rate, eye function and GI activity.
  • ANS mediates the body's response to emergency situations and maintains homeostasis.
  • The nervous system is broadly divided into CNS and PNS.
  • SMS (somatic motor system) is voluntary and acts at the neuromuscular junction.

posts.post_title: Neurotransmitter at autonomic ganglia (prega…
posts.post_content: Which neurotransmitter is released by preganglionic fibres at autonomic ganglia?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Acetylcholine

Acetylcholine (ACh) is released by preganglionic fibres of both sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.

Correct Option Explanation

This ganglionic synapse is a nicotinic cholinergic synapse, common to both autonomic divisions.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Norepinephrine is released at the sympathetic postganglionic neuroeffector junction, not at the ganglion.
  • Dopamine acts mainly as a CNS neurotransmitter and renal vasodilator, not the principal ganglionic transmitter.
  • Epinephrine is released from the adrenal medulla into blood, not at ganglionic synapses.
Know More
  • Preganglionic fibres exit the spinal cord and terminate in ganglia.
  • Postganglionic fibres innervate effector cells/organs directly.
  • The adrenal medulla is an embryological exception, acting like a sympathetic ganglion.
  • Ganglionic transmission is nicotinic; neuroeffector transmission may be nicotinic, muscarinic or adrenergic.

posts.post_title: Transmitter at parasympathetic neuroeffector…
posts.post_content: Which neurotransmitter mediates transmission at the parasympathetic postganglionic neuroeffector junction?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Acetylcholine (muscarinic)

Acetylcholine mediates muscarinic cholinergic transmission at parasympathetic neuroeffector junctions.

Correct Option Explanation

Postganglionic parasympathetic fibres release ACh, which acts on muscarinic receptors on effector cells.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Norepinephrine mediates adrenergic transmission at sympathetic, not parasympathetic, neuroeffector junctions.
  • Epinephrine is released into the blood by the adrenal medulla, not at parasympathetic synapses.
  • Serotonin is not a classical autonomic neuroeffector transmitter in this system.
Know More
  • Parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral (cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and sacral S2-S4).
  • Preganglionic:postganglionic ratio is discrete (1:1) in the parasympathetic system.
  • Function is termed 'rest and digest' or conservation of energy.
  • Postganglionic fibres are short, synapsing near or within the target organ.

posts.post_title: Transmitter at sympathetic neuroeffector jun…
posts.post_content: Which neurotransmitter is released at the sympathetic postganglionic neuroeffector junction?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Norepinephrine

Norepinephrine (NE) mediates adrenergic transmission at the sympathetic neuroeffector junction.

Correct Option Explanation

Sympathetic postganglionic fibres are generally adrenergic, releasing NE onto effector organs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Acetylcholine is the transmitter at sympathetic ganglia and at sympathetic sweat gland fibres (an exception), not the general neuroeffector transmitter.
  • GABA is a major CNS inhibitory transmitter, not a peripheral autonomic neuroeffector transmitter.
  • Histamine is an autacoid, not a classical autonomic neurotransmitter.
Know More
  • Sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar (T1-L3).
  • Preganglionic:postganglionic ratio is diffuse, up to 1:20.
  • Function is 'fight or flight', energy expenditure.
  • Postganglionic fibres are long, arising from paravertebral/prevertebral ganglia.

posts.post_title: Spinal origin of sympathetic preganglionic f…
posts.post_content: Sympathetic preganglionic fibres originate from which region of the spinal cord?

_aimcq_options.text: Entire length of the spinal cord

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1st thoracic to 3rd lumbar segments

Sympathetic preganglionic fibres arise from the intermediolateral column of the spinal cord between T1 and L3.

Correct Option Explanation

This is termed the thoracolumbar outflow, distinguishing it from parasympathetic craniosacral outflow.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sacral segments 2-4 contribute to the parasympathetic craniosacral outflow, not sympathetic.
  • Cervical segments only is incorrect; sympathetic outflow begins at T1, not the cervical cord.
  • Entire length of the spinal cord is incorrect; sympathetic outflow is restricted to the thoracolumbar region.
Know More
  • Preganglionic fibres are short, synapsing in paravertebral or prevertebral ganglia.
  • Paravertebral ganglia include 22 pairs of cervical ganglia along the vertebral column.
  • Prevertebral ganglia include the celiac, cranial and caudal mesenteric ganglia.
  • The adrenal medulla is functionally a sympathetic ganglion.

posts.post_title: Cranial nerves in parasympathetic craniosacr…
posts.post_content: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres arise from which of the following cranial nerves?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 3rd, 7th, 9th and 10th cranial nerves

Parasympathetic craniosacral outflow arises from the oculomotor (III), facial (VII), glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) cranial nerves, plus sacral segments.

Correct Option Explanation

These nerves carry preganglionic fibres from the midbrain and medulla oblongata to peripheral ganglia near or within target organs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 1st, 2nd, 5th and 6th cranial nerves (olfactory, optic, trigeminal, abducens) are not part of parasympathetic outflow.
  • 4th, 8th, 11th and 12th cranial nerves (trochlear, vestibulocochlear, accessory, hypoglossal) carry no parasympathetic outflow.
  • Only the 10th cranial nerve is incomplete; III, VII and IX also contribute.
Know More
  • Vagus (X) fibres synapse in terminal ganglia in the heart, lungs, liver, spleen, GI tract, kidney.
  • 3rd cranial nerve fibres synapse in the ciliary ganglion for eye control.
  • 7th cranial nerve fibres synapse in the submandibular ganglia.
  • 9th cranial nerve fibres synapse in the otic ganglion.

posts.post_title: Preganglionic:postganglionic neuron ratio in…
posts.post_content: What is the typical ratio of preganglionic to postganglionic neurons in the sympathetic nervous system?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Diffuse, up to 1:20

Sympathetic innervation is diffuse, with one preganglionic neuron synapsing on up to 20 postganglionic neurons.

Correct Option Explanation

This diffuse arrangement lets a small sympathetic stimulus produce a widespread "fight or flight" response.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Discrete, 1:1 describes the parasympathetic system, which acts on a more localised, precise basis.
  • Fixed at 1:5 is not the ratio described for either autonomic division.
  • 1:2 exactly does not match the described diffuse sympathetic ratio of up to 1:20.
Know More
  • Parasympathetic ganglia synapse discretely (1:1) close to the effector organ.
  • Sympathetic ganglia are paravertebral or prevertebral, close to the CNS.
  • Sympathetic postganglionic fibres are long; parasympathetic postganglionic fibres are short.
  • Diffuse innervation supports mass sympathetic discharge during stress.

posts.post_title: Functional equivalence of the adrenal medulla
posts.post_content: The adrenal medulla is embryologically and functionally equivalent to which structure?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A sympathetic ganglion

The adrenal medulla is embryologically and functionally a sympathetic ganglion.

Correct Option Explanation

It is innervated by typical sympathetic preganglionic neurons releasing ACh, but instead of a postganglionic neuron it releases epinephrine directly into the blood.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A parasympathetic ganglion is innervated by craniosacral, not thoracolumbar, preganglionic fibres — not the adrenal medulla's origin.
  • A somatic motor nerve innervates skeletal muscle voluntarily, unlike the adrenal medulla's endocrine-like function.
  • A dorsal root ganglion houses cell bodies of sensory afferent fibres, not sympathetic efferents.
Know More
  • This is the one case where ganglionic transmission causes release of epinephrine (adrenaline) into circulation.
  • Cell bodies of afferent fibres lie in the dorsal root ganglia of spinal nerves.
  • The hypothalamus is the principal CNS locus of autonomic integration.
  • The medulla oblongata controls blood pressure and respiration reflexes.

posts.post_title: Predominant tone at the SA node
posts.post_content: Which division of the autonomic nervous system exerts the predominant tone at the sino-atrial (SA) node?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Parasympathetic (cholinergic)

The SA node is predominantly under parasympathetic (cholinergic) tone.

Correct Option Explanation

Vagal cholinergic tone normally restrains heart rate; loss of this tone raises resting heart rate.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sympathetic (adrenergic) tone predominates at arterioles, veins and the ventricles, not the SA node.
  • Both equally is incorrect; the text specifies a clear predominant tone per site, not a balanced one for the SA node.
  • Neither division is wrong since the SA node is actively under parasympathetic control.
Know More
  • The atrium is also predominantly parasympathetic (cholinergic).
  • The ventricle is predominantly sympathetic (adrenergic).
  • Iris and ciliary muscle tone is predominantly parasympathetic.
  • Sweat glands are predominantly sympathetic despite using ACh as transmitter.

posts.post_title: Effect of sympathetic activation on bronchi
posts.post_content: Sympathetic activation produces which effect on the bronchi?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bronchodilation

Sympathetic activation causes the bronchi to dilate.

Correct Option Explanation

This supports increased airflow during the 'fight or flight' response, complementing increased heart rate and force.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bronchoconstriction is the parasympathetic effect on bronchi, the opposite of sympathetic action.
  • No change is incorrect; the bronchi are dually innervated with clear opposing effects.
  • Increased mucus secretion only is not the described bronchial effect; secretion changes relate to glands, not bronchial smooth muscle tone.
Know More
  • Sympathetic activation increases heart rate and force of ventricular contraction.
  • Sympathetic activation decreases intestinal tone and motility.
  • Parasympathetic activation increases intestinal tone and motility.
  • Bronchial and intestinal smooth muscle show classic antagonistic dual innervation.

posts.post_title: Structures without parasympathetic innervati…
posts.post_content: Which of the following structures receives NO parasympathetic innervation?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sweat glands

Sweat glands receive no parasympathetic innervation.

Correct Option Explanation

They are innervated solely by sympathetic (cholinergic) fibres, an exception where sympathetic nerves use ACh.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Urinary bladder receives predominant parasympathetic innervation controlling micturition.
  • Salivary glands receive dual innervation, with parasympathetic tone producing profuse watery secretion.
  • Iris receives parasympathetic innervation to its sphincter (constrictor) muscle.
Know More
  • Other structures lacking parasympathetic supply include systemic blood vessels, erector pili, the adrenal gland, and smooth muscle of the upper eyelid/nictitating membrane.
  • These structures are controlled solely by increasing or decreasing sympathetic activity.
  • The pupil shows opposing tonic control: sympathetic dilator vs parasympathetic constrictor muscle.
  • In a frightened animal, the pupil dilates even in bright light due to increased sympathetic activity.

posts.post_title: Nature of dual innervation of salivary glands
posts.post_content: The sympathetic and parasympathetic effects on salivary secretion are best described as

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Complementary

Salivary gland innervation is complementary: both divisions increase secretion, but of different character.

Correct Option Explanation

Sympathetic tone gives scanty, viscous secretion; parasympathetic tone gives profuse, watery secretion — same direction, different quality.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Antagonistic describes organs like the heart, bladder or bronchi, where the two divisions oppose each other, unlike the salivary gland.
  • Absent is wrong; salivary glands are actively and dually innervated.
  • Identical in volume and viscosity is incorrect; the two divisions differ markedly in the character of secretion produced.
Know More
  • Heart, bladder, bronchi and GI tract show antagonistic dual innervation, with one division usually predominant.
  • The pupil is controlled by opposing muscles (dilator vs constrictor) rather than by opposing action on the same cells.
  • Organs with single innervation are controlled purely by increasing/decreasing that one division's activity.
  • Lacrimal glands show increased lacrimation with both sympathetic and parasympathetic activation.

posts.post_title: Cause of pupil dilation in dim light
posts.post_content: Pupil dilation in dim light occurs primarily due to

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Reduced parasympathetic activity

In dim light, the pupil dilates because of reduced parasympathetic tone to the constrictor muscle.

Correct Option Explanation

The constrictor (sphincter) muscle of the pupil is normally kept in tonic contraction by parasympathetic fibres; less light reduces this tone, allowing dilation.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Increased parasympathetic activity would constrict, not dilate, the pupil, the opposite of the observed effect.
  • Reduced sympathetic activity would reduce dilator muscle tone and favour constriction, not dilation.
  • Loss of adrenal medullary secretion is unrelated to the direct neural reflex controlling pupil size in dim light.
Know More
  • In a frightened animal, the pupil dilates even in bright light due to increased sympathetic activity.
  • The dilator muscle is under sympathetic tonic contraction; the constrictor muscle under parasympathetic tonic contraction.
  • This is an example of opposing ANS branches acting on different cells of the same organ.
  • The iris illustrates functional antagonism through separate effector muscles rather than a single shared cell type.

posts.post_title: Nerves classified as cholinergic
posts.post_content: Which of the following nerve groups is classified as cholinergic?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All postganglionic parasympathetic nerves

All postganglionic parasympathetic nerves are cholinergic.

Correct Option Explanation

Cholinergic nerves also include all motor nerves to skeletal muscle and all preganglionic autonomic nerves (including to the adrenal medulla).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Most postganglionic sympathetic nerves are classified as adrenergic, not cholinergic.
  • Adrenal medullary secretory cells are innervated by cholinergic preganglionic fibres but themselves secrete catecholamines, not acting as cholinergic effector nerves.
  • Cardiovascular sympathetic innervation is predominantly adrenergic.
Know More
  • All motor nerves to skeletal muscle are cholinergic (nicotinic, neuromuscular junction).
  • All preganglionic autonomic nerves, both sympathetic and parasympathetic, are cholinergic.
  • Sweat glands are an adrenergic-system exception innervated by cholinergic sympathetic fibres.
  • Adrenergic innervation predominates in the cardiovascular system.

posts.post_title: Adrenal medulla secretion on sympathetic act…
posts.post_content: Sympathetic activation causes the adrenal medulla to secrete

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Epinephrine and norepinephrine

Sympathetic activation of the adrenal medulla causes secretion of epinephrine and norepinephrine into the blood.

Correct Option Explanation

Preganglionic sympathetic fibres release ACh onto medullary chromaffin cells, which then release these catecholamines systemically.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Acetylcholine only is the ganglionic input signal, not the medulla's secretory output.
  • Dopamine only is a catecholamine precursor but not the principal secreted product of the adrenal medulla.
  • Serotonin and histamine are autacoids unrelated to adrenal medullary sympathetic secretion.
Know More
  • There is no parasympathetic innervation to the adrenal gland.
  • Sympathetic activation causes vasoconstriction and contraction of the vas deferens, seminal vesicle and prostatic musculature for ejaculation.
  • Parasympathetic activation causes vasodilatation and erection of sex organs.
  • The adrenal medulla is functionally a modified sympathetic ganglion.

posts.post_title: Otto Loewi's key contribution (1920)
posts.post_content: Otto Loewi, in 1920, provided

_aimcq_options.text: The first real proof of chemical neurotransmission
The discovery of nitric oxide as a transmitter

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: The first real proof of chemical neurotransmission

Otto Loewi (1920) obtained the first real experimental proof of chemical neurotransmission.

Correct Option Explanation

His work, along with Dale's, earned the Nobel Prize in 1936 for fundamental contributions to chemical neurotransmission.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The concept of quantal release is credited to Katz (1970 Nobel laureate), not Loewi.
  • The discovery of nitric oxide as a transmitter is credited to Furchgott, Murad and Ignarro (1998 Nobel).
  • Classification of adrenergic receptor-related work such as β-blockers is credited to Black (1988 Nobel).
Know More
  • Sir Henry Dale (1914) coined the terms 'muscarinic' and 'nicotinic'.
  • Von Euler (1970) established norepinephrine as the adrenergic neurotransmitter.
  • Axelrod (1970) established major catecholamine inactivation pathways.
  • Dale and Loewi jointly received the 1936 Nobel Prize.

posts.post_title: Resting membrane potential of the axon
posts.post_content: The resting membrane potential of a typical axon is approximately

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: -85 mV

The axonal resting membrane potential is approximately -85 mV.

Correct Option Explanation

This electronegativity arises from potassium ion leakage against its concentration gradient from inside to outside the cell.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • -40 mV is not the described resting value; it is closer to a partially depolarized state.
  • 0 mV describes the transient point during depolarization as the potential moves toward and crosses zero, not the resting state.
  • +30 mV approximates the overshoot phase of the action potential, not the resting potential.
Know More
  • A supra-threshold stimulus sharply increases membrane permeability to Na+ relative to K+.
  • Repolarisation restores relative impermeability to Na+ and higher permeability to K+.
  • The axonal membrane is briefly refractory after an action potential, preventing antidromic conduction.
  • Axonal conduction itself is largely insensitive to most drugs.

posts.post_title: Ion triggering neurotransmitter exocytosis
posts.post_content: Which ion couples membrane excitation to the discharge of neurotransmitter from the nerve terminal?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Calcium (Ca++)

Ca++ links excitation of the nerve terminal membrane to exocytotic discharge of neurotransmitter.

Correct Option Explanation

The action potential triggers inward Ca++ movement from interstitial space and membrane binding sites, which then triggers vesicular exocytosis into the junctional cleft.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sodium (Na+) drives the depolarising phase of the axonal action potential itself, not vesicular release.
  • Potassium (K+) efflux underlies repolarisation and the resting potential, not the release-coupling step.
  • Chloride (Cl-) permeability changes underlie inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSP), not release coupling.
Know More
  • Nitric oxide is a unique co-transmitter not stored in vesicles; its synthesis is also Ca++-activated, via nitric oxide synthase.
  • An EPSP involves net inward Na+ movement and K+ efflux causing depolarization.
  • An IPSP involves selective increased permeability to K+ and Cl-, causing hyperpolarization.
  • Co-transmitters such as ATP, VIP, Neuropeptide Y and Substance P are stored in distinct vesicles from the primary transmitter.

posts.post_title: Neurotransmitter not stored in synaptic vesi…
posts.post_content: Which neurotransmitter is NOT stored in synaptic vesicles and instead diffuses rapidly due to high lipophilicity?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Nitric oxide

Nitric oxide is not stored in vesicles; being highly lipophilic, it diffuses rapidly to effector cells.

Correct Option Explanation

Its formation is Ca++-activated via the enzyme nitric oxide synthase, generating it on demand rather than storing it.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Acetylcholine is synthesized and stored in vesicles at the nerve terminal, released by exocytosis.
  • Norepinephrine is also stored in vesicles and metabolized by intraneuronal and extraneuronal enzymes after release.
  • Dopamine is a classical catecholamine that is vesicle-stored like norepinephrine.
Know More
  • Nitric oxide is a highly reactive free radical, oxidised within seconds to nitrites and nitrates.
  • Nitric oxide is the transmitter of non-adrenergic non-cholinergic (NANC) transmission.
  • NANC transmission occurs in the gut, vas deferens, urinary tract, salivary glands and some blood vessels.
  • Nitric oxide, not acetylcholine, is likely responsible for penile erection despite parasympathetic genital supply.

posts.post_title: Rate-limiting step in acetylcholine synthesis
posts.post_content: The rate-limiting step in the synthesis of acetylcholine at the cholinergic nerve terminal is

_aimcq_options.text: Uptake of choline into the axonal membrane

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Uptake of choline into the axonal membrane

Active uptake of choline into the nerve terminal is the rate-limiting step in ACh synthesis.

Correct Option Explanation

This uptake is selectively blocked by hemicholinium, which depletes acetylcholine stores by cutting off precursor supply.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Acetylation by choline acetylase uses ATP and coenzyme-A but is not the described rate-limiting step; choline uptake precedes and limits it.
  • Hydrolysis by cholinesterase terminates ACh action after release, unrelated to the synthesis rate.
  • Storage in synaptic vesicles is blocked by vesamicol, a separate step from the rate-limiting uptake.
Know More
  • Choline acetylase acetylates choline in the axoplasm using ATP and coenzyme-A.
  • Ca++ facilitates vesicle fusion and ACh release; Mg++ inhibits release.
  • Botulinum toxin inhibits ACh release causing paralysis; black widow spider venom causes massive release.
  • ACh release occurs in quanta, each corresponding to one vesicle's contents.

posts.post_title: Drug blocking vesicular transport of acetylc…
posts.post_content: Which drug blocks the transport of acetylcholine into synaptic vesicles?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Vesamicol

Vesamicol blocks transport of acetylcholine into the synaptic vesicles.

Correct Option Explanation

This prevents vesicular storage of ACh even though cytoplasmic ACh synthesis may continue.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Hemicholinium blocks choline uptake, the precursor supply step, not vesicular loading.
  • Physostigmine inhibits cholinesterase, prolonging ACh action rather than blocking its storage.
  • Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors postjunctionally, unrelated to presynaptic vesicular transport.
Know More
  • Most ACh is stored in ionic solution in small synaptic vesicles; some remains free in the cytoplasm.
  • Release occurs by exocytosis in quantal packets after Ca++ influx.
  • Ca++ ionophores can also stimulate ACh release directly.
  • Hydrolysis of released ACh yields choline and acetate; choline is recycled by active uptake.

posts.post_title: True cholinesterase distribution
posts.post_content: True (specific) acetylcholinesterase is characteristically found at

_aimcq_options.text: Cholinergic nerve sites, RBCs and gray matter

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cholinergic nerve sites, RBCs and gray matter

True cholinesterase is distributed at all cholinergic nerve sites, in red blood cells and in gray matter.

Correct Option Explanation

It hydrolyses acetylcholine very fast and is primarily responsible for terminating ACh action at synapses.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Plasma, liver and intestine describe the distribution of pseudocholinesterase, not true cholinesterase.
  • Only in skeletal muscle cytoplasm is not an accurate distribution site for either enzyme type.
  • Only in the adrenal cortex is unrelated to cholinesterase distribution, which is neural and hematologic.
Know More
  • True cholinesterase is more sensitive to inhibition by physostigmine.
  • Pseudocholinesterase is more sensitive to organophosphates and hydrolyses benzoylcholine and butyrylcholine.
  • True cholinesterase hydrolyses methacholine slower than ACh; pseudocholinesterase does not hydrolyse it at all.
  • Pseudocholinesterase functions mainly in hydrolysis of ingested esters, found in white matter too.

posts.post_title: Toxin that massively increases acetylcholine…
posts.post_content: Which toxin causes massive release of acetylcholine from nerve terminals?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Black widow spider venom

Black widow spider venom induces massive release of acetylcholine.

Correct Option Explanation

It acts oppositely to botulinum toxin, triggering exocytosis rather than blocking it.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Botulinum toxin inhibits ACh release, causing flaccid paralysis — the opposite effect.
  • Tetanus toxin acts centrally on inhibitory neurons in the spinal cord, not by increasing peripheral ACh release.
  • Curare (d-tubocurarine) blocks nicotinic receptors postjunctionally rather than affecting presynaptic ACh release.
Know More
  • Botulinum toxin causes paralysis by inhibiting ACh release from cholinergic terminals.
  • ACh is normally removed with 'flash-like suddenness' after release.
  • Mg++ physiologically inhibits ACh release, opposing the facilitatory action of Ca++.
  • Release occurs by exocytosis in discrete quantal packets.

posts.post_title: Naming basis of muscarinic and nicotinic rec…
posts.post_content: Muscarinic and nicotinic cholinergic receptors are named after

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: The alkaloids muscarine and nicotine

These receptors are named for selective activation by the alkaloids muscarine and nicotine respectively.

Correct Option Explanation

Muscarinic receptors are additionally linked historically to Amanita muscaria, the mushroom source of muscarine.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Naming after Dale and Loewi is incorrect; though Dale coined the terms, the receptors are named for the alkaloids, not the scientists.
  • CNS location is not the naming basis; both receptor types occur centrally and peripherally.
  • Molecular weight was never the naming criterion for these receptor classes.
Know More
  • Muscarinic receptors are G-protein coupled; nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels.
  • Muscarinic receptors are blocked by atropine, from Atropa belladonna.
  • Nicotinic receptors are blocked by d-tubocurarine (NM) or hexamethonium (NN).
  • There are five muscarinic subtypes (M1-M5); M1, M2 and M3 are pharmacologically most important.

posts.post_title: M2 muscarinic receptor agonist
posts.post_content: Which agent is the classical agonist at M2 muscarinic receptors of the SA node?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Methacholine

Methacholine is the agonist at M2 receptors, producing SA node hyperpolarization.

Correct Option Explanation

M2 activation decreases the rate of impulse generation at the SA node and decreases AV conduction velocity and atrial/ventricular contractility.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Oxotremorine is the agonist at M1 receptors of autonomic ganglia, not M2.
  • Bethanechol is the agonist at M3 receptors on visceral smooth muscle, causing contraction.
  • Phenyl trimethyl ammonium stimulates nicotinic (NM and NN), not muscarinic, receptors.
Know More
  • M2 receptors are blocked by the antagonist methoctramine.
  • M1 receptors are blocked by pirenzepine and mediate late EPSP in autonomic ganglia.
  • M3 receptors also increase secretion from exocrine glands.
  • All muscarinic receptor subtypes are G-protein coupled.

posts.post_title: Location of NM nicotinic receptors
posts.post_content: NM nicotinic receptors are located at the

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Skeletal muscle motor end plate

NM receptors are located at the skeletal muscle motor end plate and mediate skeletal muscle contraction.

Correct Option Explanation

They are blocked by d-tubocurarine, producing neuromuscular blockade and flaccid paralysis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Autonomic ganglia contain NN, not NM, receptors, blocked instead by hexamethonium.
  • Adrenal medulla also carries NN receptors, mediating catecholamine release, not NM receptors.
  • The SA node carries muscarinic M2 receptors, not nicotinic NM receptors.
Know More
  • Both NM and NN receptors are stimulated by phenyl trimethyl ammonium.
  • NN receptors occur in sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia, adrenal medulla, spinal cord and certain brain areas.
  • NN receptors are blocked by hexamethonium.
  • Nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated cation channels, causing rapid depolarization on ACh binding.

posts.post_title: Choline ester acting purely as a muscarinic …
posts.post_content: Which choline ester acts purely as a muscarinic agonist with no nicotinic activity?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bethanechol

Bethanechol is only a muscarinic agonist, with no nicotinic effects on skeletal muscle.

Correct Option Explanation

It is resistant to hydrolysis by acetylcholinesterase, giving it a longer duration of action and greater selectivity for GI and bladder smooth muscle.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Carbachol activates both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors and can cause fasciculation and paralysis at high doses.
  • Acetylcholine acts on both receptor types and is rapidly hydrolysed, so it is not selectively muscarinic in duration or effect.
  • Arecoline retains some nicotinic agonist activity in addition to its muscarinic effects.
Know More
  • Bethanechol has essentially no cardiovascular effects compared with methacholine or carbachol.
  • Bethanechol is used therapeutically in atrial tachycardia to inhibit pacemaker activity.
  • Both carbachol and bethanechol resist hydrolysis by acetylcholinesterase.
  • Bethanechol and carbachol act more on GI and bladder smooth muscle than the cardiovascular system.

posts.post_title: Choline ester activating both muscarinic and…
posts.post_content: Which choline ester activates both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors and is used as an eye drop to reduce intraocular pressure in glaucoma?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Carbachol

Carbachol activates both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors and is used as eye drops in glaucoma.

Correct Option Explanation

Its dual receptor action and resistance to acetylcholinesterase give it effects broadly similar to acetylcholine but with a longer duration.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bethanechol is purely muscarinic, lacking the nicotinic activity that carbachol shows.
  • Muscarine is a naturally occurring alkaloid, not a therapeutic glaucoma agent, and is not used clinically.
  • Oxotremorine is a synthetic M1 agonist used experimentally, not a standard glaucoma therapy.
Know More
  • Methacholine is also used for glaucoma, typically with a cholinesterase inhibitor such as neostigmine.
  • Carbachol induces profuse salivation and increased peristalsis in the GI tract.
  • In late gestation, carbachol can cause uterine contractions, useful post-partum.

posts.post_title: Source plant of pilocarpine
posts.post_content: Pilocarpine, a parasympathomimetic alkaloid, is obtained from

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pilocarpus jaborandi

Pilocarpine is obtained from Pilocarpus jaborandi and Pilocarpus microphyllus.

Correct Option Explanation

It is a potent parasympathomimetic that produces all the muscarinic responses of ACh, with pupillary constriction being its most important effect.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Areca catechu is the source of arecoline, a related but distinct cholinomimetic alkaloid.
  • Amanita muscaria is the mushroom source of muscarine, not pilocarpine.
  • Atropa belladonna is the source of atropine, a muscarinic antagonist, the opposite pharmacological class.

  • Pilocarpine increases secretion of salivary, sweat, mucous, gastric and pancreatic glands.

posts.post_title: Source and anthelmintic use of arecoline
posts.post_content: Arecoline, obtained from Areca catechu, has been used clinically as an anthelmintic to

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

Arecoline has been used as an anthelmintic to paralyze tapeworms.

It acts on muscarinic receptors of glands, smooth muscle and myocardium, and is more potent than pilocarpine, with additional nicotinic agonist activity.

  • Roundworms and ganglionic block are not the described mechanism or target parasite for arecoline in the text.

  • Arecoline depresses heart rate and blood pressure and can cause dyspnoea.

posts.post_title: Antidote for muscarine poisoning
posts.post_content: The antidote of choice for accidental muscarine poisoning is

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Atropine

Atropine is the antidote of choice for muscarine poisoning.

Correct Option Explanation

As a muscarinic antagonist, atropine directly blocks the excess muscarinic stimulation (colic, diarrhoea, miosis, hypotension, bradycardia) caused by muscarine.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Neostigmine inhibits cholinesterase, which would worsen, not reverse, muscarinic toxicity.
  • Hexamethonium blocks nicotinic ganglionic receptors, not the muscarinic receptors responsible for muscarine's toxic effects.
  • d-Tubocurarine blocks nicotinic NM receptors at the neuromuscular junction, irrelevant to muscarinic toxicity.
Know More
  • Muscarine is obtained from the mushroom Amanita muscaria and is not used clinically.
  • Toxic signs include severe colic, diarrhoea, miosis, dyspnoea, hypotension and bradycardia.
  • Oxotremorine is a synthetic muscarinic agonist related in action to muscarine.
  • Muscarine is a potent naturally occurring parasympathomimetic.

posts.post_title: Effect of large intravenous doses of acetylc…
posts.post_content: Large intravenous doses of acetylcholine, especially after atropine pretreatment, tend to

_aimcq_options.text: Increase blood pressure via ganglionic and adrenal medullary nicotinic stimulation
Further decrease blood pressure via endothelial NO release
Have no effect on blood pressure
Cause isolated bradycardia without pressure change

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Increase blood pressure via ganglionic and adrenal medullary nicotinic stimulation

Large ACh doses raise BP by stimulating nicotinic receptors in autonomic ganglia and the adrenal medulla.

Correct Option Explanation

This pressor effect is masked at normal doses by the dominant muscarinic vasodilator response, but becomes evident when muscarinic receptors are blocked by atropine.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Further muscarinic-mediated NO-driven vasodilation would lower, not raise, BP, and is blocked once atropine is given.
  • 'No effect' is incorrect; large doses clearly produce a measurable pressor response through ganglionic stimulation.
  • 'Isolated bradycardia' ignores the described tachycardia and other sympathetic responses seen at high doses.
Know More
  • Small IV doses of ACh cause a rapid fall in BP due to vasodilatation mediated by endothelial M3 receptors releasing NO.
  • In the presence of atropine, ACh's remaining effects are purely sympathetic (tachycardia, raised BP).
  • Nicotinic ganglionic effects of ACh are normally evident only at very high doses.
  • Sympathetic responses generally predominate at ganglia except in the GI and urinary tract.

posts.post_title: Diagnostic use of methacholine
posts.post_content: Subcutaneous methacholine is used clinically to help diagnose

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Atropine poisoning

Methacholine is given subcutaneously to test for loss of flush/sweating or miotic response when atropine poisoning is suspected.

Correct Option Explanation

If muscarinic receptors are already blocked by atropine, methacholine will fail to elicit its normal muscarinic responses, confirming the diagnosis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Organophosphate poisoning is diagnosed by cholinesterase activity assays, not by a methacholine challenge test.
  • Botulism is diagnosed by toxin assays and clinical signs of flaccid paralysis, unrelated to methacholine testing.
  • Myasthenia gravis is diagnosed using edrophonium (Tensilon test), not methacholine.
Know More
  • Methacholine is more active on the CNS and cardiovascular system than the GI tract compared to other choline esters.
  • It is resistant to pseudocholinesterase, giving a longer duration of action than acetylcholine.
  • Its action is potentiated by anticholinesterase drugs.
  • Methacholine is also used with neostigmine as eye drops for glaucoma.

posts.post_title: Reversible cholinesterase inhibitor example
posts.post_content: Which of the following is classified as a reversible inhibitor of cholinesterase?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Neostigmine

Neostigmine is a reversible inhibitor of cholinesterase.

Correct Option Explanation

Other reversible inhibitors include physostigmine and edrophonium, all forming a temporary bond with the enzyme.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Malathion is an irreversible organophosphorus cholinesterase inhibitor.
  • Parathion is likewise an irreversible organophosphorus inhibitor.
  • Sarin is an irreversible organophosphorus nerve agent that permanently inactivates cholinesterase.
Know More
  • Irreversible inhibitors also include di-isopropyl fluorophosphate and tetraethyl pyrophosphate.
  • Indirectly acting cholinergic drugs raise ACh concentration at nerve endings by blocking its breakdown.
  • Directly acting cholinergic drugs include choline esters (ACh, methacholine, carbachol, bethanechol) and alkaloids (muscarine, pilocarpine, arecoline).
  • Edrophonium is notable for its short duration of action, useful diagnostically.

posts.post_title: Effect of acetylcholine on the eye
posts.post_content: Acetylcholine's principal ocular effect is

_aimcq_options.text: Miosis and accommodation for near vision

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Miosis and accommodation for near vision

ACh causes contraction of the iris sphincter (miosis) and ciliary muscle, producing accommodation for near vision.

Correct Option Explanation

It also aids drainage of intraocular fluid, thereby reducing intraocular pressure — the basis of its use in glaucoma-related choline esters.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Mydriasis and cycloplegia are effects of muscarinic antagonists like atropine, the opposite of ACh's action.
  • ACh decreases, rather than increases, intraocular pressure by improving fluid drainage.
  • Corneal anaesthesia is a local anaesthetic effect, unrelated to cholinergic action on the eye.
Know More
  • Pilocarpine's most important ocular effect is also pupillary constriction.
  • Carbachol and methacholine eye drops are used therapeutically to reduce IOP in glaucoma.
  • ACh is lipophobic and poorly crosses the blood-brain barrier.
  • Direct intracerebral ACh injection can cause excitation and convulsions.

posts.post_title: Bethanechol's therapeutic use in atrial tach…
posts.post_content: Bethanechol is used systemically in atrial tachycardia because it

_aimcq_options.text: Inhibits atrial pacemaker activity via muscarinic stimulation
Directly blocks calcium channels in the SA node
Stimulates adrenal catecholamine release to slow the heart

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Inhibits atrial pacemaker activity via muscarinic stimulation

Bethanechol is administered systemically to inhibit atrial pacemaker activity in atrial tachycardia.

Correct Option Explanation

Its muscarinic agonist action mimics vagal tone, slowing pacemaker discharge, similar in principle to methacholine's cardiac depressant effect.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bethanechol has no significant nicotinic ganglionic blocking action; its selectivity is for muscarinic receptors.
  • It does not act by directly blocking calcium channels; its mechanism is muscarinic receptor agonism.
  • Bethanechol does not stimulate adrenal catecholamine release; that effect is associated with carbachol and acetylcholine, not the cardioselectively-inert bethanechol.
Know More
  • Bethanechol otherwise has essentially no cardiovascular effects, unlike methacholine and carbachol.
  • Methacholine, by contrast, is the most cardioactive choline ester, causing depression and slowing of the heart.
  • Large doses of methacholine can cause heart block, reversible by atropine.
  • Carbachol is comparatively less potent than methacholine on the cardiovascular system.

posts.post_title: Source of physostigmine
posts.post_content: Physostigmine (eserine) is obtained from

_aimcq_options.text: Dried ripe seeds of Physostigma venenosum

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Dried ripe seeds of Physostigma venenosum

Physostigmine is obtained from the dried ripe seeds of Physostigma venenosum.

Correct Option Explanation

As a tertiary amine, it is well absorbed orally and readily crosses the blood-brain barrier, unlike quaternary anticholinesterases.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Areca catechu is the source of arecoline, a directly-acting cholinomimetic alkaloid, not physostigmine.
  • Pilocarpus jaborandi yields pilocarpine, a different directly-acting parasympathomimetic.
  • Atropa belladonna yields atropine, a muscarinic antagonist, pharmacologically opposite to physostigmine.
Know More
  • Physostigmine is used as a miotic and to treat glaucoma.
  • It effectively antagonizes atropine poisoning, both centrally and peripherally.
  • It is also absorbed from the conjunctiva when applied to the eye.
  • It is used in ruminal atony as well.

posts.post_title: Primary diagnostic use of edrophonium
posts.post_content: Edrophonium is primarily used clinically for

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Diagnosis of myasthenia gravis

Edrophonium is primarily used in the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis.

Correct Option Explanation

Its very short duration of action makes it ideal as a diagnostic test agent: improvement suggests myasthenia gravis, while worsening suggests cholinergic over-treatment.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Alzheimer's disease treatment uses tacrine, a lipophilic anticholinesterase that crosses the BBB, not edrophonium.
  • Atropine poisoning is treated with physostigmine, which crosses the blood-brain barrier for CNS effects.
  • Organophosphate poisoning reversal relies on pralidoxime (2-PAM), not edrophonium.
Know More
  • Edrophonium primarily binds the anionic site of AChE; its reactivation doesn't require hydrolysis.
  • It is a short-acting, less potent reversible anticholinesterase compared to neostigmine.
  • If edrophonium worsens muscle weakness, this indicates cholinergic weakness from anticholinesterase over-treatment.
  • Neostigmine improves myasthenic muscle contraction by prejunctional ACh accumulation.

posts.post_title: Drug used for symptomatic treatment of Alzhe…
posts.post_content: Which anticholinesterase, due to its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier, is used in the symptomatic treatment of Alzheimer's disease?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Tacrine

Tacrine, a lipophilic acridine compound, crosses the blood-brain barrier easily and is used in Alzheimer's disease.

Correct Option Explanation

By increasing brain ACh levels, it provides symptomatic relief in this human neurodegenerative disorder.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Neostigmine is a quaternary ammonium compound that cannot penetrate the BBB, ruling out CNS use.
  • Pyridostigmine is similarly a quaternary compound with poor CNS penetration, used for myasthenia gravis instead.
  • Edrophonium is used diagnostically for myasthenia gravis, not for CNS disorders like Alzheimer's disease.
Know More
  • Reversible anticholinesterases are subgrouped into quaternary ammonium, tertiary amine alkaloids, acridine derivatives and carbamates.
  • Tacrine belongs to the acridine derivative subgroup.
  • Physostigmine (tertiary amine) also crosses the BBB, unlike neostigmine.
  • Carbamates like carbaryl and carbofuran are used as insecticides, not CNS drugs.

posts.post_title: Antidote used to reactivate cholinesterase i…
posts.post_content: Which compound is commonly used as an antidote to reactivate cholinesterase inhibited by organophosphorus compounds?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pralidoxime (2-PAM)

Pralidoxime (2-PAM) is commonly used to reactivate cholinesterase inhibited by organophosphorus compounds.

Correct Option Explanation

Its oxime group reacts with the phosphorylated esteratic site, splitting off as an oxime-phosphonate and regenerating active enzyme, if given before aging occurs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Atropine blocks muscarinic symptoms but does not chemically reactivate the inhibited enzyme itself.
  • Neostigmine is itself a cholinesterase inhibitor and would worsen, not treat, OP poisoning.
  • Physostigmine is likewise a cholinesterase inhibitor, inappropriate as an OP poisoning antidote.
Know More
  • Obidoxime is a more potent oxime alternative to pralidoxime.
  • Diacetylmonoxime (DAM) is lipophilic and can reactivate cholinesterase in the brain.
  • Oximes are contraindicated in carbamate poisoning as they can aggravate toxicity.
  • Oximes must be given before aging, the loss of an alkyl group that makes the enzyme resistant to reactivation.

posts.post_title: Why oximes are contraindicated in carbamate …
posts.post_content: Oximes such as pralidoxime are contraindicated in carbamate poisoning because

_aimcq_options.text: They have weak anticholinesterase activity and can aggravate the toxicity
They are ineffective against all cholinesterase inhibitors

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: They have weak anticholinesterase activity and can aggravate the toxicity

Oximes possess weak anticholinesterase activity of their own, and in carbamate poisoning this aggravates the condition.

Correct Option Explanation

In carbamate poisoning, the enzyme's anionic site is not free for oxime attachment, so oximes cannot exert their reactivating benefit, leaving only their harmful weak anticholinesterase effect.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Immediate fatal bronchospasm' is not the documented mechanism for the oxime-carbamate contraindication.
  • Oximes ARE effective against organophosphate inhibition specifically; the statement 'ineffective against all' overgeneralizes and misstates the actual reason.
  • Oximes do not chemically convert carbamates into organophosphates; no such transformation is described.
Know More
  • Carbamate poisoning is generally of shorter duration than organophosphate poisoning.
  • Carbamates are non-polar, highly soluble compounds easily absorbed at the exposure site.
  • In OP poisoning, oximes must be given before aging occurs for effective reactivation.
  • Atropine remains the mainstay treatment for muscarinic symptoms in both OP and carbamate poisoning.

posts.post_title: Limitation of atropine in treating OPC poiso…
posts.post_content: In organophosphate compound (OPC) poisoning, atropine effectively controls muscarinic symptoms but does NOT reverse

_aimcq_options.text: Peripheral skeletal muscle paralysis mediated by nicotinic action

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Peripheral skeletal muscle paralysis mediated by nicotinic action

Atropine does not reverse peripheral muscular paralysis, which is mediated by nicotinic, not muscarinic, receptors.

Correct Option Explanation

Since atropine is a selective muscarinic antagonist, it cannot counter the nicotinic fasciculations and paralysis seen at the neuromuscular junction in OPC poisoning.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Salivation and bronchial secretions are muscarinic effects that atropine effectively blocks.
  • Bradycardia and hypotension are muscarinic cardiovascular effects reversed by atropine.
  • Miosis is a classic muscarinic sign of OPC poisoning that atropine reverses, with pupil dilation used as an endpoint of atropinisation.
Know More
  • Atropine must be given by slow intravenous injection and continued until pupils dilate.
  • In high doses, atropine can also control some central effects of OPC poisoning.
  • Cholinesterase reactivators (oximes) should follow atropinisation as early as possible, before aging.
  • Death in OPC poisoning is usually due to respiratory failure from bronchoconstriction and paralysis.

posts.post_title: Conditions in which neostigmine is contraind…
posts.post_content: Neostigmine is contraindicated in which of the following conditions?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Intestinal and urinary obstruction

Neostigmine is contraindicated in intestinal and urinary obstruction, along with late pregnancy, bronchial asthma, epilepsy, peptic ulcer and arrhythmias.

Correct Option Explanation

Its cholinergic stimulation of smooth muscle can dangerously worsen an existing mechanical obstruction.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Myasthenia gravis is a primary therapeutic indication for neostigmine, not a contraindication.
  • Ruminal atony is a clinical use of neostigmine to restore motility, not a contraindication.
  • Post-operative decurarization (reversing non-depolarising muscle relaxants) is a standard neostigmine indication.
Know More
  • Neostigmine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier and is poorly absorbed orally.
  • It has a stronger action on nicotinic than muscarinic receptors, giving it a powerful anticurare effect.
  • It is metabolized in the liver and hydrolyzed by plasma cholinesterase.
  • Pyridostigmine is similar to neostigmine but has a slower onset of action.

posts.post_title: Meaning of 'aging' in organophosphate poison…
posts.post_content: In organophosphate poisoning, 'aging' of the inhibited cholinesterase enzyme refers to

_aimcq_options.text: Loss of an alkyl group making the enzyme resistant to oxime reactivation
Gradual spontaneous full recovery of enzyme activity
Conversion of the drug into a less toxic metabolite
The natural breakdown of unbound organophosphate in plasma

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Loss of an alkyl group making the enzyme resistant to oxime reactivation

Aging is the loss of one alkyl group from the phosphorylated enzyme, occurring faster than spontaneous hydrolysis.

Correct Option Explanation

Once aged, the enzyme-inhibitor complex becomes resistant to regeneration by oximes such as pralidoxime, making early oxime treatment critical.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Aging does not represent spontaneous full recovery — it is the opposite, making recovery harder.
  • Aging is a change in the enzyme-inhibitor complex, not metabolism of the organophosphate drug itself.
  • Aging occurs at the enzyme level, not as breakdown of free plasma organophosphate.
Know More
  • The four stages of anticholinesterase action are phosphorylation, reactivation, aging and regeneration.
  • Without reactivation, new enzyme must be synthesized, taking weeks to months.
  • Pralidoxime combines with the cation-binding site to orient its oxime group toward the phosphorus atom.
  • Organophosphates react only at the esteratic site, lacking the cationic group of carbamates.

posts.post_title: Chemical nature of atropine
posts.post_content: Atropine is chemically best described as

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A racemic mixture of dl-hyoscyamine

Atropine is a racemic mixture of dl-hyoscyamine, a tertiary amine alkaloid.

Correct Option Explanation

It is obtained from Atropa belladonna and Datura stramonium, plants that also contain hyoscyamine and hyoscine.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Atropine is racemic, not a pure L-isomer; and hyoscine is a chemically distinct compound, not another name for atropine.
  • Atropine is a tertiary amine, not a quaternary ammonium compound — this is why it crosses the CNS unlike quaternary antimuscarinics.
  • Atropine is a belladonna alkaloid, not a synthetic carbamate; carbamates are a distinct anticholinesterase class.
Know More
  • Atropine is well absorbed orally and parenterally, with a duration of action of 4 to 6 hours in most species.
  • About 30-50% of absorbed atropine is excreted unchanged in urine.
  • High doses of atropine can also block nicotinic receptors.
  • Belladonna also contains hyoscyamine and hyoscine alongside atropine.

posts.post_title: Effect of low-dose atropine on heart rate
posts.post_content: At low doses, atropine typically produces which initial cardiac effect?

_aimcq_options.text: No cardiac effect at any dose

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Transient bradycardia

Low doses of atropine produce transient bradycardia before the more familiar tachycardia appears.

Correct Option Explanation

This is attributed to blockade of M1 muscarinic autoreceptors on vagal nerve endings, which paradoxically increases vagal ACh discharge at low doses.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Sustained tachycardia only' ignores the initial bradycardic phase seen at low doses, caused by M1 autoreceptor blockade.
  • 'Complete heart block' is not a described atropine effect; atropine instead shortens the AV nodal refractory period, facilitating conduction.
  • 'No cardiac effect' is incorrect; atropine has clear, dose-dependent cardiac effects.
Know More
  • At normal or higher doses, atropine causes tachycardia via blockade of M2 receptors on the SA node.
  • Atropine shortens the AV node refractory period, facilitating AV conduction.
  • Degree of tachycardia depends on vagal tone, which is high in horses and dogs.
  • Atropine alone has little effect on blood pressure since vascular smooth muscle lacks parasympathetic innervation.

posts.post_title: Drug of choice for producing mydriasis in op…
posts.post_content: Which drug is preferred over atropine for producing mydriasis for ophthalmoscopic examination, owing to only weak cycloplegia?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Homatropine

Homatropine is the drug of choice for mydriasis, producing only weak cycloplegia with a shorter duration than atropine.

Correct Option Explanation

It is a semisynthetic derivative of atropine, about 10 times less potent, with rapid onset (30-45 min) and short duration of action.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Scopolamine is a CNS-active alkaloid used for sedation and anti-motion sickness effects, not the preferred mydriatic.
  • Pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist that causes miosis, the opposite ocular effect.
  • Neostigmine is an anticholinesterase used for myasthenia gravis, unrelated to producing mydriasis.
Know More
  • Atropine is no longer first choice for mydriasis because its effects are too long lasting.
  • Eucatropine produces mydriasis without cycloplegia, lasting about 1 hour.
  • Cyclopentolate and tropicamide were developed specifically for ophthalmic use with rapid recovery.
  • Atropine raises intraocular pressure, making it contraindicated in glaucoma.

posts.post_title: Preferred preanaesthetic antimuscarinic due …
posts.post_content: Which antimuscarinic drug is preferred as a preanaesthetic because of its comparatively minimal effect on the heart?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Glycopyrrolate

Glycopyrrolate is preferred as a preanaesthetic because of its less significant effect on the heart.

Correct Option Explanation

As a quaternary compound it is poorly absorbed from the gut and penetrates the CNS poorly, and at usual doses has little effect on resting heart rate or blood pressure.

  • Atropine, while useful for reducing secretions, also blocks vagal cardiac reflexes and can cause inappetance/rumen stasis in cattle.
  • Scopolamine has more pronounced CNS effects (tranquility, amnesia), not chosen specifically for cardiac safety.
  • Nicotine is not an antimuscarinic preanaesthetic; it is a nicotinic ganglionic stimulant/blocker with no such therapeutic use.
Know More
  • Glycopyrrolate is less effective than atropine at blocking gastric secretions.
  • It produces less sedation than scopolamine.
  • Preanaesthetic antimuscarinics reduce salivary and airway secretions and block vagal reflexes during anaesthesia.
  • Scopolamine combined with morphine produces analgesia and amnesia.

posts.post_title: Selective M1 muscarinic antagonist used in p…
posts.post_content: Which drug is a selective M1 muscarinic receptor antagonist that inhibits gastric acid secretion with minimal CNS effects?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pirenzepine

Pirenzepine is a selective M1 antagonist that inhibits gastric acid secretion at doses producing minimal other effects.

Correct Option Explanation

It has minimal CNS effects because it cannot pass the blood-brain barrier despite its selective peripheral M1 action.

  • Darifenacin is a selective M3 antagonist, useful for smooth muscle and epithelial secretion effects, not primarily gastric acid.
  • Tripitamine is a selective M2 antagonist with potential to block cholinergic bradycardia, not a gastric acid inhibitor.
  • Ipratropium is a non-selective quaternary antimuscarinic used as a bronchodilator, not an M1-selective gastric drug.

  • Telenzepine is a more potent analogue of pirenzepine, also used for peptic ulcer.
  • Ipratropium acts selectively on bronchial muscle without altering respiratory secretion volume, useful in COPD.

posts.post_title: Species resistant to oral atropine/belladonn…
posts.post_content: Certain strains of which species are resistant to a diet of belladonna leaves because their liver contains the enzyme atropinase?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rabbits

Certain strains of rabbits are resistant to belladonna leaves because their liver contains the enzyme atropinase.

Correct Option Explanation

Despite this resistance, the meat of such rabbits can still be toxic if eaten by dogs, cats or humans, since those species lack the same enzyme.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Dogs are described as susceptible (carnivora are more sensitive than herbivora) and can be poisoned even by eating resistant rabbit meat.
  • Cats, like dogs, are carnivora and are relatively more susceptible to atropine toxicity, not resistant.
