Know More
  • Herbivora are generally more resistant than carnivora to atropine toxicity.
  • Horses, cattle and goats are relatively resistant orally but susceptible when given parenterally.
  • Urine from an atropine-poisoned animal instilled into a cat's eye can cause pupil dilatation — a diagnostic test.
  • Signs of atropine toxicity include dry mouth, mydriasis, tachycardia, delirium and respiratory failure.

posts.post_title: Mechanism of nicotine's ganglionic action at…
posts.post_content: At high doses, nicotine ultimately blocks autonomic ganglia by

_aimcq_options.text: Producing persistent depolarization of nicotinic receptors
Competitively antagonizing acetylcholine at the anionic site
Directly damaging the ganglionic cell membrane

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Producing persistent depolarization of nicotinic receptors

Nicotine first stimulates ganglionic nicotinic receptors, then blocks them via persistent depolarization at high doses.

Correct Option Explanation

This depolarizing block explains its biphasic effect: initial stimulation (e.g., transient BP rise) followed by ganglionic blockade and falling BP/motor tone.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Nicotine is an agonist, not a competitive antagonist, at nicotinic receptors — its blockade arises from over-stimulation, not receptor competition.
  • Nicotine has no described action on acetylcholinesterase; its effect is purely receptor-mediated.
  • There is no described mechanism of nicotine physically damaging ganglionic cell membranes.
Know More
  • IV nicotine initially raises BP via sympathetic ganglionic and adrenal medullary stimulation.
  • High doses paralyze the diaphragm and chest muscles via depolarizing neuromuscular block, causing respiratory paralysis and death.
  • Small doses enhance parasympathetic GI tone, causing vomiting and increased peristalsis.
  • Nicotine is obtained from the tobacco plant Nicotiana tobaccum and has no therapeutic use.

posts.post_title: Selective bronchodilator antimuscarinic spar…
posts.post_content: Which antimuscarinic drug acts selectively on bronchial smooth muscle without altering the volume or consistency of respiratory secretions, and is used in COPD?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ipratropium

Ipratropium acts selectively on bronchial muscle as a bronchodilator without changing respiratory secretions.

Correct Option Explanation

This selectivity makes it useful in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), where drying secretions further would be undesirable.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Atropine reduces bronchial secretions broadly while causing bronchodilation, lacking Ipratropium's secretion-sparing selectivity.
  • Isopropamide is used mainly for its antiemetic and antidiarrhoeal anticholinergic effects, not selective bronchodilation.
  • Dicyclomine is a tertiary amine antispasmodic with direct smooth muscle relaxant action, not the described selective bronchial agent.
Know More
  • Ipratropium is a quaternary compound, so it is poorly absorbed from the gut and has minimal CNS/eye side effects.
  • Atropine is used for temporary relief in heaves (equine bronchoconstriction) but is not preferred in true bronchial asthma.
  • Quaternary antimuscarinics have some inherent ganglionic blocking activity contributing to antispasmodic effects.
  • Propantheline and glycopyrrolate are other quaternary antisecretory-antispasmodic agents.

posts.post_title: Precursor for catecholamine synthesis
posts.post_content: The precursor amino acid for the synthesis of catecholamines is

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Tyrosine

Tyrosine is the precursor for catecholamine synthesis.

Correct Option Explanation

Tyrosine is converted to DOPA and then dopamine in the neuronal cytoplasm, then to norepinephrine in granules, and finally to epinephrine in the adrenal medulla.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Tryptophan is the precursor for serotonin synthesis, an unrelated pathway.
  • Phenylalanine only is incomplete; phenylalanine is converted to tyrosine in the liver, which is the actual direct precursor for catecholamine synthesis.
  • Glutamate is a CNS excitatory neurotransmitter, unrelated to catecholamine biosynthesis.
Know More
  • Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme, inhibited by alpha-methyl-p-tyrosine.
  • Conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine occurs in the liver.
  • Storage granules complex catecholamines with ATP and chromogranin, keeping them inactive until release.
  • Granular uptake of catecholamines is an ATP and Mg++ dependent active transport process.

posts.post_title: Enzyme responsible for intraneuronal deamina…
posts.post_content: Which enzyme, located on the outer surface of mitochondria, inactivates catecholamines by deamination?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Monoamine oxidase (MAO)

MAO, located on the mitochondrial outer surface, deaminates catecholamines to aldehydes.

Correct Option Explanation

These aldehydes are further metabolized by aldehyde reductase (to alcohols) or aldehyde dehydrogenase (to acids), ultimately forming VMA or MOPEG.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • COMT is an extraneuronal enzyme that methylates catecholamines, a different reaction from MAO's deamination.
  • Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis, not catabolism.
  • Dopamine beta hydroxylase converts dopamine to norepinephrine in storage granules, a synthetic, not catabolic, step.
Know More
  • Active reuptake (Uptake I) accounts for up to 65% of norepinephrine removal from the synaptic cleft — the most important termination pathway.
  • Diffusion (Uptake II) accounts for about 15% of removal.
  • Enzymatic breakdown accounts for about 20% of norepinephrine inactivation.
  • Major final catecholamine metabolites are VMA and MOPEG.

posts.post_title: Most potent alpha-adrenergic stimulant among…
posts.post_content: Among epinephrine (EPI), norepinephrine (NE) and isoproterenol (ISO), which is the most potent alpha-adrenergic stimulant?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Epinephrine

Epinephrine is the most potent alpha-adrenergic stimulant among the three catecholamines.

Correct Option Explanation

The alpha-adrenergic potency order is EPI ≥ NE >> ISO, while the beta-adrenergic order is reversed: ISO > EPI.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Norepinephrine is a potent alpha stimulant but generally somewhat less potent than epinephrine at alpha receptors.
  • Isoproterenol is the least potent alpha stimulant of the three, being instead the most potent beta stimulant.
  • 'All are equally potent' contradicts the clearly described differential potency order among the three agents.
Know More
  • Isoproterenol is the most potent beta stimulant of the three catecholamines.
  • NE is a weak stimulant of vascular β2 receptors but a potent stimulant of cardiac β1 receptors.
  • NE and EPI are roughly equipotent at β1 receptors.
  • Alpha action causes smooth muscle contraction; beta action causes smooth muscle relaxation.

posts.post_title: Receptor mediating adrenaline-induced mydria…
posts.post_content: Adrenaline causes mydriasis by acting on which receptor and muscle?

_aimcq_options.text: Alpha-1 receptors on the radial muscle of the iris
Beta-2 receptors on the ciliary muscle
M3 muscarinic receptors on the sphincter muscle
Alpha-2 receptors on the lacrimal gland

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Alpha-1 receptors on the radial muscle of the iris

Adrenaline causes mydriasis via α1 receptor-mediated contraction of the radial muscle of the iris.

Correct Option Explanation

This effect is minimal when adrenaline is applied topically, since it penetrates the cornea very poorly.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Beta-2 on the ciliary muscle is not the described mechanism for adrenaline-induced pupil changes.
  • M3 muscarinic receptors on the sphincter muscle mediate miosis from cholinergic agonists, the opposite effect and receptor system.
  • Alpha-2 on the lacrimal gland is unrelated to the described mydriatic mechanism.
Know More
  • Adrenaline interacts with all subtypes (α1, α2, β1, β2, β3) of adrenergic receptors.
  • Norepinephrine also contracts the radial muscle (α1 action), producing mydriasis.
  • Adrenaline reduces intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma as a 2% topical solution.
  • Adrenaline causes piloerection via α1-mediated contraction of piloerector muscles.

posts.post_title: Low-dose dopamine's predominant receptor act…
posts.post_content: At very low intravenous doses (0.5-2 µg/kg/min), dopamine acts predominantly on

_aimcq_options.text: Vascular D1 dopaminergic receptors, dilating renal and mesenteric beds
Cardiac β1 receptors, increasing heart rate

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Vascular D1 dopaminergic receptors, dilating renal and mesenteric beds

At very low doses, dopamine acts mainly on vascular D1 receptors, dilating renal, mesenteric and coronary beds.

Correct Option Explanation

This increases renal blood flow, glomerular filtration rate and sodium excretion, the basis for its use in shock with oliguria.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cardiac β1 stimulation with positive inotropy occurs at somewhat higher doses (2-10 µg/kg/min), not the very low dose range.
  • Vascular α1 vasoconstriction predominates only at high doses (≥10 µg/kg/min), countering dopamine's useful effects.
  • Dopamine has no significant action on non-vascular β2 (bronchial) receptors at any described dose.
Know More
  • Dopamine is unique in having direct (α and β), indirect (norepinephrine release) and dopaminergic (D1/D2) actions.
  • Exogenous dopamine has no central effects since it cannot cross the blood-brain barrier.
  • Dopamine is useful in cardiogenic or septic shock, oliguria and severe congestive heart failure.
  • Dopamine is the immediate metabolic precursor of norepinephrine.

posts.post_title: Mechanism of action of amphetamine
posts.post_content: Amphetamine produces its sympathomimetic effects mainly by

_aimcq_options.text: Indirectly releasing endogenous noradrenaline from nerve terminals
Directly and potently stimulating alpha and beta receptors

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Indirectly releasing endogenous noradrenaline from nerve terminals

Amphetamine acts indirectly, displacing noradrenaline from storage vesicles into the cytosol for release.

Correct Option Explanation

Its structural resemblance to noradrenaline allows uptake into nerve terminals via Uptake I, after which it displaces the transmitter without requiring exocytosis or Ca++ entry.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Amphetamine is not a potent direct agonist at adrenergic receptors; its action is predominantly indirect via NE release.
  • Amphetamine has no described action on acetylcholinesterase; it is a purely adrenergic/CNS stimulant agent.
  • Amphetamine does not block dopamine receptors; rather it enhances catecholaminergic transmission.
Know More
  • Amphetamine also blocks MAO and decreases Uptake I, both raising synaptic NE further.
  • D-amphetamine is 3-4 times more potent than the l-isomer for CNS effects; the l-isomer is more potent peripherally.
  • Amphetamine is resistant to MAO, giving it a prolonged duration of action.
  • In humans, it is used for depression, narcolepsy and hyperkinesis.

posts.post_title: Phenomenon of diminishing response with repe…
posts.post_content: The progressively diminishing response seen with repeated injections of ephedrine is termed

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Tachyphylaxis

Repeated ephedrine injections produce a progressively diminishing response called tachyphylaxis.

Correct Option Explanation

This occurs because repeated dosing depletes stores of endogenous noradrenaline that ephedrine relies on to release, and because previously occupied adrenergic receptors become less available.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Tolerance typically develops over a longer time course with chronic use, distinct from the rapid, repeated-dose phenomenon described here as tachyphylaxis.
  • Idiosyncrasy refers to an unusual individual reaction to a drug, not a reproducible diminishing response pattern.
  • Cross-sensitization describes increased response to a related agent after exposure to another, the opposite of the diminishing effect described.
Know More
  • Ephedrine is a mixed-acting sympathomimetic — it directly stimulates α and β receptors and also releases endogenous NE.
  • It is 7-10 times longer acting than adrenaline and effective orally.
  • Reflex mechanisms triggered by cardiovascular stimulation also contribute to tachyphylaxis.
  • Ephedrine is a poor substrate for MAO or COMT and is largely excreted unchanged.

posts.post_title: Drug of choice in acute anaphylaxis
posts.post_content: The drug of choice to counter both hypotension and bronchospasm in acute anaphylactic reaction is

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Epinephrine

Epinephrine is the drug of choice in acute anaphylaxis, countering hypotension (α action) and bronchospasm (β action).

Correct Option Explanation

Its combined alpha and beta agonist activity addresses both the vascular collapse and airway constriction that characterize anaphylactic shock.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Norepinephrine has negligible β2 (bronchodilator) activity, making it unsuitable for the bronchospasm component of anaphylaxis.
  • Dopamine is preferred in cardiogenic, traumatic or hypovolemic shock for renal perfusion benefits, not the first-line anaphylaxis drug.
  • Ephedrine is long-acting but far less potent and slower in onset, unsuitable for an acute emergency.
Know More
  • Epinephrine is also used to restore cardiac rhythm in asystole and to control local bleeding from arterioles/capillaries.
  • It is combined with local anaesthetics (1:100,000) to prolong their action by local vasoconstriction.
  • Epinephrine reduces intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma.
  • It is contraindicated in narrow-angle glaucoma and during anaesthesia with halogenated hydrocarbons.

posts.post_title: Key structural feature distinguishing catech…
posts.post_content: Catecholamines are structurally distinguished from non-catecholamine adrenergic drugs by

_aimcq_options.text: Hydroxyl groups at positions 3 and 4 on the benzene ring

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Hydroxyl groups at positions 3 and 4 on the benzene ring

True catecholamines contain hydroxyl groups at the 3 and 4 positions of the benzene ring (the catechol structure).

Correct Option Explanation

Non-catecholamines lack one or both of these hydroxyl groups, which changes their pharmacokinetics — better oral absorption, longer half-life, and CNS penetration.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A quaternary nitrogen is not the defining catechol feature; catecholamines like epinephrine have a secondary/tertiary amine, not quaternary nitrogen.
  • A carboxylic acid side chain is not part of the catechol structural definition described.
  • An indole ring is characteristic of serotonin-related compounds, not catecholamines.
Know More
  • Catecholamines are usually metabolised mainly by MAO or COMT, giving them a short half-life.
  • Non-catecholamines are poor substrates for MAO and resistant to COMT, giving longer half-lives.
  • Catecholamines are polar and poorly cross the CNS; non-catecholamines like amphetamine readily cross the BBB.
  • Catecholamine effects persist after adrenergic denervation, while non-catecholamines lose activity after denervation.

posts.post_title: Selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor agonist
posts.post_content: Which drug is a selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor agonist commonly used to produce mydriasis and treat hypotension?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Phenylephrine

Phenylephrine is a direct-acting, non-catecholamine α1 agonist with negligible β or CNS actions.

Correct Option Explanation

It produces peripheral vasoconstriction, raising BP, and causes mydriasis with reduced intraocular pressure.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Clonidine is a selective α2 agonist, not α1, with an opposite net cardiovascular effect (sustained hypotension).
  • Dobutamine is a selective β1 agonist used as an inotrope, not for vasoconstriction/mydriasis.
  • Salbutamol is a selective β2 agonist used as a bronchodilator, unrelated to α1 mydriatic action.
Know More
  • Phenylephrine lacks the 4-OH group present on adrenaline's benzene ring, distinguishing it chemically.
  • It is given parenterally since oral phenylephrine is rapidly metabolized in the GI tract.
  • Prazosin is the selective α1 receptor antagonist.
  • Methoxamine is another selective α1 agonist, notable for some β-blocking action reducing arrhythmia risk.

posts.post_title: Selective alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonis…
posts.post_content: Which drug is a selective alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist used to treat hypertension via central sympathetic outflow reduction?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Clonidine

Clonidine is a partial α2 agonist used to treat hypertension by reducing central sympathetic outflow.

Correct Option Explanation

Rapid IV injection causes a transient pressor response via peripheral postjunctional α2 receptors, followed by sustained hypotension via central presynaptic α2 activation in the medulla.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Phenylephrine is a selective α1 agonist, causing vasoconstriction and hypertension, the opposite therapeutic use.
  • Prazosin is a selective α1 antagonist, also used in hypertension but via a completely different mechanism.
  • Yohimbine is the selective α2 antagonist, pharmacologically opposite to clonidine.
Know More
  • Clonidine also produces central sedation, analgesia and stimulates parasympathetic outflow causing bradycardia.
  • It is also used to treat addiction to narcotics, alcohol and tobacco.
  • Xylazine is structurally related to clonidine and is a veterinary α2 sedative-analgesic.
  • α2 activation in CNS opens K+ channels, hyperpolarizing neurons, producing sedation similar to opioids.

posts.post_title: Selective beta-1 agonist used as an inotrope
posts.post_content: Which selective β1-adrenergic agonist is primarily used as an inotropic agent in severe congestive heart failure?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Dobutamine

Dobutamine is a relatively selective β1 agonist used as an inotrope in severe congestive heart failure.

Correct Option Explanation

Unlike dopamine, it does not cause noradrenaline release and produces purely β1 effects, increasing contractility without major changes in heart rate or peripheral resistance.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Salbutamol is a selective β2 agonist used as a bronchodilator, not a cardiac inotrope.
  • Terbutaline is also a selective β2 bronchodilator/tocolytic, not primarily an inotrope.
  • Isoproterenol is a nonselective β agonist (β1 and β2), lacking dobutamine's cardiac selectivity.
Know More
  • Dobutamine, unlike dopamine, does not dilate the renal vascular bed.
  • It is given by continuous IV infusion due to its brief half-life and rapid hepatic metabolism.
  • Its selective antagonist is atenolol (β1-selective blocker).
  • Dobutamine structurally resembles dopamine but lacks the indirect noradrenaline-releasing action.

posts.post_title: Beta receptor with highest beta2:beta1 selec…
posts.post_content: Which β2-selective adrenergic agonist has the highest β2:β1 selectivity ratio, about 10 times, among the group?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Salbutamol

Salbutamol (albuterol) has the highest β2:β1 selectivity ratio, about 10 times, among selective β2 agonists.

Correct Option Explanation

This high selectivity minimizes cardiac β1 stimulation while providing effective bronchodilation.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Clenbuterol is also β2-selective but is not described as having the highest selectivity ratio in this text.
  • Isoxuprine is used mainly as a uterine relaxant (tocolytic), not noted for the highest β2:β1 ratio.
  • Terbutaline is a standard β2 agonist bronchodilator/tocolytic but not credited with the highest selectivity ratio here.
Know More
  • β2 agonists relax bronchial, uterine and skeletal-muscle vascular smooth muscle.
  • At high doses, β2 agonists may exhibit β1 cardiac action, causing tachycardia.
  • Long-term use of β2 agonists can cause receptor down-regulation and reduced response.
  • β2 agonists are used as bronchodilators and to delay premature labour (tocolysis).

posts.post_title: Mechanism producing sedation and analgesia w…
posts.post_content: Xylazine produces sedation and analgesia in the CNS mainly by

_aimcq_options.text: Activating α2 receptors, opening K+ channels and hyperpolarizing neurons
Blocking α1 receptors, reducing sympathetic tone
Inhibiting GABA reuptake in the spinal cord

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Activating α2 receptors, opening K+ channels and hyperpolarizing neurons

Xylazine, an α2 agonist, opens K+ channels via G-proteins, hyperpolarizing neurons to block excitatory transmission.

Correct Option Explanation

This mechanism parallels opioid receptor signalling, as both α2 and opioid receptors share the same effector pathway and brain regions, explaining xylazine's opioid-like sedative/analgesic profile.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Xylazine is an α2 agonist, not an α1 antagonist; its mechanism is receptor activation, not blockade.
  • Xylazine does not act directly on opioid receptors; it merely shares a downstream signalling mechanism with them.
  • There is no described action of xylazine on GABA reuptake; its mechanism is purely α2-receptor mediated.
Know More
  • Xylazine is structurally related to clonidine.
  • It causes transient hypertension followed by more sustained hypotension and decreased cardiac output.
  • It causes emesis in cats and is often combined with ketamine as a general anaesthetic.
  • Other veterinary α2 agonists include detomidine, medetomidine and romifidine.

posts.post_title: Prejunctional receptor mediating auto-inhibi…
posts.post_content: Which receptor subtype, located prejunctionally on adrenergic nerve terminals, inhibits further release of norepinephrine as an auto-inhibitory feedback mechanism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Alpha-2 receptor

Prejunctional α2 receptors mediate auto-inhibitory feedback, reducing further norepinephrine release.

Correct Option Explanation

This allows the released neurotransmitter itself to modulate its own subsequent release, an important regulatory mechanism for catecholamine output.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Alpha-1 receptors are located postjunctionally on effector organs, mediating excitatory/contractile responses, not presynaptic feedback.
  • Beta-1 receptors mediate cardiac stimulation and renin release, not presynaptic auto-inhibition of NE release.
  • Beta-2 receptors mediate smooth muscle relaxation (bronchi, blood vessels, uterus), unrelated to this presynaptic feedback loop.
Know More
  • α2 receptors are also found postjunctionally in the brain, on pancreatic β cells and platelets.
  • α2 activation decreases insulin release and promotes platelet aggregation.
  • The selective α2 agonist is clonidine; the selective antagonist is yohimbine.
  • In general, α receptors mediate excitatory/contractile responses; β receptors mediate cardiac stimulation, smooth muscle relaxation and metabolic effects.

posts.post_title: Receptor mediating renin release from the ki…
posts.post_content: Renin release from the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney is mediated by which adrenergic receptor?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Beta-1 receptor

Renin release from juxtaglomerular cells is mediated by β1 receptors.

Correct Option Explanation

β1 receptors also mediate increased heart rate, force of contraction and AV nodal conduction velocity in the heart.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Alpha-1 receptors mediate vasoconstriction and glandular secretion decreases, not renin release.
  • Beta-2 receptors mediate bronchial, uterine, GI and urinary tract relaxation, plus skeletal muscle/liver glycogenolysis, not renin release.
  • Alpha-2 receptors mediate prejunctional inhibition of transmitter release and decreased insulin release, not renin secretion.
Know More
  • The selective β1 agonist is dobutamine; the selective β1 antagonist is atenolol.
  • β2 receptors mediate lipolysis in adipose tissue is actually attributed to β3 receptors specifically.
  • β2 selective agonist is salbutamol; selective antagonist is butoxamine.
  • ADH secretion from the posterior pituitary is also a described β-receptor mediated effect.

posts.post_title: Mechanism producing Dale's adrenaline revers…
posts.post_content: The phenomenon of 'Dale's adrenaline reversal', where the pressor response to adrenaline is converted to a depressor response, occurs after administration of

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A non-selective alpha-adrenergic receptor antagonist

Drugs like phenoxybenzamine block α receptors, converting adrenaline's pressor response into a depressor response.

Correct Option Explanation

With α receptors blocked, adrenaline acts only on β receptors, which dilate blood vessels, so blood pressure falls instead of rising — this is Dale's adrenaline reversal.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A beta-blocker would leave α-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, producing an even greater pressor response, not a reversal.
  • A selective α2 agonist like clonidine reduces sympathetic outflow centrally, an unrelated mechanism to receptor blockade-based reversal.
  • An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor raises ACh levels and has no described role in adrenaline pressor reversal.
Know More
  • Phenoxybenzamine is a non-competitive antagonist of both α1 and α2 receptors.
  • Noradrenaline's pressor response is only diminished, not reversed, since it has little β2 action.
  • Phenoxybenzamine is used clinically for urinary retention and hypertension from phaeochromocytoma.
  • Reflex tachycardia after phenoxybenzamine is accentuated by blocked prejunctional α2 auto-inhibition.

posts.post_title: Selective alpha-1 antagonist that avoids ref…
posts.post_content: Which selective α1-adrenergic antagonist does NOT cause reflex tachycardia, unlike non-selective α-blockers?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Prazosin

Prazosin, a highly selective α1 blocker, does not cause reflex tachycardia.

Correct Option Explanation

Since it spares prejunctional α2 receptors, it does not increase noradrenaline release from sympathetic nerve endings in the myocardium, and it also reduces cardiac pre-load.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Phenoxybenzamine blocks both α1 and α2, so prejunctional α2 blockade increases noradrenaline release, causing marked reflex tachycardia.
  • Tolazoline is a weak-to-modest non-selective α1/α2 blocker with additional direct cardiac stimulant action.
  • Phentolamine is likewise a non-selective α-blocker, a close congener of tolazoline.
Know More
  • Prazosin has about 1000 times greater affinity for α1 than α2 receptors.
  • It is used to treat systemic or pulmonary hypertension.
  • Prazosin causes minimal change in cardiac output, renal blood flow and GFR.
  • The selective α2 antagonist is yohimbine.

posts.post_title: Selective alpha-2 antagonist used to reverse…
posts.post_content: Which selective α2-adrenergic antagonist, obtained from Pausinystalia yohimbe, is used to antagonize xylazine overdose?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Yohimbine

Yohimbine is a selective α2 antagonist used to reverse xylazine overdose.

Correct Option Explanation

By blocking peripheral postjunctional α2 receptors it causes vasodilatation and hypotension, and its central α2 blockade increases sympathetic outflow, reversing xylazine's sedative effects.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Prazosin is a selective α1, not α2, antagonist, and is not used for xylazine reversal.
  • Propranolol is a non-selective β blocker, an entirely different receptor class from α2 antagonism.
  • Atenolol is a selective β1 blocker, unrelated to α2 receptor antagonism or xylazine reversal.
Know More
  • Yohimbine's vasodilator effect in male genitalia can cause penile erection.
  • It readily crosses the blood-brain barrier, producing CNS excitation, ADH release, nausea and vomiting.
  • Tolazoline is also used as an antidote to xylazine overdose, via non-selective α blockade plus direct vasodilation.
  • Yohimbine also blocks 5-HT receptors with short-duration competitive action.

posts.post_title: Cardioselective beta-1 blocker useful for ul…
posts.post_content: Which β1-selective adrenergic antagonist is ultra-short acting and given IV for immediate control of tachycardia?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Esmolol

Esmolol is an ultra-short-acting β1-selective blocker, given IV for rapid, short-duration therapy of tachycardia.

Correct Option Explanation

Its brief action makes it ideal for acute investigation and immediate management of tachyarrhythmias where prolonged β-blockade is undesirable.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Metoprolol is the prototype cardioselective β1 blocker but has a longer duration, not ultra-short acting.
  • Atenolol is notable for very low lipid solubility (limited CNS penetration), not for ultra-short duration.
  • Propranolol is a non-selective β1/β2 blocker, not cardioselective and not ultra-short acting.
Know More
  • Metoprolol requires 50-100 times higher doses to block β2 compared with β1 receptors.
  • Atenolol penetrates the brain only to a very limited extent due to low lipid solubility.
  • Non-selective β-blockers like propranolol can cause dangerous bronchoconstriction in asthmatics.
  • Butoxamine is a selective β2 antagonist with no clinical use, as β2 blockade causes bronchoconstriction.

posts.post_title: Adrenergic antagonist that blocks both alpha…
posts.post_content: Which drug blocks β1 and β2 receptors non-selectively and also blocks α1 receptors at higher doses?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Labetalol

Labetalol blocks β1 and β2 receptors non-selectively, and at higher doses also blocks α1 receptors.

Correct Option Explanation

This combined action lowers blood pressure without the peripheral vasoconstriction seen with pure β-blockade, since some α1 blockade offsets it.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Prazosin is a purely selective α1 antagonist, with no β-blocking activity.
  • Atenolol is a purely selective β1 antagonist, with no α-blocking activity.
  • Yohimbine is a selective α2 antagonist, unrelated to β receptor blockade.
Know More
  • Labetalol's α-blockade is limited to α1 receptors only, sparing α2.
  • It is used for treating hypertension and as an experimental pharmacological tool.
  • Non-selective β-blockers like propranolol can aggravate heart failure and worsen bronchoconstriction.
  • β-blockers are useful in glaucoma by reducing aqueous humor production.

posts.post_title: Mechanism of reserpine's antihypertensive ac…
posts.post_content: Reserpine, obtained from Rauwolfia serpentina, lowers blood pressure primarily by

_aimcq_options.text: Blocking vesicular storage of noradrenaline, leading to its depletion
Competitively antagonizing beta-1 receptors on the heart
Stimulating central alpha-2 receptors to reduce sympathetic outflow

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Blocking vesicular storage of noradrenaline, leading to its depletion

Reserpine blocks the Mg++-ATP dependent transport of noradrenaline into storage vesicles, causing its depletion.

Correct Option Explanation

Unstored noradrenaline leaks into the cytoplasm where it is metabolized by MAO, progressively depleting sympathetic nerve terminal stores and causing a slow, sustained fall in BP.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Reserpine does not act as a receptor antagonist; it works presynaptically on storage vesicles, not by blocking α1 receptors.
  • Reserpine has no direct action on β1 receptors; its effect is entirely presynaptic on catecholamine storage.
  • The central α2-mediated sympathetic reduction mechanism describes clonidine or α-methyldopa, not reserpine.
Know More
  • High doses of reserpine also deplete brain catecholamines and 5-HT, causing sedation and depression.
  • Side effects include bradycardia, diarrhoea and increased gastric acid secretion from unopposed parasympathetic activity.
  • Reserpine is rarely used clinically today because of its adverse effect profile.
  • Guanethidine is another adrenergic neuron blocker acting mainly by inhibiting noradrenaline release.

posts.post_title: Category of ganglionic blockers exemplified …
posts.post_content: Hexamethonium is a classical example of a

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Non-depolarizing ganglionic blocking drug

Hexamethonium is a classical non-depolarizing ganglionic blocking drug.

Correct Option Explanation

It competitively blocks nicotinic receptors at autonomic ganglia without causing initial depolarization/stimulation, unlike nicotine at high doses.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Nicotine (large doses), not hexamethonium, is the example given of a persisting depolarizing ganglionic blocker.
  • Hexamethonium is a blocker, not a nicotinic agonist like DMPP or tetramethylammonium.
  • Muscarinic ganglionic agonists include acetylcholine, carbachol and pilocarpine — hexamethonium is nicotinic-selective and inhibitory, not muscarinic/stimulatory.
Know More
  • Other non-depolarizing ganglionic blockers include pentolinium, mecamylamine, pempidine and trimethaphan.
  • Ganglionic blockade causes tachycardia (since the heart is normally under predominant parasympathetic tone) but hypotension in vessels (predominant sympathetic tone).
  • Ganglionic blockade also causes mydriasis, cycloplegia and urinary retention, since these organs are predominantly parasympathetic.
  • Ganglionic blockers cause anhydrosis since sweat glands are predominantly sympathetic (adrenergic).

posts.post_title: Ocular effect of atropine mediated by iris s…
posts.post_content: Atropine's effect of relaxing the iris sphincter muscle produces

_aimcq_options.text: Mydriasis with a very long duration of action
Miosis with a short duration of action
Cycloplegia without any change in pupil size

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mydriasis with a very long duration of action

Atropine relaxes the iris sphincter, producing mydriasis with a very long duration of action on the eye.

Correct Option Explanation

It also relaxes the ciliary muscle, causing paralysis of accommodation (cycloplegia), also long-lasting — together these long durations make atropine less favoured than homatropine for routine ophthalmic use.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Miosis is produced by pilocarpine, a muscarinic agonist, the pharmacological opposite of atropine.
  • 'No change in pupil diameter' contradicts atropine's well-documented mydriatic effect.
  • Atropine does cause pupil size change (mydriasis) in addition to cycloplegia — the pupil is not unaffected.
Know More
  • Pilocarpine can counter atropine-induced mydriasis by contracting the iris sphincter.
  • The iris sphincter (constrictor pupillae) is parasympathetically innervated; the radial muscle is sympathetically innervated.
  • Parasympathetic activity normally predominates in controlling pupil diameter.
  • Shorter-acting antimuscarinics like tropicamide are preferred for routine ophthalmic examination.

posts.post_title: Drugs useful in narrow-angle (acute congesti…
posts.post_content: Which group of drugs is useful in reducing pressure during an attack of narrow-angle (acute congestive) glaucoma?

_aimcq_options.text: Parasympathomimetics such as pilocarpine and physostigmine

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Parasympathomimetics such as pilocarpine and physostigmine

Parasympathomimetic and anticholinesterase drugs like pilocarpine and physostigmine reduce intraocular pressure in narrow-angle glaucoma.

Correct Option Explanation

By inducing miosis and ciliary muscle contraction, they free the trabecular space at the canal of Schlemm from iris tissue blockade, facilitating aqueous humor outflow.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Atropine is contraindicated in narrow-angle glaucoma, as it can precipitate an acute attack by causing mydriasis.
  • Phenylephrine, a sympathomimetic, is also contraindicated as it can worsen angle closure via mydriasis.
  • Antihistaminics are listed among agents contraindicated in narrow-angle glaucoma, not useful treatments.
Know More
  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors like acetazolamide reduce aqueous humor formation.
  • Osmotic diuretics like mannitol and glycerine produce intraocular dehydration.
  • Wide-angle (chronic) glaucoma is managed long-term with pilocarpine, physostigmine or carbachol.
  • Echothiophate and diisopropylfluorophosphate offer the advantage of infrequent ocular dosing in wide-angle glaucoma.

posts.post_title: Predominant autonomic tone at sweat glands
posts.post_content: Sweat glands are under predominant control of which autonomic division and neurotransmitter?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sympathetic, using acetylcholine

Sweat glands are under predominant sympathetic (adrenergic) tone but are innervated using acetylcholine as the transmitter — a notable exception.

Correct Option Explanation

This unusual combination means ganglionic blockade produces anhydrosis despite sweat glands being classed as sympathetically predominant structures.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sweat glands are NOT primarily parasympathetic-controlled structures despite their cholinergic transmitter.
  • The transmitter at sweat glands is acetylcholine, not norepinephrine, despite the sympathetic classification.
  • Sweat glands are not parasympathetically dominant, and their transmitter is cholinergic, not noradrenergic.
Know More
  • Ganglionic stimulation increases sweating; ganglionic blockade causes anhydrosis.
  • The heart, GI tract, eye, urinary bladder and salivary glands are all predominantly parasympathetic.
  • Cardiovascular smooth muscle (arterioles, veins) is predominantly sympathetic with classical adrenergic transmission.
  • Ganglionic blockade causes tachycardia because the heart's predominant parasympathetic (vagal) tone is removed.

posts.post_title: Meaning of the term 'autacoid'
posts.post_content: The term 'autacoid' is derived from Greek words meaning

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Self remedy

'Autacoid' derives from Greek autos (self) and akos (remedy/healing substance), meaning 'self remedy'.

Correct Option Explanation

Autacoids are diverse substances produced locally by many cell types, acting fast at their site of synthesis, unlike hormones.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Tissue substance' describes the etymology of histamine (from 'histos', tissue), not the general term 'autacoid'.
  • 'Distant messenger' describes hormones, which travel via circulation to distant targets — the opposite of autacoid action.
  • 'Blood healer' is not the accepted etymological meaning of autacoid.
Know More
  • Autacoids are also known as local hormones.
  • Unlike hormones (specific cells, distant action, slow), autacoids are made by diverse cells, act locally and act fast.
  • Amine autacoids include histamine and serotonin; peptide autacoids include bradykinin and angiotensin.
  • Lipid-derived autacoids include prostaglandins, leukotrienes and PAF.

posts.post_title: Receptor mediating histamine-induced gastric…
posts.post_content: Histamine stimulates gastric acid secretion from parietal cells mainly through

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: H2 receptors

Histamine increases gastric acid secretion through H2 receptors on parietal cells.

Correct Option Explanation

H2 receptor activation stimulates adenylyl cyclase, raising intracellular cAMP, which drives acid secretion.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • H1 receptors mediate bronchoconstriction, vasodilatation and increased vascular permeability, not gastric acid secretion.
  • H3 receptors are autoreceptors providing feedback regulation of histamine synthesis and release, not gastric acid control.
  • Muscarinic M3 receptors mediate cholinergic, not histaminergic, gastric secretory stimulation.
Know More
  • H1 receptor activation works via phospholipase C and increased intracellular Ca2+.
  • H2 blockers reduce acid secretion and also diminish the response to acetylcholine and gastrin.
  • H2 receptors on vascular smooth muscle contribute a slower, more sustained vasodilator response to histamine.
  • H3 receptors are found on autonomic nerve terminals, arterial tissue and CNS.

posts.post_title: Components of the 'triple response of Lewis'
posts.post_content: Intradermal injection of histamine produces the 'triple response of Lewis', consisting of

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Flush, flare and wheal

The triple response of Lewis consists of flush, flare and wheal.

Correct Option Explanation

Flush is intense capillary dilatation; flare is surrounding arteriolar dilatation via axon reflex; wheal is fluid exudation causing local swelling.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Rash, itch and swelling' are related histamine effects but not the specific named triad of the Lewis response.
  • 'Pallor, cyanosis and erythema' are not the components described for the triple response.
  • 'Fever, chills and sweating' are systemic signs unrelated to the localized triple response.
Know More
  • The flare component is mediated by an axon reflex causing arteriolar dilatation in surrounding tissue.
  • The triple response is used to test the integrity of sensory innervation, e.g., in leprosy (leprotic spots).
  • Higher histamine concentrations injected deeply cause pain, while superficial injection causes itching.
  • Histamine-induced vasodilatation is partly mediated by EDRF (nitric oxide).

posts.post_title: Mechanism of action of cromolyn sodium
posts.post_content: Cromolyn sodium (sodium cromoglycate) prevents allergic bronchospasm by

_aimcq_options.text: Stabilizing the mast cell membrane, preventing degranulation

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Stabilizing the mast cell membrane, preventing degranulation

Cromolyn sodium stabilizes the mast cell membrane, preventing degranulation after an antigen-antibody reaction.

Correct Option Explanation

By blocking mast cell degranulation, it inhibits release of histamine and other allergic mediators before they are released, making it a prophylactic, not a reversal, agent.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cromolyn does not act as an H1 antagonist; it works upstream, preventing mediator release altogether rather than blocking their receptor.
  • Cromolyn has no direct bronchodilator action on smooth muscle; its benefit is purely preventive.
  • Cromolyn has no described action on acetylcholinesterase; its mechanism is mast cell membrane stabilization.
Know More
  • Cromolyn is not effective once an acute asthmatic attack has already started.
  • It is useful only in the prophylaxis of asthma, not in non-allergic asthma.
  • It is available as dry powder or solution for inhalation, and as eye drops.
  • Drugs that increase intracellular cAMP (e.g., adrenaline) also inhibit histamine release from mast cells.

posts.post_title: Diagnostic use of histamine in pheochromocyt…
posts.post_content: In patients with pheochromocytoma, administration of histamine characteristically causes

_aimcq_options.text: A paradoxical rise in blood pressure
A greater fall in blood pressure than in normal individuals

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A paradoxical rise in blood pressure

In pheochromocytoma, histamine causes a rise in blood pressure, unlike the fall seen in normal individuals.

Correct Option Explanation

Histamine stimulates the tumour-affected adrenal medulla to release excess catecholamines, producing a pressor rather than depressor response — historically used as a diagnostic test.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A 'greater fall' is the opposite of the actual paradoxical pressor response documented for pheochromocytoma patients.
  • 'No change' contradicts the described diagnostic rise in blood pressure used clinically.
  • 'Immediate bradycardia without pressure change' does not match the described pressor diagnostic response.
Know More
  • Histamine stimulates autonomic ganglia and the adrenal medulla, inducing adrenaline release and raised BP.
  • Histamine itself has no direct clinical therapeutic use beyond diagnostic testing.
  • For diagnosing achlorhydria, H2 agonists like pentagastrin are preferred over histamine to avoid systemic side effects.
  • The triple response tests sensory nerve and circulatory integrity, useful in conditions like leprosy.

posts.post_title: Storage of histamine within mast cell granul…
posts.post_content: Within mast cell granules, histamine is held in an inactive complex bound to

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: An acidic protein and heparin

Positively charged histamine is held within granules bound to an acidic protein and heparin (both negatively charged).

Correct Option Explanation

Upon exocytosis, sodium ions from extracellular fluid exchange with histamine, releasing it in free, active form.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Albumin and sodium ions is incorrect; sodium ions are involved only in the release-phase exchange, not in the storage complex itself.
  • Chromogranin and ATP describes storage of catecholamines in adrenergic vesicles, not histamine's storage mechanism.
  • Globulin and calcium ions is not the described mast cell granule storage complex for histamine.
Know More
  • Increased intracellular cAMP inhibits histamine release, which is why adrenaline inhibits histamine release.
  • Histamine is synthesized locally from the amino acid histidine.
  • Histamine is inactive orally because it is degraded by the liver upon intestinal absorption.
  • Tissues rich in histamine include skin, gastric/intestinal mucosa, lungs, liver and placenta.

posts.post_title: Drug of choice for anaphylactic shock despit…
posts.post_content: Even though antihistamines control many allergic manifestations, the drug of choice for anaphylactic shock is

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Epinephrine

Epinephrine remains the drug of choice for anaphylactic shock, as antihistamines only partially prevent the anaphylactic fall in blood pressure.

Correct Option Explanation

Antihistamines block histamine-induced bronchoconstriction and urticaria well, but they cannot substitute for epinephrine's combined pressor and bronchodilator action in true anaphylaxis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Diphenhydramine, a first-generation H1 antagonist, only partially controls anaphylactic hypotension, not a substitute for epinephrine.
  • Cetirizine, a second-generation antihistamine, is non-sedating but still inadequate alone for anaphylactic shock.
  • Chlorpheniramine is a low-sedation first-generation antihistamine, also insufficient as sole anaphylaxis therapy.
Know More
  • Antihistamines well control urticaria, itching and angioedema.
  • Antihistamines block histamine action on smooth muscle and the triple response but do not affect histamine-induced gastric secretion.
  • Complete blockade of the histamine BP fall requires both H1 and H2 antagonists.
  • Pretreatment with antihistamines can abolish adrenaline release from the adrenal medulla triggered by histamine.

posts.post_title: H1 antihistamines causing cardiac arrhythmia…
posts.post_content: Which second-generation antihistamines were found to cause cardiac arrhythmias and were banned in some countries?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Terfenadine and astemizole

Terfenadine and astemizole were found to cause cardiac arrhythmias and were banned in some countries.

Correct Option Explanation

Despite being non-sedating second-generation agents, their cardiotoxic potential led to restricted or withdrawn use.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cetirizine and loratadine are second-generation antihistamines not associated with the described arrhythmia bans.
  • Chlorpheniramine and diphenhydramine are first-generation sedating antihistamines, not the ones flagged for arrhythmias in this text.
  • Cimetidine and ranitidine are H2 receptor antagonists for peptic ulcer, an unrelated drug class.
Know More
  • Second-generation antihistamines are generally practically non-sedating and not anticholinergic.
  • First-generation agents like diphenhydramine and promethazine cause high sedation.
  • Chlorpheniramine and mepyramine cause low sedation among first-generation agents.
  • Cinnarizine is a second-generation agent notable for anti-vertigo activity.

posts.post_title: H2 antagonist considered the prototype
posts.post_content: Which H2 receptor antagonist is considered the prototype of this drug class?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cimetidine

Cimetidine is the prototype H2 receptor antagonist.

Correct Option Explanation

It acts competitively, like ranitidine, nizatidine and roxatidine, to block histamine-mediated gastric acid secretion.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Ranitidine is 5 times more potent than cimetidine but is not the class prototype.
  • Famotidine is both competitive and non-competitive in action, notably more potent and longer-acting, but not the prototype.
  • Roxatidine is twice as potent and longer-acting than ranitidine, but again not the original prototype drug.
Know More
  • Loxatidine is uniquely non-competitive in its H2 antagonist action.
  • Ranitidine, unlike cimetidine, has no antiandrogenic action and does not inhibit hepatic drug metabolism.
  • Famotidine's higher potency and longer duration make it particularly suited for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
  • H2 antagonists cause marked inhibition of gastric secretion without affecting vitamin B12 absorption.

posts.post_title: H2 antagonist most suitable for Zollinger-El…
posts.post_content: Which H2 antagonist, being 8 times more potent than ranitidine with a longer duration of action, is considered particularly suitable for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Famotidine

Famotidine is 8 times more potent than ranitidine with a longer duration, making it especially suitable for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Correct Option Explanation

Its higher potency and prolonged action also make it useful for prophylaxis of aspiration pneumonia.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cimetidine is the original, less potent prototype H2 blocker, not the drug singled out for this indication by potency.
  • Nizatidine is a competitive H2 antagonist but not highlighted for the described 8x potency advantage over ranitidine.
  • Roxatidine is twice as potent as ranitidine, less potent than famotidine's described 8-fold advantage.
Know More
  • Famotidine, like ranitidine, has no antiandrogenic action.
  • H2 antagonists suppress basal, psychic, neurogenic and gastric secretion phases dose-dependently.
  • H2 antagonists provide 60-70% inhibition of 24-hour acid output (antiulcerogenic effect).
  • H2 antagonists have no direct effect on gastric or oesophageal motility or sphincter tone.

posts.post_title: Pharmacological action of antihistamines NOT…
posts.post_content: Which histamine effect is NOT significantly affected by conventional H1 antihistamines?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Gastric acid secretion

Histamine's action on gastric secretion is singularly not affected by conventional H1 antihistamines.

Correct Option Explanation

Gastric acid secretion is mediated via H2 receptors, which are unaffected by classical (H1-selective) antihistamines, requiring a separate H2 antagonist class.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bronchoconstriction from histamine IS blocked by H1 antihistamines, as it is H1-receptor mediated.
  • The triple response is well blocked by H1 antihistamines, since it is largely H1-mediated.
  • Intestinal smooth muscle contraction from histamine is blocked by H1 antihistamines as described in the text.
Know More
  • Complete reversal of the histamine BP fall needs both H1 and H2 blockers.
  • H1 antihistamines can abolish histamine-triggered adrenaline release from the adrenal medulla.
  • Second-generation H1 antihistamines are not anticholinergic, unlike many first-generation agents.
  • Antihistamines are useful for motion sickness, vertigo and Parkinsonism symptoms due to CNS effects.

posts.post_title: Why serotonin is also called 'enteramine'
posts.post_content: Serotonin is also historically known as 'enteramine' because

_aimcq_options.text: About 90% of it is found in the intestines
It was first isolated from enteric neurons
It only acts on intestinal receptors
It is synthesized exclusively in the gut wall

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: About 90% of it is found in the intestines

Serotonin is called 'enteramine' because roughly 90% of body serotonin is present in the intestines.

Correct Option Explanation

The remaining serotonin is distributed in platelets and the brain, and it is also found in wasp/scorpion venom and certain fruits like banana, pineapple and plums.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The naming reflects distribution, not the site of first isolation from enteric neurons.
  • Serotonin acts on multiple tissues beyond the intestine — cardiovascular, respiratory, CNS and platelets — not exclusively intestinal receptors.
  • Serotonin is not exclusively synthesized in the gut; it is also formed and stored in platelets and the CNS.
Know More
  • Serotonin's chemical name is β-aminoethyl 5-hydroxyindole.
  • It is synthesized from the amino acid tryptophan.
  • It is degraded by monoamine oxidases and dehydrogenases.
  • Serotonin crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly, limiting direct peripheral-to-central effects.

posts.post_title: Rate-limiting step in serotonin synthesis
posts.post_content: The rate-limiting step in the synthesis of serotonin is

_aimcq_options.text: Deamination of serotonin by monoamine oxidase

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Conversion of 5-hydroxytryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptamine by decarboxylase

The rate-limiting step is conversion of 5-hydroxytryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptamine (serotonin) by the enzyme decarboxylase.

Correct Option Explanation

This final decarboxylation step controls the overall rate of serotonin production from its tryptophan precursor.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Hydroxylation of tryptophan is an earlier step in the pathway but is not identified as the rate-limiting step in this text.
  • Deamination by MAO is a catabolic (breakdown), not synthetic, step, producing 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid.
  • Dehydrogenation to 5-hydroxytryptophol is also a catabolic pathway, not part of synthesis.
Know More
  • Serotonin has two catabolic pathways: MAO (to 5-HIAA) and dehydrogenases (to 5-hydroxytryptophol).
  • Serotonin receptors are broadly classed as musculotropic (D type) and neurotropic (M type), or numerically as 5-HT1, 5-HT2, 5-HT3, etc.
  • Serotonin is a potent depolarizer of nerve endings, and tachyphylaxis is very common with repeated dosing.
  • Serotonin release from platelets occurs during aggregation at the site of injury.

posts.post_title: Serotonin's effect on gastric secretion
posts.post_content: Serotonin's action on gastric glands is generally considered

_aimcq_options.text: Ulcer protective, inhibiting acid/pepsin and increasing mucous
Neutral, with no effect on gastric secretion
Purely stimulatory to pepsin release only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ulcer protective, inhibiting acid/pepsin and increasing mucous

Serotonin inhibits gastric acid and pepsin secretion while increasing mucous production, giving it an ulcer protective effect.

Correct Option Explanation

This contrasts with histamine, which stimulates gastric acid secretion via H2 receptors — an important pharmacological distinction between the two amine autacoids.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Serotonin is described as ulcer protective, the opposite of an ulcerogenic action.
  • 'No effect' contradicts its documented inhibitory action on acid and pepsin secretion.
  • Serotonin inhibits, rather than stimulates, pepsin secretion, contrary to a purely stimulatory claim.
Know More
  • Serotonin stimulates the GI tract, increasing peristalsis and causing diarrhoea.
  • It constricts bronchial smooth muscle, though it is less potent than histamine in this action.
  • On the cardiovascular system, rapid IV injection produces a characteristic triphasic blood pressure curve.
  • Continuous slow infusion of serotonin instead causes a prolonged fall in arterial pressure.

posts.post_title: Serotonin antagonist used clinically to incr…
posts.post_content: Which 5-HT receptor antagonist is used clinically to increase appetite and promote weight gain, despite causing drowsiness?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cyproheptadine

Cyproheptadine is used to increase appetite and weight gain, though drowsiness is a major side effect.

Correct Option Explanation

Its appetite-stimulating effect is exploited clinically despite its sedative liability, making it useful in underweight patients.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Methysergide is used specifically for migraine prophylaxis, not appetite stimulation.
  • Ketanserine is used as an antihypertensive agent, unrelated to appetite effects.
  • Ondansetron is used to control vomiting, particularly in cancer chemotherapy/radiotherapy patients.
Know More
  • 5-HT agonists include LSD, azapirones and cisapride.
  • Other 5-HT antagonists include phenoxybenzamine, cinnarizine, chlorpromazine and clozapine.
  • Serotonin initiates the vasoconstrictor phase of migraine.
  • Nausea and vomiting from cytotoxic drugs and radiotherapy are mediated by serotonin, explaining ondansetron's mechanism.

posts.post_title: Effect of thromboxane A2 on platelets and ve…
posts.post_content: Thromboxane A2 (TxA2), released from activated platelets, characteristically causes

_aimcq_options.text: No effect on platelets, only bronchodilation

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Vasoconstriction and pro-aggregatory platelet effects

TxA2 is a potent vasoconstrictor and is pro-aggregatory, promoting further platelet aggregation.

Correct Option Explanation

Due to its short half-life, it acts immediately at the site of release, reducing blood flow to a damaged site and forming a platelet plug.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Vasodilation and anti-aggregatory effects describe prostacyclin (PGI2), the physiological antagonist of TxA2, not TxA2 itself.
  • TxA2 has clear pro-aggregatory platelet effects, not 'no effect'.
  • TxA2 is a vasoconstrictor, not selectively a venodilator.

  • TxA2 spontaneously degrades into the inactive metabolite TxB2.
  • Prostacyclin (PGI2) is produced by the endothelium and degrades into inactive 6-keto-PGF1.
  • Only TxA2 and PGI2 are the major vasoactive prostaglandins; normally their opposing actions balance.
  • Platelets primarily synthesize TxA2, while the vessel wall mainly generates PGI2.

posts.post_title: Prostaglandin causing bronchial contraction …
posts.post_content: Nearly all prostaglandins cause bronchial relaxation, but which one is the notable exception, causing bronchoconstriction?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: PGD2

PGD2 is the exception among prostaglandins, causing contraction of bronchial smooth muscle rather than relaxation.

Correct Option Explanation

All other prostaglandins cause bronchial relaxation, making PGD2's bronchoconstrictor action pharmacologically notable.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • PGE2 follows the general rule of prostaglandin-induced bronchial relaxation, unlike PGD2.
  • PGI2 is a vasodilator that also causes bronchial relaxation, consistent with the general rule.
  • PGF2α also causes bronchial relaxation like most prostaglandins, not constriction.

  • Leukotrienes, unlike most prostaglandins, are implicated as bronchoconstrictors in asthma.
  • PGE2 and PGF2α cause strong contraction of the pregnant uterus and GI tract.
  • PGE2 and PGI2 can inhibit gastric acid secretion and increase gastric mucosal blood flow.
  • PGE2 and PGI2 are hyperalgesic, sensitizing pain receptors to chemicals like bradykinin, rather than causing pain directly.

posts.post_title: Enzyme distinguishing COX and LOX pathways o…
posts.post_content: The cyclooxygenase (COX) and lipoxygenase (LOX) pathways of arachidonic acid metabolism differ in that

_aimcq_options.text: COX generates ring-structured eicosanoids while LOX produces open-chain leukotrienes
COX produces leukotrienes while LOX produces prostaglandins
Both pathways produce identical end products
LOX operates only in vascular endothelium

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: COX generates ring-structured eicosanoids while LOX produces open-chain leukotrienes

The COX pathway generates ring-structured eicosanoids (PGs, TXs, prostacyclin), while LOX produces open-chain leukotrienes.

Correct Option Explanation

The lipoxygenase pathway operates mainly in the lung, WBCs and platelets, producing leukotrienes such as the potent chemotactic LTB4 and the SRS-A components LTC4/LTD4.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • This statement reverses the actual pathway-product relationship described in the text.
  • The two pathways clearly produce chemically distinct classes of eicosanoids, not identical products.
  • LOX operates mainly in lung, WBC and platelets, not specifically or exclusively in vascular endothelium.
Know More
  • COX exists in two forms: COX1 (constitutive, physiological) and COX2 (inducible, inflammatory).
  • Aspirin is a selective COX1 inhibitor causing irreversible acetylation; nabumetone, meloxicam and nimesulide are selective COX2 inhibitors.
  • LTB4, LTC4 and LTD4 together constitute the slow reacting substance of anaphylaxis (SRS-A).
  • Leukotrienes are named for being first obtained from leukocytes.

posts.post_title: Clinical use of PGF2α for oestrous synchroni…
posts.post_content: PGF2α is used for oestrous synchronization in cattle because it

_aimcq_options.text: Causes luteolysis, converting the uterus to an oxytocin-responsive state

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Causes luteolysis, converting the uterus to an oxytocin-responsive state

PGF2α causes luteolysis and converts an oxytocin-resistant midterm uterus to an oxytocin-responsive state, enabling oestrous synchronization.

Correct Option Explanation

Despite this useful reproductive action, it can cause side effects like cramps and diarrhoea, and abortion induction may be delayed/erratic or incomplete, sometimes requiring surgery.

  • PGF2α does not directly stimulate follicular development; its role is luteolytic, ending the luteal phase.
  • PGF2α causes regression of the corpus luteum, which decreases, not increases, progesterone secretion.
  • PGF2α does not prevent ovulation; rather, by ending the luteal phase it permits a new cycle to begin.
Know More
  • Prostaglandins offer no advantage over oxytocin for inducing labour at full term, and show more variable action.
  • 15-methyl-PGF2α can be used for post-partum haemorrhage unresponsive to ergometrine or oxytocin.
  • Misoprostol (a PGE1 analogue) is used to protect against NSAID-induced peptic ulcers.
  • Prostaglandins can maintain patency of the ductus arteriosus in newborns with certain congenital aortic abnormalities.

posts.post_title: Reason paracetamol is contraindicated in cats
posts.post_content: Paracetamol is contraindicated in cats mainly because

_aimcq_options.text: Cats have poor glucuronidation capacity, leading to hepatotoxic metabolite accumulation
Paracetamol causes immediate cardiac arrest in cats

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cats have poor glucuronidation capacity, leading to hepatotoxic metabolite accumulation

Paracetamol's major elimination pathway is glucuronidation, which is poor in cats, causing a hepatotoxic metabolite to accumulate.

Correct Option Explanation

This deficiency makes cats particularly susceptible to paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity, unlike dogs where glucuronidation is more efficient.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cats retain functional COX enzymes; paracetamol's action is notably not primarily through COX inhibition anyway.
  • 'Immediate cardiac arrest' is not the documented toxicity mechanism; hepatotoxicity via poor glucuronidation is the key issue.
  • Cats can absorb paracetamol orally; the problem lies in metabolism, not absorption.
Know More
  • Paracetamol acts mainly as an antipyretic with essentially no anti-inflammatory effect.
  • It is the most popular NSAID-class drug in humans.
  • Hepatotoxicity is possible with all NSAIDs, but paracetamol's alternate metabolic pathway makes this especially relevant.
  • Its mechanism of antipyretic action is not primarily through COX inhibition, unlike classical NSAIDs.

posts.post_title: NSAID prohibited for veterinary use in the I…
posts.post_content: Which NSAID's residues in livestock carcasses caused mass mortality of vultures in North-West India and Pakistan, leading to a ban on its veterinary use in the region?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Diclofenac

Diclofenac residues in food-animal carcasses were responsible for wiping out vulture populations, leading to its ban for veterinary use in the Indian subcontinent.

Correct Option Explanation

Vultures feeding on treated carcasses suffered fatal renal failure from diclofenac exposure, a landmark case of pharmaceutical-driven wildlife mortality.

  • Meloxicam was found to be relatively vulture-safe and has instead been promoted as an alternative to diclofenac.
  • Ketoprofen is not described as the causative drug for vulture deaths; its main documented risk is laminitis in horses at overdose.
