  • Meclofenamic acid, used in horses for osteoarthritis, may cause GI irritation and colic.
  • Ketoprofen's major veterinary use is in horses at 2.2 mg/kg; overdose may cause laminitis.

posts.post_title: Species in which phenylbutazone is popular, …
posts.post_content: Phenylbutazone, popular in horses and dogs, is particularly associated with which serious toxicity?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Blood dyscrasias

Phenylbutazone is specifically noted to cause blood dyscrasias as a toxic effect.

Correct Option Explanation

It has combined analgesic, antipyretic, anti-inflammatory and uricosuric actions, but this haematologic toxicity is a key limitation, and it is also irritating if given IM or SC.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Vulture-lethal renal failure' is specifically associated with diclofenac, not phenylbutazone.
  • Cardiac arrhythmia is not the toxicity highlighted for phenylbutazone in this text.
  • Corneal ulceration is not a documented phenylbutazone toxicity in this material.
Know More
  • Phenylbutazone uniquely also has uricosuric action among the listed NSAIDs.
  • Ibuprofen is more anti-inflammatory and less analgesic, with a low tendency to cause GI ulcers.
  • Flunixin meglumine is widely used for colic and musculoskeletal pain in horses at a low dose (1.1 mg/kg).
  • Hepatotoxicity is possible with all NSAIDs, though the specific mechanism varies by drug.

posts.post_title: Mechanism of NSAID-induced gastric ulceration
posts.post_content: NSAIDs cause gastric ulceration primarily because they

_aimcq_options.text: Inhibit cytoprotective prostaglandins that protect gastric mucosa from acid
Directly corrode the gastric mucosal lining chemically
Stimulate excess gastrin release from G cells

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Inhibit cytoprotective prostaglandins that protect gastric mucosa from acid

NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandins that normally exert a cytoprotective effect on the gastric mucous membrane, exposing it to acid attack.

Correct Option Explanation

This leads to erosion, ulcers and bleeding, with typical ulcers reported in dogs and horses from NSAID use.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • NSAIDs do not directly corrode the mucosa chemically; their ulcerogenic effect is via prostaglandin inhibition.
  • NSAIDs decrease, not increase, protective mucus secretion by inhibiting prostaglandins.
  • NSAIDs have no described action of stimulating gastrin release; the mechanism is prostaglandin-mediated cytoprotection loss.
Know More
  • NSAIDs also carry renal toxicity risk, since prostaglandins regulate local renal blood flow.
  • NSAIDs can delay labour by inhibiting prostaglandins involved in parturition.
  • Some individuals develop asthma or anaphylactic reactions from NSAID-induced overproduction of leukotrienes.
  • NSAIDs are useful adjunct therapy in mastitis alongside antibiotics in veterinary practice.

posts.post_title: NSAID mechanism responsible for increased bl…
posts.post_content: NSAIDs increase bleeding time primarily because their inhibitory effect on

_aimcq_options.text: Thromboxane A2 predominates over their effect on prostacyclin
Prostacyclin predominates over their effect on thromboxane A2

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Thromboxane A2 predominates over their effect on prostacyclin

NSAIDs inhibit both pro-aggregatory TXA2 and anti-aggregatory PGI2, but the effect on TXA2 predominates, increasing bleeding time.

Correct Option Explanation

This relative sparing of the anti-aggregatory PGI2 pathway tips the balance toward reduced platelet aggregation overall.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • If the effect on PGI2 predominated, the net effect would favour clotting/aggregation rather than bleeding.
  • NSAIDs do not act by blocking fibrinogen synthesis; their antithrombotic action is via the eicosanoid pathway.
  • NSAIDs have no described effect on vitamin K absorption; this is unrelated to their antiplatelet mechanism.
Know More
  • This antithrombotic property underlies low-dose aspirin use in humans to prevent arterial thrombus and heart attacks.
  • NSAIDs can also help close a patent ductus arteriosus by inhibiting the prostaglandins that normally maintain its patency.
  • Aspirin causes irreversible COX inhibition via acetylation, unlike most other NSAIDs which are reversible.
  • Selective COX2 inhibitors (nimesulide, valdecoxib, rofecoxib) have less GI ulcer risk since COX1's protective role is spared.

posts.post_title: NSAID with major veterinary use in horses at…
posts.post_content: Which powerful anti-inflammatory NSAID is used mainly in horses at 2.2 mg/kg, with overdose risking laminitis?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ketoprofen

Ketoprofen is a powerful anti-inflammatory, with its major veterinary use in horses at 2.2 mg/kg; overdose may cause laminitis.

Correct Option Explanation

This makes accurate dosing critical in equine practice given the serious risk of laminitis with excess dosing.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Meloxicam is noted for its low potency to induce GI side effects, not the specific 2.2 mg/kg equine dosing/laminitis risk described for ketoprofen.
  • Paracetamol has essentially no anti-inflammatory effect and is not the drug described for equine anti-inflammatory dosing.
  • Nimesulide is a selective COX2 inhibitor with an injectable form, not associated with the described equine laminitis risk.
Know More
  • Aspirin is mostly preferred in cats among the classical NSAIDs, available in enteric-coated and other formulations.
  • Flunixin meglumine is widely used for colic and musculoskeletal pain in horses at a low dose (1.1 mg/kg).
  • Meclofenamic acid is used in horses for osteoarthritis, but may cause GI irritation and colic.
  • Ibuprofen has a low tendency to produce GI ulcers compared with many other NSAIDs.

posts.post_title: Origin of the name 'bradykinin'
posts.post_content: Bradykinin is so named because early experiments showed it causes

_aimcq_options.text: A slow-developing contraction of the gut
A rapid dilation of the pupil
A fast pressor response in blood pressure

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A slow-developing contraction of the gut

Bradykinin ('brady' = slow, 'kinin' = to move) was named for its slow-developing contraction of gut smooth muscle, discovered when trypsin and certain snake venoms acted on plasma globulin.

Correct Option Explanation

This same substance also lowered blood pressure, distinguishing it as a novel local mediator distinct from other known agents at the time.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bradykinin's naming was based on gut contraction speed, not any described pupil effect.
  • Bradykinin causes a fall, not a rapid pressor rise, in blood pressure — the opposite direction.
  • Bradykinin's naming and identification relate to gut motility and blood pressure, not blood clotting speed.
Know More
  • The blood-pressure-lowering activity in pancreas extracts led to the term 'kallikreins'.
  • Kallidin is a decapeptide with almost similar actions to bradykinin.
  • Bradykinin and kallidin together are called plasma kinins.
  • Kininogens, the precursors of kinins, are liver-derived alpha2 globulins.

posts.post_title: Enzyme responsible for degrading kinins, als…
posts.post_content: Which enzyme metabolizes kinins and is also identical to angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE)?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Kininase II

Kininase II, a carboxypeptidase, is identical to angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) and degrades kinins.

Correct Option Explanation

This explains why ACE inhibitors increase kinin levels in tissue and plasma, since they simultaneously prevent kinin breakdown.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Kininase I is a separate carboxypeptidase enzyme, distinct from ACE/Kininase II.
  • Aminopeptidase converts kallidin to bradykinin, a different metabolic action, not equivalent to ACE.
  • Plasma kallikrein is involved in kinin production (converting kininogen to bradykinin), not in ACE-related degradation.
Know More
  • Tissue damage activates Hageman factor, initiating the kinin cascade.
  • Plasma kallikrein converts high molecular weight kininogen to bradykinin; tissue kallikrein converts low molecular weight kininogen to kallidin.
  • ACE inhibitor-induced cough is thought to be mediated by elevated kinin levels.
  • Kinins are implicated in shock, angioedema, rhinitis, asthma and acute pancreatitis.

posts.post_title: Cardiovascular effect of plasma kinins
posts.post_content: Plasma kinins such as bradykinin exert which effect on the cardiovascular system?

_aimcq_options.text: Potent vasodilatation causing a sharp fall in blood pressure

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Potent vasodilatation causing a sharp fall in blood pressure

Plasma kinins are potent vasodilators, dilating renal, cardiac and other visceral vessels and causing a sharp fall in blood pressure.

Correct Option Explanation

This vasodilator action explains why ACE inhibitors, by raising kinin levels, can contribute additional hypotensive benefit beyond their angiotensin-related effects.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Kinins produce vasodilatation, not vasoconstriction, so hypertension is the opposite of the described effect.
  • Kinins have a clear, significant vascular effect, contrary to 'no significant effect'.
  • Kinins dilate a broad range of vascular beds, not selectively constricting coronary vessels.
Know More
  • Kinins increase renal blood flow and regulate urine volume and composition.
  • Kinins promote sperm motility and play a role in spermatogenesis.
  • Kinins help the transition from fetal to neonatal circulation via femoral artery dilatation, ductus arteriosus closure and umbilical vessel constriction.
  • Kinins produce all cardinal signs of inflammation: redness, exudation, pain and leukocyte mobilization.

posts.post_title: Platelet activating factor's effect on the s…
posts.post_content: Platelet activating factor (PAF) has which characteristic effect on the stomach?

_aimcq_options.text: Ulcerogenic, causing erosions and mucosal bleeding

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ulcerogenic, causing erosions and mucosal bleeding

PAF is ulcerogenic, causing gastric erosions and mucosal bleeding.

Correct Option Explanation

This adds to PAF's broad pathological role alongside its effects on platelets, white blood cells and smooth muscle in inflammatory and allergic states.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • PAF is damaging, not cytoprotective, to gastric mucosa — the opposite of the correct description.
  • PAF has a clear, documented harmful gastric effect, not 'no effect'.
  • PAF does not increase protective mucus; instead it causes erosive damage to the mucosa.
Know More
  • PAF causes platelet aggregation and release of TXA2.
  • PAF is chemotactic to neutrophils, eosinophils and monocytes, promoting their migration to infection sites.
  • PAF causes vasodilatation likely via EDRF release, but contracts intestinal/uterine smooth muscle and bronchi.
  • PAF plays a role in inflammation, bronchial asthma, anaphylactic shock, haemostasis and thrombosis.

posts.post_title: Rate-limiting enzyme in angiotensin II gener…
posts.post_content: Which enzyme is the rate-limiting factor for angiotensin II generation?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Renin

Renin is the rate-limiting factor for angiotensin II generation.

Correct Option Explanation

Renin converts angiotensinogen (plasma alpha globulin) to angiotensin I, which has a very short biological potency, and ACE then rapidly converts it to the potent vasoconstrictor angiotensin II.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • ACE converts angiotensin I to II but is not described as the limiting factor for the overall pathway; renin holds that role.
  • Angiotensinase inactivates angiotensin III, a degradative rather than rate-limiting synthetic role.
  • Chymase is not discussed in this text as the rate-limiting enzyme for angiotensin generation.
Know More
  • The plasma half-life of renin is about 15 minutes.
  • Angiotensin II has a very short half-life of less than a minute.
  • ACE is a dipeptidyl carboxypeptidase located mainly on vascular endothelial cells in the lungs.
  • Angiotensin III is less potent than angiotensin II but still stimulates aldosterone secretion.

posts.post_title: Angiotensin receptor subtype through which a…
posts.post_content: All the major effects of angiotensin II — vasoconstriction, aldosterone release, sympathetic outflow — are mediated through which receptor subtype?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: AT1 receptor

All the effects of angiotensin II are mediated through AT1 receptors.

Correct Option Explanation

AT1 is a G-protein coupled receptor using phospholipase C/IP3/DAG signalling, driving vascular and visceral smooth muscle contraction via myosin light chain kinase activation.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • AT2 receptors are found in the adrenal medulla and CNS but do not mediate the classic angiotensin II actions described.
  • An 'AT3 receptor' is not a described angiotensin receptor subtype in this material.
  • The bradykinin B2 receptor is an unrelated receptor system for a different autacoid (kinins), not angiotensin.
Know More
  • Losartan is the specific antagonist for the AT1 receptor.
  • DAG activates protein kinase C, which promotes cell growth via protein phosphorylation.
  • In liver and kidney, angiotensin II inhibits adenylyl cyclase.
  • AT1 receptor activation has a sustained effect on cell growth and intracellular matrix synthesis in myocardium and vascular smooth muscle.

posts.post_title: Prototype ACE inhibitor
posts.post_content: Which drug is considered the prototype orally active ACE inhibitor?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Captopril

Captopril, an orally active dipeptide analogue, is the prototype ACE inhibitor.

Correct Option Explanation

It abolishes the pressor action of angiotensin I (but not angiotensin II directly), and increases plasma kinin levels, potentiating bradykinin's hypotensive action.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Losartan is an AT1 receptor antagonist, a mechanistically different drug class from ACE inhibitors.
  • Saralasin is a partial agonist angiotensin II analogue, requiring parenteral administration, not the ACE inhibitor prototype.
  • Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist, blocking mineralocorticoid receptors, not an ACE inhibitor.
Know More
  • Teprotide, from pit viper venom bradykinin-potentiating factor, was the first ACE inhibitor discovered.
  • Captopril's cough side effect is attributed to elevated kinin and prostaglandin levels.
  • About 70% of orally administered captopril is absorbed, and food reduces its bioavailability.
  • Other ACE inhibitors include enalapril, lisinopril, perindopril and ramipril.

posts.post_title: Advantage of losartan over ACE inhibitors re…
posts.post_content: Compared to ACE inhibitors, losartan has the therapeutic advantage of

_aimcq_options.text: No recurrence of cough, since it does not raise kinin levels
Requiring dose reduction only in renal failure

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: No recurrence of cough, since it does not raise kinin levels

Losartan shows no recurrence of cough, unlike ACE inhibitors, since it acts by blocking AT1 receptors rather than by inhibiting kinin breakdown.

Correct Option Explanation

As a competitive AT1 antagonist without partial agonist activity, it blocks all angiotensin II actions without the kinin-mediated side effects seen with ACE inhibitors like captopril.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • ACE inhibitors as a class are noted to cause no postural hypotension; losartan is not singled out as causing profound postural hypotension either.
  • Losartan's advantage described is oral administration with food not interfering with absorption, not a parenteral-only requirement (that describes saralasin).
  • Losartan's dose should be reduced in hepatic dysfunction, not specifically renal failure, since it undergoes first-pass metabolism.
Know More
  • Losartan's blood pressure lowering effect lasts about 24 hours.
  • It regresses hypertensive left ventricular hypertrophy.
  • Fetal abnormalities have been recorded with losartan, similar to ACE inhibitor risk in pregnancy.
  • Saralasin, an earlier angiotensin antagonist, exhibits partial agonist activity, unlike losartan.

posts.post_title: Effect of loop diuretics on renin release
posts.post_content: Loop diuretics stimulate renin release primarily by

_aimcq_options.text: Reducing sodium ion delivery to the macula densa
Directly stimulating beta-1 receptors on juxtaglomerular cells
Increasing prostaglandin synthesis in the kidney

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Reducing sodium ion delivery to the macula densa

Loop diuretics reduce sodium ion delivery to the macula densa, which triggers renin release.

Correct Option Explanation

This macula densa sensing pathway is one of the key physiological triggers for renin secretion from juxtaglomerular cells, alongside baroreceptor and sympathetic pathways.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sympathetic outflow acting via beta-adrenoreceptors is a separate mechanism, described as sensed through the baroreceptor pathway, not the direct diuretic action described.
  • NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis and thereby decrease renin release — the opposite relationship to what loop diuretics do.
  • Loop diuretics do not act by blocking ACE; that is the separate mechanism of ACE inhibitor drugs.
Know More
  • Vasodilators and diuretics in general stimulate renin release by lowering blood pressure.
  • Central sympatholytics and beta-blockers decrease renin release.
  • ACE inhibitors and AT1 antagonists enhance renin release by interfering with negative feedback.
  • NSAIDs decrease renin release by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis.

posts.post_title: Predominant molecular mechanism of barbitura…
posts.post_content: Barbiturates, benzodiazepines and most inhalational anaesthetics are now understood to act mainly by

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Potentiating GABA-A receptor activity

Barbiturates, benzodiazepines and most inhalational anaesthetics act primarily by potentiating GABA-A receptor activity.

Correct Option Explanation

Since GABA is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter, potentiating its receptor increases inhibitory tone throughout the CNS, producing sedation, hypnosis and anaesthesia.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • NMDA receptor inhibition is the specific mechanism of ketamine (a dissociative anaesthetic), not barbiturates/benzodiazepines.
  • Closing nicotinic ACh receptor channels is described for some fluorinated general anaesthetics specifically, not the primary GABA-A mechanism.
  • Local anaesthetics, not general anaesthetics like barbiturates, work by blocking voltage-gated Na+ channels.
Know More
  • Ketamine (dissociative anaesthetic) acts via inhibition of the NMDA glutamate receptor.
  • No single unitary theory of narcosis fully explains general anaesthetic action.
  • The Meyer-Overton theory links anaesthetic potency to oil (lipid) solubility.
  • Receptor-operated ion channels are considered the major overall site of general anaesthetic action.

posts.post_title: Stage of anaesthesia characterized by involu…
posts.post_content: Which stage of anaesthesia is also known as the stage of delirium or involuntary excitement, marked by struggling, jerky breathing and pupillary dilatation?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Stage II

Stage II (delirium/involuntary excitement) extends from loss of consciousness to onset of automatic respiration.

Correct Option Explanation

During this stage, sympathetic stimulation causes pupillary dilatation, increased heart rate and blood pressure, along with involuntary struggling, jerky breathing, and sometimes vomiting or involuntary micturition/defecation.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Stage I (analgesia/voluntary excitement) precedes loss of consciousness, with voluntary rather than involuntary resistance.
  • Stage III, Plane 2 is part of surgical anaesthesia, characterized by loss of corneal and laryngeal reflexes, not delirium.
  • Stage IV is medullary/respiratory paralysis, between respiratory and cardiac arrest — a very different, dangerous stage.
Know More
  • Stage III (surgical anaesthesia) is divided into 4 planes, from light to excessive surgical anaesthesia.
  • Dissociative anaesthetics uniquely induce only Stages I and II, not full surgical anaesthesia in the classical sense.
  • Ether is notable for inducing all four classical stages of anaesthesia.
  • Ultra-short acting barbiturates induce stages I, III and IV, effectively skipping the excitement of Stage II.

posts.post_title: Order of sensory modality blockade by local …
posts.post_content: Local anaesthetics typically block sensory modalities in which order?

_aimcq_options.text: Pain, then temperature, then touch, then deep pressure
Deep pressure, then touch, then temperature, then pain
Touch, then pain, then temperature, then deep pressure

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pain, then temperature, then touch, then deep pressure

Local anaesthetics block sensory modalities in the order: pain, temperature, touch, deep pressure.

Correct Option Explanation

This occurs because small, non-myelinated fibres (carrying pain/temperature) are more sensitive to blockade than larger, myelinated fibres (carrying touch/pressure).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The reverse order ('deep pressure first') contradicts the documented fibre-size-dependent sensitivity pattern.
  • 'Touch before pain' is inconsistent with the described order, where pain sensation is lost first.
  • 'All modalities simultaneously' contradicts the graded, sequential blockade pattern based on fibre type and size.
Know More
  • Small sensory fibres are more vulnerable to local anaesthetic block than motor fibres.
  • Autonomic nerves are more susceptible to blockade than somatic fibres.
  • Blockade is more efficient at a rapidly stimulated nerve than a resting nerve.
  • Local anaesthetics stabilize the Na+ channel in its inactivated state after entering the cell in unionized form and becoming ionized (cationic).

posts.post_title: Local anaesthetic hydrolyzed by cholinestera…
posts.post_content: Which local anaesthetic is hydrolyzed by cholinesterase into alcohol and PABA, and should not be used concurrently with sulphonamides?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Procaine

Procaine, introduced in 1905, is hydrolysed by cholinesterase to alcohol and PABA, and is not to be used when sulphonamides are given.

Correct Option Explanation

PABA competitively antagonizes sulphonamide antibacterial action, making concurrent use counterproductive against infection.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Lidocaine is an amide-type LA, resistant to cholinesterase, and is not associated with the PABA-sulphonamide interaction.
  • Bupivacaine is a long-acting amide-type LA, roughly 4 times more potent than lidocaine, unrelated to this specific ester-hydrolysis interaction.
  • Ropivacaine is an amide-type long-acting LA with less CVS/CNS toxicity than bupivacaine, also not the PABA-forming ester agent.
Know More
  • Procaine is short-acting, being rapidly metabolized in plasma, and also has antiarrhythmic effect.
  • Ester-type LAs include cocaine, procaine, chloroprocaine, tetracaine, benzocaine.
  • Amide-type LAs include lidocaine, bupivacaine, dibucaine, prilocaine.
  • Amide LAs are more intense/longer-lasting, bind to α1 acid glycoprotein and rarely cause hypersensitivity.

posts.post_title: Definition of MAC (minimum alveolar concentr…
posts.post_content: MAC (minimum alveolar concentration) of an inhalant anaesthetic is defined as

_aimcq_options.text: The lowest alveolar concentration producing immobility to a painful stimulus in 50% of subjects
The highest alveolar concentration tolerable without cardiac arrest
The blood concentration producing surgical anaesthesia in all subjects
The concentration required to produce unconsciousness in 100% of subjects

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: The lowest alveolar concentration producing immobility to a painful stimulus in 50% of subjects

MAC is the lowest alveolar concentration of anaesthetic needed to produce immobility to a painful stimulus in 50% of individuals.

Correct Option Explanation

MAC correlates excellently with the oil/gas partition coefficient, and anaesthetic potency is inversely related to MAC — a very potent agent has a low MAC.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • MAC is not defined by the 'highest tolerable concentration'; it is specifically the concentration producing immobility in half the population.
  • MAC is an alveolar (gas phase) concentration measure, not a blood concentration measure.
  • MAC applies to 50%, not 100%, of subjects by definition.
Know More
  • MAC values vary greatly by species — e.g., nitrous oxide MAC ranges from about 104% in man to 255% in cats.
  • A low blood/gas partition coefficient favours rapid induction and recovery.
  • Oil/gas partition coefficient correlates inversely with anaesthetic potency (i.e., directly with MAC being low for potent agents).
  • Nitrous oxide has a MAC >100%, making it a weak anaesthetic but a strong analgesic, used as an adjuvant.

posts.post_title: Inhalant anaesthetic notable for causing mal…
posts.post_content: Which inhalant anaesthetic is specifically noted to cause malignant hyperthermia in pigs (and other species)?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Halothane

Halothane can cause malignant hyperthermia in pigs and other species, including man.

Correct Option Explanation

Halothane also sensitizes the heart to catecholamines, potentially causing arrhythmia, and depresses cardiac output with bradycardia due to vagal activity.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Isoflurane is explicitly noted to not be used in animals with known susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia, implying it is comparatively safer in this regard, though desflurane also has this tendency.
  • Nitrous oxide is a weak anaesthetic with no described malignant hyperthermia risk in this text.
  • Methoxyflurane is known for polyuric renal dysfunction from fluoride metabolites (leading to its withdrawal), not malignant hyperthermia.
Know More
  • Halothane is about 20% metabolized, with a MAC of 0.85%, and is not irritating to mucous membranes.
  • Desflurane also has a tendency to cause malignant hyperthermia.
  • Isoflurane offers better muscle relaxation than halothane and a wider margin of cardiovascular safety.
  • Chloroform, now discontinued, sensitizes the myocardium to adrenaline causing ventricular fibrillation, and is 20-30 times more potent than ether.

posts.post_title: Basis of Meyer-Overton theory of anaesthetic…
posts.post_content: The Meyer-Overton theory of general anaesthesia proposes that anaesthetic potency correlates with

_aimcq_options.text: Degree of ionization at body pH

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Oil (lipid) solubility of the agent

The Meyer-Overton theory proposes that the higher the oil solubility of an agent, the greater its anaesthetic potency.

Correct Option Explanation

Ether and chloroform fit this hypothesis reasonably well, though the theory has faced several objections since its original proposal.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Molecular weight is not the basis of the Meyer-Overton hypothesis; lipid solubility is the key correlate proposed.
  • Water solubility is essentially the opposite consideration; the theory specifically emphasizes lipid/oil solubility.
  • Degree of ionization is more relevant to local anaesthetic action at the Na+ channel, not the classical general anaesthetic potency theory.
Know More
  • Other historical theories include the colloidal theory, surface tension theory, and permeability theory.
  • The Pauling and Miller theory proposed microcrystal (clathrate) formation reducing conductance.
  • The cell membrane expansion theory explains the phenomenon of pressure reversal of anaesthesia.
  • No single unitary theory of narcosis is currently accepted as fully satisfactory.

posts.post_title: Purpose of cholinolytics like atropine as pr…
posts.post_content: Atropine and glycopyrrolate are used as preanaesthetic medications mainly to

_aimcq_options.text: Inhibit salivary gland secretion and help prevent regurgitation
Directly potentiate the anaesthetic's hypnotic effect
Provide the primary analgesia during surgery

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Inhibit salivary gland secretion and help prevent regurgitation

Cholinolytics like atropine and glycopyrrolate inhibit secretory activity of salivary glands, helping prevent regurgitation during anaesthesia.

Correct Option Explanation

This antisecretory action reduces airway complications from excess salivation and reflex-related regurgitation during the anaesthetic procedure.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cholinolytics are not described as potentiating hypnotic depth; their preanaesthetic role is antisecretory/anti-vagal, not sedative.
  • Cholinolytics provide no analgesia; opioid analgesics are the class used for that purpose among preanaesthetics.
  • Malignant hyperthermia prevention is not a described function of cholinolytic preanaesthetics.
Know More
  • A notable complication of atropine as preanaesthetic is mydriasis.
  • α2 agonists (e.g., xylazine) used as preanaesthetics can cause cardiac depression.
  • Opioids used as preanaesthetics can cause respiratory depression and hypotension.
  • Preanaesthetic classes also include tranquilizer-sedatives (acepromazine, diazepam) and dissociatives (ketamine).

posts.post_title: Combination defining 'neuroleptic analgesia'
posts.post_content: 'Neuroleptic analgesia', a state of deep sedation with analgesia sometimes sufficient for surgical anaesthesia, is produced by combining

_aimcq_options.text: A neuroleptic drug with an opioid derivative
An NSAID with a local anaesthetic
A muscle relaxant with an antihistamine

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A neuroleptic drug with an opioid derivative

Neuroleptic analgesia is produced by combining a neuroleptic (benzodiazepine, butyrophenone or phenothiazine) with an opioid derivative.

Correct Option Explanation

At lower doses this combination produces a preanaesthetic effect; at higher doses it can produce sufficient depression for surgical anaesthesia, as with popular combinations like fentanyl + droperidol.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Combining two inhalant anaesthetics describes balanced inhalation anaesthesia, a different concept from neuroleptic analgesia.
  • An NSAID with a local anaesthetic is not the defined combination for neuroleptic analgesia.
  • A muscle relaxant with an antihistamine does not match the described neuroleptic-opioid combination.
Know More
  • Popular neuroleptic analgesia combinations include fentanyl + droperidol, fentanyl + fluanisone, and etorphine + acepromazine.
  • Neuroleptics used include benzodiazepines, butyrophenones and phenothiazines.
  • An ideal general anaesthetic should be non-irritant, free from disagreeable odour, and allow rapid, smooth induction and recovery.
  • Excretion/metabolism of anaesthetics should be rapid enough to avoid tissue residues in food animals.

posts.post_title: Nitrous oxide's 'second gas effect'
posts.post_content: The 'second gas effect' of nitrous oxide refers to its ability to

_aimcq_options.text: Increase the uptake and alveolar concentration of a concurrently administered anaesthetic like halothane
Reduce the toxicity of any concurrent anaesthetic
Convert into a more potent anaesthetic in the lungs
Decrease pulmonary ventilation to prolong anaesthetic contact time

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Increase the uptake and alveolar concentration of a concurrently administered anaesthetic like halothane

Nitrous oxide's rapid uptake increases the concentration and uptake of a co-administered agent (e.g., halothane, enflurane, or oxygen) — the 'second gas effect'.

Correct Option Explanation

This is distinct from, but related to, the 'concentration effect', where N2O increases its own inhalation and pulmonary ventilation due to direct respiratory stimulation.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The second gas effect is not about reducing toxicity; it concerns uptake dynamics of the co-administered gas.
  • Nitrous oxide is not chemically converted into a more potent agent in the lungs; the effect is a physical uptake phenomenon.
  • N2O actually increases, not decreases, pulmonary ventilation via direct respiratory stimulation.
Know More
  • Nitrous oxide has a very high MAC (over 100%), making it a weak anaesthetic but a strong analgesic, so it is used as an anaesthetic adjuvant.
  • It is kept compressed as a colourless gas at 40 atmospheres.
  • Ether, unlike N2O, can produce nausea and vomiting during inhalation and has slow, unpleasant induction.
  • Chloroform was discontinued due to hepatotoxicity and myocardial sensitization causing sudden death.

posts.post_title: Effect of replacing oxygen with sulphur at c…
posts.post_content: Replacing the oxygen atom at carbon 2 with a sulphur atom in the barbiturate structure produces a thiobarbiturate with

_aimcq_options.text: Increased potency and shorter duration of action
Decreased potency and longer duration of action
No change in any pharmacological property

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Increased potency and shorter duration of action

Sulphur substitution at carbon 2 increases potency and instability, shortening the compound's duration of action (thiobarbiturates).

Correct Option Explanation

This structure-activity relationship explains why ultra-short-acting agents like thiopental (a thiobarbiturate) are used for rapid induction of anaesthesia.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sulphur substitution increases, rather than decreases, potency, and shortens rather than lengthens duration.
  • Complete loss of hypnotic activity is caused instead by replacing the carbon-2 oxygen with an HN= group, not sulphur.
  • The change produces significant, well-documented alterations, not 'no change'.
Know More
  • Barbiturates with oxygen at carbon 2 are called oxybarbiturates; those with sulphur are thiobarbiturates.
  • Both hydrogen atoms on carbon 5 must be replaced by alkyl/aryl groups for hypnotic activity.
  • Adding an alkyl group to an N-atom (position 1 or 3) increases anaesthetic potency and stimulates the CNS; substitution at both N-atoms produces a convulsant.
  • Unsaturated, long carbon chains are more readily oxidized and hence shorter acting; short, straight chains are more stable and longer acting.

posts.post_title: Species-specific sensitivity to barbiturate …
posts.post_content: Regarding barbiturate toxicity, which statement is accurate?

_aimcq_options.text: Cats are more sensitive to respiratory depression, dogs to cardiovascular depression
Dogs are more sensitive to respiratory depression, cats to cardiovascular depression
Both species show identical sensitivity patterns
Neither species shows any barbiturate-related organ sensitivity

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cats are more sensitive to respiratory depression, dogs to cardiovascular depression

Cats are sensitive to the respiratory depression, and dogs to the cardiovascular depression, of barbiturates.

Correct Option Explanation

This species-specific pattern is clinically important for dosing and monitoring priorities during barbiturate anaesthesia in these two common companion species.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • This option reverses the actual documented species-sensitivity pattern.
  • The two species show distinct, not identical, sensitivity patterns as specifically documented.
  • There is a described species-specific sensitivity pattern; this is not absent.
Know More
  • The antidote for barbiturate overdose is bemegride, a CNS stimulant.
  • Barbiturates are known inducers of microsomal enzymes, inducing their own metabolism and causing tolerance.
  • Barbiturates cross the placenta and depress fetal respiration, making them not preferred for caesarean sections.
  • Repeated barbiturate doses cause cumulation due to storage in adipose tissue with slow redistribution back into circulation.

posts.post_title: Most popular thiobarbiturate for induction o…
posts.post_content: Which thiobarbiturate is described as the most popular agent for induction of anaesthesia, followed by maintenance with inhalational agents?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Thiopental sodium

Thiopental sodium is the most popular intravenous barbiturate, used for induction followed by maintenance with inhalational agents.

Correct Option Explanation

Its single-dose effect lasts 10-15 minutes, but maintenance dosing is not recommended since it accumulates in tissues with repeated administration.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Methohexital sodium, though not a true thiobarbiturate, is 2-3 times more potent with faster recovery but can cause tremors/convulsions on recovery, making it less the described 'most popular' choice.
  • Pentobarbital sodium was widely used historically but is now used mainly for control of convulsions, not primary induction.
  • Thiamylal sodium is ultra-short acting but is described as not used clinically.
Know More
  • Thiopental is typically given as a 2.5% solution in dogs, at 20-25 mg/kg in non-premedicated animals.
  • If xylazine is used as premedication, the thiopental dose is decreased by 75-90%.
  • Rapid injection commonly causes apnea; the dose should be given slowly over 30-40 seconds.
  • Thiopental causes severe sloughing/necrosis if injected perivascularly.

posts.post_title: Mechanism of propofol's anaesthetic action
posts.post_content: Propofol produces its anaesthetic effect mainly by

_aimcq_options.text: Enhancing GABA's inhibitory effects via a pathway distinct from benzodiazepines

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Enhancing GABA's inhibitory effects via a pathway distinct from benzodiazepines

Propofol enhances the inhibitory effects of GABA through a pathway different from that used by benzodiazepines.

Correct Option Explanation

It is highly lipid soluble, rapidly taken up by the CNS after IV injection, and then rapidly redistributed, giving it a high volume of distribution and rapid recovery profile.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Propofol's described mechanism is GABAergic, not calcium channel blockade.
  • Propofol has no described action on acetylcholinesterase in this material.
  • NMDA receptor antagonism describes ketamine's mechanism, not propofol's GABA-potentiating action.
Know More
  • Propofol is chemically 2,6-diisopropylphenol, formulated as an oily emulsion with soybean oil, glycerol and egg lecithin.
  • It may cause mild hypotension and can sensitize the heart to adrenaline-induced arrhythmia.
  • It is metabolized in the liver and lungs to glucuronides and sulfates.
  • Typical dosing is 5-7 mg/kg in dogs and 5-8 mg/kg in cats, reducible with tranquilizer premedication.

posts.post_title: Reason Saffan (Althesin) is contraindicated …
posts.post_content: Saffan (Althesin), a steroid anaesthetic combination, is contraindicated in dogs because

_aimcq_options.text: It has a very narrow, dangerous therapeutic index
It causes severe hepatotoxicity unique to dogs
It cannot cross the blood-brain barrier in dogs

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Its vehicle causes histamine release

Saffan is contraindicated in dogs due to histamine release by the vehicle used in its formulation.

Correct Option Explanation

Despite this species-specific limitation, Saffan otherwise has a high therapeutic index, wide margin of safety, and good muscle relaxation with mild cardiovascular/respiratory depression.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Saffan actually has a high therapeutic index with a wide margin of safety, not a narrow one.
  • Hepatotoxicity is not the documented reason for its canine contraindication; histamine release from the vehicle is.
  • Saffan does cross the blood-brain barrier to exert its anaesthetic effect; that is not the reason for the contraindication.
Know More
  • Saffan is a combination of 9 mg alphaxolone + 3 mg alphadolone, both steroids.
  • It can be given both intravenously or intramuscularly, typically at 5-6 mg/kg.
  • It causes no irritation on accidental escape into subcutaneous tissue, unlike thiopental.
  • Metomidate, a non-barbiturate imidazole anaesthetic, was developed as a hypnotic specifically for pigs.

posts.post_title: Order of CNS depression in dissociative anae…
posts.post_content: Dissociative anaesthetics produce their characteristic state by

_aimcq_options.text: Depressing the cerebral cortex before causing medullary depression
Depressing the medulla before affecting the cortex
Uniformly depressing the entire CNS at once

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Depressing the cerebral cortex before causing medullary depression

Dissociative anaesthetics depress the cerebral cortex before causing medullary depression.

Correct Option Explanation

This produces a state combining profound somatic analgesia with only a light plane of unconsciousness, giving the characteristic 'dissociation' from the environment.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The order is cortex first, then medulla — the reverse sequence is not the described mechanism.
  • Dissociatives are not described as acting only on the spinal cord; their key effect is cortical.
  • The action is sequential (cortex before medulla), not uniform across the entire CNS.
Know More
  • Pharyngeal, laryngeal, corneal and pedal reflexes remain relatively unimpaired, and the eyes stay open.
  • Somatic analgesia is good, but visceral analgesia is poor with dissociative anaesthetics.
  • Catalepsy with rigidity and partial limb extension is a characteristic feature.
  • Dissociative anaesthetics are contraindicated in head trauma, space-occupying brain lesions, and corneal ulcers/laceration.

posts.post_title: Ketamine's primary receptor mechanism
posts.post_content: Ketamine produces its dissociative anaesthetic and analgesic effects mainly by

_aimcq_options.text: Inhibiting glutamate/NMDA receptors, with analgesia partly through opioid receptors

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Inhibiting glutamate/NMDA receptors, with analgesia partly through opioid receptors

Ketamine inhibits glutamate (NMDA) receptors, and its analgesia is achieved partly through opioid receptors.

Correct Option Explanation

It acts primarily on the cortex, and this distinct receptor mechanism differentiates it from GABA-A potentiating agents like barbiturates and benzodiazepines.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • GABA-A potentiation is the mechanism of barbiturates, benzodiazepines and propofol, not ketamine.
  • Ketamine's mechanism is not primarily peripheral nicotinic receptor blockade.
  • Central alpha-2 stimulation describes agents like xylazine, sometimes co-administered with ketamine but not ketamine's own mechanism.
Know More
  • Ketamine's induction is rapid, though slower than thiopental's.
  • Its major metabolite, norketamine, is hypnotic and can cause long-standing drowsiness/prolonged recovery in large doses.
  • Ketamine centrally stimulates the sympathetic system, causing tachycardia and high blood pressure.
  • It is popularly combined with xylazine (or xylazine-diazepam) for improved muscle relaxation.

posts.post_title: Special concern with ketamine use in cats
posts.post_content: A particular concern with ketamine use in cats is that they

_aimcq_options.text: May be thrown into convulsions if subjected to noise or other disturbances
Develop malignant hyperthermia uniquely to this drug
Show no analgesic response to ketamine

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: May be thrown into convulsions if subjected to noise or other disturbances

In cats, ketamine anaesthesia carries the risk that the animal may be thrown into convulsions if subjected to noise or other disturbances.

Correct Option Explanation

This makes a quiet recovery environment important when ketamine is used in feline patients.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Malignant hyperthermia with ketamine specifically in cats is not a documented issue in this text (that risk is linked to halothane/desflurane in pigs).
  • Cats do metabolize ketamine; the concern described is about seizure risk from external stimuli, not an inability to metabolize it.
  • Ketamine does produce good analgesia in cats as in other species; that is not the specific documented concern.
Know More
  • Ketamine causes corneal drying due to open eyes during anaesthesia, requiring bland ophthalmic ointment.
  • Judging the depth of anaesthesia with ketamine is difficult, risking overdosing by inexperienced users.
  • Combining ketamine with an alpha-2 agonist may lead to vomition in some cases.
  • Tiletamine is more potent, longer acting, and has greater side effects than ketamine; it is often combined with zolazepam.

posts.post_title: Acepromazine's adverse effect on the male re…
posts.post_content: Acepromazine can adversely affect the reproductive market value of stallions and bulls by causing

_aimcq_options.text: Paralysis of the retractor penis muscle, resulting in priapism

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Paralysis of the retractor penis muscle, resulting in priapism

Acepromazine causes paralysis of the retractor penis muscle, resulting in priapism and penile paralysis in stallions and bulls.

Correct Option Explanation

This complication can affect their market/breeding value, an important consideration before using acepromazine in breeding animals.

  • 'Complete testicular atrophy' is not the documented mechanism; the effect described is muscular paralysis causing priapism.
  • 'Irreversible infertility from testicular necrosis' overstates and mischaracterizes the actual documented penile paralysis effect.

Know More
  • Acepromazine is a good sedative lasting 4-6 hours (longer in dogs), sometimes with initial excitement.

  • Phenothiazines act broadly on dopamine, norepinephrine, 5-HT and histamine receptors.

posts.post_title: Popular sedative for pigs among butyrophenon…
posts.post_content: Which butyrophenone tranquilizer is a popular sedative specifically used in pigs, with the animal ideally undisturbed for 20 minutes post-injection?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Azaperone

Azaperone is a popular sedative in pigs; the animal should not be disturbed for 20 minutes after injection, as this may cause excitation.

Correct Option Explanation

It is used to prevent fighting, avoid piglet rejection by mothers, and for fostering, but it is not recommended in horses due to a tendency to cause excitement in that species.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Haloperidol is primarily a human antipsychotic drug, not the described pig sedative.
  • Droperidol's main use is in neuroleptanalgesia combinations (e.g., with fentanyl), not specifically as the described pig sedative.
  • Fluanisone is likewise used in neuroleptanalgesia combinations, not as the primary pig sedative described.
Know More
  • Butyrophenones cause central blockade of DA and NE actions, are potent antiemetics, and reduce motor activity causing catalepsy.
  • Butyrophenones have little cardiovascular or respiratory effect.
  • Popular neuroleptanalgesia combinations include droperidol + fentanyl or with benzodiazepines.
  • In humans, butyrophenones may cause unusual behavioural side effects.

posts.post_title: Benzodiazepine receptor binding site relativ…
posts.post_content: Benzodiazepines act on the GABA-gated Cl- channel at a site that is

_aimcq_options.text: Different from that used by barbiturates
Identical to the barbiturate binding site
Located on a completely separate ion channel unrelated to GABA

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Different from that used by barbiturates

Benzodiazepines act at a specific benzodiazepine receptor site, different from the site used by barbiturates on the same GABA-gated Cl- channel.

Correct Option Explanation

This is an important example of a receptor site for a non-endogenous drug, distinguishing benzodiazepines' pharmacology from barbiturates despite both ultimately affecting the same chloride channel complex.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The site is explicitly described as different from, not identical to, the barbiturate site.
  • Benzodiazepines act on the same GABA-gated Cl- channel complex, not an unrelated channel.
  • Benzodiazepines are not described as acting at nicotinic receptors; their action is GABAergic.
Know More
  • Chlordiazepoxide (1955) was the first benzodiazepine discovered.
  • Benzodiazepines act on the limbic system and produce muscle relaxation via inhibition of spinal neurons.
  • Flumazenil is the benzodiazepine antagonist used to reverse benzodiazepine toxicity.
  • Benzodiazepines can act as appetite stimulants in children and animals.

posts.post_title: Species most resistant to xylazine, requirin…
posts.post_content: Which species is most resistant to xylazine, requiring 20-30 times the ruminant dose, and in which the drug is therefore rarely used?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Swine

Swine are very resistant to xylazine, requiring 20-30 times the ruminant dose, so xylazine is rarely used in this species.

Correct Option Explanation

This is the opposite extreme from ruminants, which are extremely sensitive to xylazine's effects, requiring only 1/10 the equine dose.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Ruminants are the most sensitive, not resistant, species — the opposite of the described dosing pattern.
  • Horses serve as the reference dose in comparisons but are not described as the most resistant species.
  • Cats show sedation with xylazine and are notably used for its emetic effect, not described as highly resistant like swine.
Know More
  • Xylazine causes visceral analgesia in horses better than meperidine, butorphanol, or pentazocine.
  • In cats, xylazine is used as an emetic agent in poisoning cases, producing emesis within 3-5 minutes.
  • In cattle, xylazine may cause polyuria, thought to be from decreased ADH release/activity.
  • In ruminants, xylazine may abolish ruminal movements, leading to tympany and ruminal distension.

posts.post_title: Opioid receptor mediating spinally-originate…
posts.post_content: Which opioid receptor subtype is primarily responsible for analgesia of spinal origin, along with miosis and sedation?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Kappa (κ)

Kappa receptors are responsible for spinally-originated analgesia, miosis and sedation.

Correct Option Explanation

Morphine's characteristic pinpoint pupil (miosis) results from kappa-receptor mediated stimulation of the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Mu receptors give rise to analgesia and sedation above and in the spinal cord, along with euphoria, respiratory depression and physical dependence — a distinct profile from kappa.
  • Delta receptors modulate emotional behaviour and immunomodulation, and may contribute to analgesia, but are not specifically credited with miosis.
  • Sigma receptors mediate adverse effects like dysphoria, hallucinations and respiratory stimulation, and if blocked, mydriasis (opposite of miosis) can result via sigma effect.
Know More
  • All opioid receptors are linked via G-protein to inhibition of adenylate cyclase and opening of K+ channels (hyperpolarization).
  • Sigma receptors are no longer recognized as a truly separate opioid receptor class.
  • Pure agonists have high affinity for delta and kappa sites.
  • High doses of many opioids cause convulsions via stimulation at the sigma receptor.

posts.post_title: Endogenous opioid most implicated in nocicep…
posts.post_content: Which family of endogenous opioids is believed to play the greatest role in modulating nociception during stress and acupuncture?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Beta endorphins

Beta endorphins most likely play the greatest role in modulation of nociception during stress and acupuncture.

Correct Option Explanation

They are found in the pituitary gland, hypothalamus, small intestine, placenta and plasma, consistent with a systemic stress-response role.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Enkephalins act as inhibitory neurotransmitters, modulating substance P release, and are specifically implicated in acupuncture-mediated analgesia rather than the stress-response role attributed to beta endorphins.
  • Dynorphins are believed most important in spinal cord nociception via kappa receptor activation, a different described role.
  • Substance P is a pain-transmitting peptide, not an endogenous opioid, and its release is modulated by enkephalins rather than being an opioid itself.
Know More
  • Enkephalins are widely distributed in CNS areas receiving afferent nociceptive information, and also occur in the PNS, GI tract and plasma.
  • Dynorphins function primarily as neuromodulators through mu, kappa and delta receptor interaction.
  • The three endogenous opioid families are beta endorphins, enkephalins and dynorphins.
  • Species differences exist in opioid receptor number, location, specificity and selectivity, affecting drug response.

posts.post_title: Effect of morphine on the biliary tract
posts.post_content: Morphine's effect on the biliary tract is to

_aimcq_options.text: Markedly increase pressure via contraction of the sphincter of Oddi
Relax the sphincter of Oddi, decreasing biliary pressure
Have no significant effect on biliary pressure
Cause biliary tract atony and dilation

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Markedly increase pressure via contraction of the sphincter of Oddi

Morphine causes a marked increase in biliary tract pressure due to contraction of the sphincter of Oddi.

Correct Option Explanation

This effect parallels morphine's action on other smooth muscle sphincters, such as increased detrusor muscle tone in the urinary bladder leading to urinary retention.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Morphine contracts, rather than relaxes, the sphincter of Oddi, increasing rather than decreasing biliary pressure.
  • Morphine has a clear, significant effect on biliary pressure, not 'no significant effect'.
  • Morphine causes increased tone/spasm, not atony and dilation, of biliary smooth muscle.
Know More
  • Morphine increases tone and decreases motility in the GI tract, leading to constipation.
  • It also increases detrusor muscle tone, causing urinary urgency but urinary retention due to sphincter closure.
  • Morphine can cause bronchoconstriction, making it contraindicated in asthmatics, especially before surgery.
  • Morphine causes histamine release and suppression of central adrenergic tone, contributing to vasodilatation.

posts.post_title: Neuroendocrine hormone unaffected by morphine
posts.post_content: Among the pituitary hormones affected by morphine, which one remains unaffected?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)

Morphine decreases LH, FSH, ACTH and beta endorphin levels, but TSH is unaffected.

Correct Option Explanation

This selective neuroendocrine effect arises because morphine inhibits GnRH and CRF release, which govern the gonadal and adrenal axes, but does not similarly suppress the thyrotropic axis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • LH is decreased by morphine, secondary to inhibited GnRH release, not unaffected.
  • FSH is also decreased by morphine via the same GnRH suppression mechanism.
  • ACTH is decreased by morphine via inhibited CRF release, not left unaffected.
Know More
  • Morphine inhibits release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) and corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF).
  • Circulating beta endorphin levels are also decreased alongside LH, FSH and ACTH.
  • Morphine can prolong labour via effects on uterine contraction.
  • The half-life of morphine is about 2.5 to 3 hours, and it does not persist in body tissue long-term.

posts.post_title: Most lipophilic opioid, allowing rapid blood…
posts.post_content: Which opioid is the most lipophilic, allowing it to cross the blood-brain barrier rapidly and contributing to its higher potency than morphine?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Heroin (diacetylmorphine)

Heroin is the most lipophilic of all opioids, crossing the blood-brain barrier rapidly, unlike morphine which crosses slowly.

Correct Option Explanation

Heroin is hydrolyzed to monoacetylmorphine then to morphine, delivering more active drug to the brain and making it 3-4 times more potent than morphine.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Morphine is explicitly described as the least lipophilic of all opioids, the opposite extreme from heroin.
  • Codeine has about one-tenth the analgesic potency of morphine, and is not noted for high lipophilicity.
  • Meperidine has addictive liability and potency similar to morphine, but is not described as the most lipophilic opioid.
Know More
  • Heroin's withdrawal symptoms are similar to but more intense than morphine's (rebound effect, mydriasis, diarrhoea, vasoconstriction, dysphoria).
  • Codeine results from substituting the hydroxyl at position 3 with a methyl group.
  • Heroin results from acetyl group substitution at both the 3 and 6 hydroxy positions.
  • Hydromorphone, with a ketone substitution at the 6-hydroxyl position, is more sedative and less euphoric than morphine, and does not produce miosis.

posts.post_title: Dangerous drug interaction between meperidin…
posts.post_content: Concurrent use of meperidine and MAO inhibitors can result in

_aimcq_options.text: Severe excitation, rigidity, hypertension and respiratory depression
Complete loss of analgesic effect with no other symptoms
Rapid onset sedation with mild hypotension
Enhanced antitussive effect with no other change

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Severe excitation, rigidity, hypertension and respiratory depression

Meperidine combined with MAO inhibitors can cause severe, immediate reactions including excitation, rigidity, hypertension and severe respiratory depression.

Correct Option Explanation

This dangerous interaction is a specific concern with meperidine among opioids and MAO inhibitor combinations, distinct from milder interactions seen with other CNS depressant combinations.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The interaction is severe and dangerous, not a simple loss of analgesic effect without other symptoms.
  • The reaction is characterized by excitation/hypertension, not sedation with mild hypotension.
  • There is no described enhanced antitussive benefit; the interaction is a serious adverse reaction.
Know More
  • Opioids with phenothiazines produce additive CNS depression and greater orthostatic hypotension.
  • Opioids with tricyclic antidepressants produce increased hypotension.
  • Opioids with barbiturates show increased clearance of opioids.
  • Opioids with amphetamine show enhanced analgesic effect.

posts.post_title: Extremely potent opioid used for immobilizin…
posts.post_content: Which extremely potent opioid, requiring only about 0.5 mg per 500 kg body weight, is used to sedate and immobilize large animals via dart guns?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Etorphine

Etorphine is extremely potent, needing a very small dose (about 0.5 mg per 500 kg) sufficient to sedate and anaesthetize large animals via dart guns.

Correct Option Explanation

It is very long-acting and is used in the product Immobilon for neuroleptanalgesia, typically combined with acepromazine or methotrimeprazine.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Fentanyl is about 50 times as potent as morphine and short-acting (30-45 min), used in neuroleptanalgesia and postoperative patches, but is not the drug described for large-animal dart immobilization at this extreme potency.
  • Buprenorphine is a partial agonist with a slower onset, longer duration, and a bell-shaped analgesic dose-response curve, not the described dart-gun agent.
  • Pentazocine is a standard prescription analgesic, not noted for the extreme potency and dart-gun immobilization use described for etorphine.
Know More
  • Naloxone is used to reverse etorphine and other opioid toxicity or delayed sedation.
  • Diphenoxylate is used as an antidiarrhoeal opioid derivative.
  • Codeine is primarily used as a cough suppressant.
  • Methadone is a synthetic agonist roughly equipotent to morphine, used in horses and dogs.

posts.post_title: Species groups typically showing mydriasis v…
posts.post_content: Regarding species differences in pupillary response to opioids, which statement is correct?

_aimcq_options.text: Rabbits, canines and primates show miosis; felines and other species show mydriasis
All species universally show miosis regardless of type
Cats show miosis while dogs show mydriasis
Pupillary response to opioids does not vary by species

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rabbits, canines and primates show miosis; felines and other species show mydriasis

Rabbits, canines and primates exhibit miosis with opioids, while felines and other species exhibit mydriasis.

Correct Option Explanation

This species-dependent pupillary response is an important clinical sign to interpret correctly when assessing opioid effects across different veterinary patients.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Pupillary response is not universal; it varies distinctly by species as described.
  • This statement reverses the actual documented pattern — dogs show miosis, cats show mydriasis, not the other way around.
  • There is a well-documented species-dependent variation in pupillary response, contrary to 'does not vary'.
Know More
  • Equine, bovine, caprine, ovine, porcine and feline patients may show CNS stimulation rather than depression with opioids.
  • Dogs may show initial defecation then decreased GI motility/constipation, and initial respiratory stimulation before typical depression.
  • Dogs exhibit coronary vasoconstriction with opiates, the opposite effect seen in humans.
  • Dogs and rabbits typically show hypothermia, while cattle, goats, horses and cats typically show hyperthermia with opiates.

posts.post_title: Naltrexone's clinical advantage over naloxon…
posts.post_content: Naltrexone is preferred over naloxone for longer-term management of opioid dependence because it

_aimcq_options.text: Is orally active with a long duration, blocking heroin's effects for up to 24 hours per dose
Has stronger analgesic activity of its own
Works only when injected intravenously every few minutes
Reverses respiratory depression faster than naloxone in acute overdose

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Is orally active with a long duration, blocking heroin's effects for up to 24 hours per dose

Naltrexone is similar to naloxone but can be given orally with a long duration, and a single dose blocks heroin's effects for 24 hours.

Correct Option Explanation

Once a patient is stabilized (often initially with naloxone for emergency treatment), giving naltrexone means the patient gets no euphoric effect from heroin, providing negative reinforcement to help them stop using it.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Naltrexone, like naloxone, has no analgesic activity of its own; both are pure antagonists.
  • Naltrexone's advantage is specifically its oral route, not a requirement for frequent IV injection (that limitation is more relevant to naloxone's short duration).
