Know More
  • Naloxone is a competitive antagonist at mu, kappa and sigma receptors, displacing opioids from their receptor sites.
  • Naloxone can precipitate withdrawal in a person dependent on heroin.
  • Naltrexone is FDA approved and is also used in alcohol rehabilitation treatment.
  • Both naloxone and naltrexone are metabolized via glucuronic acid conjugation like morphine.

posts.post_title: Effect of neostigmine on competitive versus …
posts.post_content: Regarding the effect of neostigmine on neuromuscular blockade, which statement is correct?

_aimcq_options.text: Neostigmine antagonizes competitive (non-depolarizing) block but has no effect on depolarizing block
Neostigmine antagonizes both types of block equally
Neostigmine worsens competitive block but reverses depolarizing block
Neostigmine has no effect on either type of blockade

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Neostigmine antagonizes competitive (non-depolarizing) block but has no effect on depolarizing block

Neostigmine antagonizes/reverses competitive blockade (e.g., d-tubocurarine) but has no effect on depolarizing block (e.g., succinylcholine).

Correct Option Explanation

By inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, neostigmine raises ACh levels, which can outcompete a competitive antagonist at the receptor, but cannot reverse the persistent depolarization mechanism of depolarizing blockers.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Neostigmine's effect is selective, not equal across both mechanistically distinct blocker types.
  • Neostigmine does not worsen competitive block; it reverses it — this statement inverts the actual relationship.
  • Neostigmine does have a clear, clinically important effect on competitive blockers, contrary to 'no effect on either'.
Know More
  • Inhalation anaesthetics (like ether) act synergistically with competitive blockers but have no described synergy with depolarizing blockers.
  • Species sensitivity to competitive blockers follows rat > rabbit > cat, while for depolarizing blockers it is cat > rabbit > rat.
  • Paralysis with competitive blockers is flaccid in both humans and chicks; depolarizing blockers cause flaccidity in humans but spastic paralysis in chicks.
  • Order of paralysis differs: competitive blockers affect fingers-eyes-limbs-neck-face-trunk-intercostals; depolarizing blockers affect neck-limbs-face-jaw-eyes-pharynx-trunk-intercostals.

posts.post_title: Mechanism explaining why succinylcholine is …
posts.post_content: In patients with pseudocholinesterase deficiency, succinylcholine can cause prolonged paralysis and apnoea because

_aimcq_options.text: Delayed hydrolysis allows the drug to persist and induce Phase II (desensitization) blockade
The drug is instead metabolized rapidly by an alternate pathway causing overdose
Pseudocholinesterase deficiency increases the drug's affinity for nicotinic receptors
The deficiency causes immediate anaphylaxis rather than prolonged paralysis

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Delayed hydrolysis allows the drug to persist and induce Phase II (desensitization) blockade

With pseudocholinesterase deficiency, succinylcholine is not rapidly hydrolyzed, so it persists and can transition into Phase II blockade from receptor desensitization, causing muscle paralysis and apnoea lasting hours.

Correct Option Explanation

Normally, succinylcholine is rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma pseudocholinesterase to succinylmonocholine and then succinic acid and choline, limiting its duration of action.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • There is no alternate rapid metabolic pathway described; the problem is precisely the lack of normal hydrolysis.
  • Pseudocholinesterase deficiency affects drug metabolism, not receptor affinity, which is unrelated to this enzyme.
  • The described complication is prolonged paralysis/apnoea, not an anaphylactic reaction.
Know More
  • Depolarizing blockade has two phases: Phase I (rapid onset, persistent depolarization) and Phase II (slow onset, receptor desensitization).
  • Succinylcholine is the most commonly used relaxant for passing an endotracheal tube, giving rapid, predictable, complete paralysis with spontaneous recovery in about 5 minutes normally.
  • Thiopentone and succinylcholine react chemically and should not be mixed in the same syringe.
  • In digitalized patients, succinylcholine can cause dangerous cardiac arrhythmias or arrest.

posts.post_title: Alkaloid source of d-tubocurarine and its ch…
posts.post_content: d-Tubocurarine, obtained from Chondrodendron tomentosum, is particularly noted for causing

_aimcq_options.text: Significant fall in blood pressure due to ganglionic blockade and histamine release
Marked hypertension due to sympathetic stimulation
No cardiovascular effect at any dose
Selective bradycardia without change in blood pressure

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Significant fall in blood pressure due to ganglionic blockade and histamine release

d-Tubocurarine causes a significant fall in blood pressure due to ganglionic blockade, prominent histamine release, and reduced venous return.

Correct Option Explanation

This histamine-release and hypotensive profile, along with a long duration of action, has led to it being largely superseded by newer agents with better cardiovascular stability.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • d-Tubocurarine causes a fall, not a rise, in blood pressure — the opposite of hypertension.
  • It has a clear, well-documented cardiovascular effect, not 'no effect'.
  • Its effect involves hypotension, not isolated bradycardia without BP change.
Know More
  • Gallamine triethiodide, unlike d-tubocurarine, produces marked tachycardia due to vagal muscarinic blockade.
  • Pancuronium is a synthetic steroidal compound, 5 times more potent than d-tubocurarine, with good cardiovascular stability.
  • Vecuronium, a close congener of pancuronium, has the shortest duration and even better cardiovascular stability.
  • Atracurium is unique for undergoing spontaneous non-enzymatic degradation in plasma.

posts.post_title: Mechanism distinguishing centrally acting mu…
posts.post_content: Unlike peripheral neuromuscular blockers, centrally and directly acting muscle relaxants primarily work by

_aimcq_options.text: Uncoupling contraction from depolarization without affecting the end-plate potential
Competitively blocking nicotinic receptors at the motor end-plate
Causing persistent depolarization of the muscle membrane
Directly hydrolyzing acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Uncoupling contraction from depolarization without affecting the end-plate potential

Centrally/directly acting relaxants do not affect neuromuscular transmission or the end-plate potential; instead they uncouple contraction from depolarization of the muscle membrane.

Correct Option Explanation

This works by reducing depolarization-triggered calcium ion release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, with fast-contracting twitch muscles affected more than slow-contracting ones.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Competitive nicotinic receptor blockade describes peripherally acting non-depolarizing blockers like d-tubocurarine, not centrally acting relaxants.
  • Persistent depolarization describes the mechanism of depolarizing blockers like succinylcholine, an entirely different drug class.
  • Central/direct muscle relaxants have no described action on acetylcholine hydrolysis; their site of action is different.
Know More
  • Centrally acting relaxants reduce skeletal muscle tone via selective action in the cerebrospinal axis without altering consciousness.
  • They do not have sedative action in their classical description and have no effect on neuromuscular transmission.
  • They reduce rigidity, spasticity and hyperreflexia.
  • They can be given orally or parenterally, unlike peripheral blockers which are given IV only.

posts.post_title: Drug of choice for malignant hyperthermia
posts.post_content: Which centrally acting muscle relaxant is the drug of choice for treating malignant hyperthermia?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Dantrolene

Dantrolene is the drug of choice for malignant hyperthermia, caused by persistent calcium ion release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in genetically susceptible individuals exposed to fluorinated anaesthetics or ACh.

Correct Option Explanation

Dantrolene is orally absorbed, penetrates the blood-brain barrier (producing sedation), is metabolized in the liver and excreted by the kidney, and reduces spasticity in upper motor neuron disorders.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Mephenesin is known as an internuncial neurone blocking agent, not specifically the malignant hyperthermia treatment.
  • Baclofen is a GABA derivative used as a muscle relaxant, but is not the drug of choice for malignant hyperthermia in this text.
  • Diazepam, a benzodiazepine, is used for spastic conditions but is not the specific malignant hyperthermia drug.
Know More
  • Dantrolene's adverse effects include muscle weakness, sedation, malaise and light-headedness.
  • Mephenesin's primary action is in the spinal internuncial neurone, which modulates reflexes maintaining muscle tone.
  • Other mephenesin-group relaxants include carisoprodol, chlorzoxazone, chlormezanone, methocarbamol.
  • Centrally acting muscle relaxants are used for acute muscle spasms, torticollis, lumbago, backache and tetanus.

posts.post_title: First and preferred anticonvulsant drug in d…
posts.post_content: Which drug, the first used as an antiepileptic, remains the drug of choice for long-term seizure control in dogs and cats?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Phenobarbitone

Phenobarbitone was the first drug used as an antiepileptic and remains the drug of choice in dogs and cats.

Correct Option Explanation

It has a slow onset but long duration of action, is highly protein bound, is a potent inducer of liver microsomal enzymes, and is administered once daily.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Diazepam is the drug of choice specifically for status epilepticus (acute control), not the first-choice drug for chronic maintenance therapy.
  • Diphenylhydantoin has limited clinical value due to poor absorption and high hepatotoxicity, and is used IV in status epilepticus, not as the preferred maintenance drug.
  • Trimethadione is not commonly used because of photophobia side effects seen (as in distemper), and is not the preferred choice.
Know More
  • Primidone, the 2-deoxy analogue of phenobarbitone, is not preferred due to reported hepatotoxicity.
  • Valproic acid is not used in dogs due to its short half-life in this species.
  • Carbamazepine elimination is too rapid in dogs, limiting its usefulness.
  • Drugs contraindicated in epileptic patients include reserpine, phenothiazines, butyrophenones and morphine.

posts.post_title: Drug of choice specifically for status epile…
posts.post_content: Which drug is the drug of choice for status epilepticus, acting by enhancing GABA's inhibitory effects with rapid CNS penetration?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Diazepam

Diazepam is the drug of choice in status epilepticus, enhancing GABA's inhibitory effects with rapid CNS penetration.

Correct Option Explanation

It has minimal depressant action on the cardiovascular and respiratory systems, making it particularly suitable for acute emergency control of seizures, though metabolic tolerance can occur readily.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Phenobarbitone has a slow onset, making it unsuitable for the rapid control needed in status epilepticus, despite being preferred for chronic maintenance.
  • Trimethadione is not commonly used due to its photophobia side effect, and is not designated for status epilepticus.
  • Carbamazepine is eliminated too rapidly in dogs to be clinically useful, and is not the status epilepticus drug of choice.
Know More
  • Clonazepam, unlike diazepam, does not develop metabolic tolerance, but shows decreased effectiveness with continuous treatment.
  • Bromides (ammonium, potassium, sodium) are also used to control convulsions.
  • Anticonvulsants generally enhancing GABA-Cl- channel inhibition include benzodiazepines, barbiturates, gabapentin and bromides.
  • Phenytoin, carbamazepine and zonisamide act by decreasing sodium channel-based action potential generation.

posts.post_title: Definition of 'therapeutic doping' in racing…
posts.post_content: 'Therapeutic doping' in racing animals is best described as

_aimcq_options.text: Using a drug to restore an animal's speed to its normal level after illness or injury
Administering a stimulant to artificially boost performance above normal
Giving a depressant to intentionally slow the animal down
The accidental administration of a prohibited substance

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Using a drug to restore an animal's speed to its normal level after illness or injury

'Therapeutic doping' involves using a drug to restore an animal's performance to its normal level after deterioration from illness or accident, not to artificially boost it beyond normal.

Correct Option Explanation

Examples include procaine to mitigate lameness, phenylbutazone for arthritis, or a tranquilizer to calm an obstreperous animal — all aimed at restoring rather than enhancing baseline performance.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Boosting performance above normal values describes 'doping to win', a distinct category from therapeutic doping.
  • Intentionally slowing an animal describes 'doping to lose', regarded as an 'outside job', not therapeutic doping.
  • Unintentional administration of a prohibited substance describes 'accidental doping', a separate category entirely.
Know More
  • Both doping to win and therapeutic doping are regarded as 'inside jobs', carried out by the trainer or someone in their employ.
  • 'Doping to win' includes stimulants (e.g., caffeine, amphetamine) given shortly before a race, or tonics (vitamins, hormones, anabolic steroids) given continuously.
  • Nicotine is given as an example of a substance causing accidental doping.
  • Drugs commonly used for doping to lose include tranquilizers, xylazine, morphine and barbiturates.

posts.post_title: AVMA-preferred method of euthanasia for smal…
posts.post_content: According to the AVMA panel on euthanasia, which class of drug is the 'preferred method' for euthanasia of small animals?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Barbiturates

The AVMA panel on euthanasia states that barbiturates are the preferred method of euthanasia for small animals.

Correct Option Explanation

Most euthanasia agents contain pentobarbitone for its cardiovascular and respiratory depressant actions, sometimes combined with a drug that induces arrhythmias to hasten death.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Opioids are not designated as the AVMA-preferred euthanasia agent class in this text.
  • Neuromuscular blockers alone are not the preferred euthanasia method, since they cause paralysis without necessarily causing the cardiovascular/respiratory depression needed for humane death.
  • Inhalant anaesthetics are not designated as the preferred small-animal euthanasia method in this text.
Know More
  • An ataractic (e.g., acepromazine or diazepam) may be given before pentobarbitone, especially if the animal is in pain or agitated.
  • Convulsive seizures involve spastic muscle movement with unconsciousness.
  • Seizure pathogenesis involves altered excitation-inhibition balance and the paroxysmal shift phenomenon.
  • An ideal maintenance antiepileptic drug should have long duration, minimal tolerance, and good oral/CNS penetration.

posts.post_title: Strychnine's mechanism of convulsant action
posts.post_content: Strychnine, obtained from Strychnos nuxvomica, produces convulsions by

_aimcq_options.text: Inhibiting glycine, a spinal cord inhibitory neurotransmitter
Directly stimulating nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Inhibiting glycine, a spinal cord inhibitory neurotransmitter

Strychnine inhibits glycine, a spinal cord neurotransmitter, causing loss of synaptic inhibition so that any stimulus produces hyperactivity.

Correct Option Explanation

As a potent spinal stimulant, strychnine is now banned for use, and treatment of poisoning includes depressants and anaesthetics to counter the resulting convulsions.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Blocking GABA-mediated Cl- channel opening describes picrotoxin's mechanism, not strychnine's.
  • Strychnine's described mechanism involves glycine, not direct glutamate/NMDA potentiation.
  • Strychnine acts on the spinal cord (glycine inhibition), not by directly stimulating peripheral nicotinic neuromuscular receptors.
Know More
  • Picrotoxin, from Anamirta cocculus (fish berries), causes clonic, spontaneous, asymmetrical convulsions via GABA inhibition; its antidote is diazepam.
  • Bicuculline is a synthetic GABA antagonist with picrotoxin-like action, used as a research tool.
  • Pentylenetetrazol (PTZ) causes CNS depolarization similar to picrotoxin and is now used only experimentally.
  • CNS stimulants are classed as spinal (strychnine, brucine), medullary (doxapram, bemegride) and cortical (cocaine, amphetamines) stimulants.

posts.post_title: Analeptic used to reverse barbiturate or inh…
posts.post_content: Which analeptic drug is used to stimulate respiration in the postanaesthetic period, reversing barbiturate or inhalant anaesthetic depression in dogs, cats and horses?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Doxapram

Doxapram is used to stimulate respiration postanaesthetically, reversing barbiturate or inhalant anaesthetic depression in dogs, cats and horses.

Correct Option Explanation

Analeptics like doxapram carry the risk of causing convulsions and are not considered entirely safe, so mechanical ventilation is generally preferred when available.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Nikethamide, though similar to doxapram, is no longer used because of its own respiratory suppression risk.
  • Strychnine is a spinal convulsant, not a clinically used respiratory analeptic, and is banned for use.
  • Bicuculline is a synthetic GABA antagonist used purely as a research tool, not a clinical analeptic.
Know More
  • Analeptics are used clinically in hypnotic drug poisoning (without mechanical ventilation), drowning suffocation, infant apnoea, and failure to ventilate after general anaesthesia.
  • For ordinary fainting, reflex stimulation with smelling ammonia or alcohol is sufficient — analeptics are not needed.
  • 4-Aminopyridine antagonizes d-tubocurarine and several CNS depressants including pancuronium and diazepam-ketamine.
  • Yohimbine and tolazoline are alpha2 antagonists, with yohimbine specific for reversing xylazine poisoning.

posts.post_title: Mechanism of caffeine's CNS stimulant action
posts.post_content: Caffeine stimulates the CNS cortex mainly by

_aimcq_options.text: Blocking adenosine receptors and inhibiting phosphodiesterase, raising cAMP
Stimulating nicotinic receptors in the brain

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Blocking adenosine receptors and inhibiting phosphodiesterase, raising cAMP

Caffeine irritates the CNS cortex by blocking adenosine receptors and inducing cAMP through phosphodiesterase inhibition (the enzyme that degrades cAMP).

Correct Option Explanation

This dual mechanism underlies caffeine's stimulant, vasodilator and diuretic-promoting properties, though it is rarely used clinically in animals.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Caffeine does not act by blocking GABA-A receptors; its mechanism is adenosine receptor blockade and cAMP elevation.
  • Caffeine has no described nicotinic receptor stimulant mechanism in this text.
  • Caffeine does not act by inhibiting MAO; that mechanism is unrelated to its documented CNS action here.
Know More
  • Coffee beans contain about 1% caffeine; tea leaves contain about 3% theophylline and caffeine combined.
  • Caffeine's clinical uses include migraine and apnoea in infants.
  • Theophylline, another methylxanthine, is useful as a bronchodilator.
  • Amphetamines act by releasing noradrenaline and dopamine from storage vesicles, increasing mental activity.

posts.post_title: Common mechanism of action shared by all ant…
posts.post_content: What mechanism of action is common to all antipsychotic drugs?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Potent dopamine D2 receptor blockade

All antipsychotic drugs share a potent dopamine (D2) receptor blocking action.

Correct Option Explanation

They block the limbic system and mesocortical areas; extrapyramidal effects arise from this dopaminergic blockade in the basal ganglia, and firing of dopamine neurons initially increases before diminishing over time.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Antipsychotics are not defined by serotonin reuptake inhibition; that mechanism describes a different drug class (e.g., SSRIs).
  • GABA-A potentiation is the mechanism of barbiturates and benzodiazepines, not the defining antipsychotic mechanism.
  • Antipsychotics are not defined by alpha-2 agonism; rather they have varying degrees of alpha-adrenergic blocking activity.
Know More
  • Clozapine is notable for having only a weak D2 blocking action despite being an effective atypical antipsychotic.
  • Risperidone blocks both D2 and 5HT2 receptors.
  • Antipsychotics have weak H2 antihistaminic and anti-5HT action, and weak anticholinergic properties.
  • In animals, antipsychotics selectively inhibit the 'conditioned avoidance response'.

posts.post_title: Antipsychotic drug notable for cardiac arrhy…
posts.post_content: Which phenothiazine has low potency, marked central anticholinergic action, the lowest incidence of extrapyramidal effects, but is notable for cardiac arrhythmia and interference with male sexual function?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Thioridazine

Thioridazine has low potency, marked central anticholinergic action, the lowest incidence of extrapyramidal side effects, but causes cardiac arrhythmia and interferes with male sexual function.

Correct Option Explanation

This distinct side-effect profile, especially the cardiac arrhythmia risk, differentiates it from other phenothiazines with different potency and safety profiles.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Triflupromazine is more potent than chlorpromazine and produces muscle dystonia when injected, a different profile from thioridazine's described effects.
  • Trifluoperazine is highly potent with minimum autonomic action but marked extrapyramidal side effects — the opposite extrapyramidal profile from thioridazine.
  • Haloperidol is a potent antipsychotic (butyrophenone) with few autonomic effects and is less epileptogenic, not matching thioridazine's described profile.
Know More
  • Droperidol is a short-acting neuroleptic used in combination with anaesthesia.
  • Pimozide is a specific dopamine antagonist with long duration, useful for maintenance therapy.
  • Clozapine carries a high incidence of agranulocytosis and other blood dyscrasias.
  • Loxapine acts quickly (lasting 12 hours), with less sedation but prominent cardiac and neurological toxicity.

posts.post_title: Endocrine adverse effect consistently caused…
posts.post_content: Neuroleptic (antipsychotic) drugs consistently cause which endocrine adverse effect?

_aimcq_options.text: Increased prolactin, causing galactorrhoea and gynaecomastia

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Increased prolactin, causing galactorrhoea and gynaecomastia

Neuroleptics consistently increase prolactin, resulting in galactorrhoea and gynaecomastia.

Correct Option Explanation

This occurs because dopamine normally inhibits prolactin release; D2 receptor blockade by antipsychotics removes this inhibition, raising prolactin levels.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Prolactin is increased, not decreased, by these drugs — the direction is opposite to the incorrect option.
  • There is no described effect on thyroid hormone/hyperthyroidism in this material for antipsychotics.
  • There is no described effect on cortisol/adrenal function attributed to neuroleptics in this text.
Know More
  • Tolerance to the sedative and hypotensive effects of neuroleptics develops within days to weeks.
  • Oral absorption of these drugs is unpredictable with low bioavailability, so IM or IV administration is preferred.
  • These drugs cross the blood-brain barrier, reaching higher brain than plasma concentrations.
  • High doses of chlorpromazine can directly depress the heart, causing QT prolongation and T-wave suppression.

posts.post_title: Extrapyramidal side effect characterized by …
posts.post_content: Which extrapyramidal adverse effect of antipsychotics is characterized by purposeless involuntary facial and limb movements such as constant chewing, lip licking and cheek puffing?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Tardive dyskinesia

Tardive dyskinesia is characterized by purposeless involuntary facial and limb movements — constant chewing, pouting, cheek puffing and lip licking.

Correct Option Explanation

This is one of several distinct extrapyramidal syndromes seen with chronic antipsychotic use, alongside rigidity, tremor and shuffling gait.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Akathisia is characterized by restlessness, discomfort and apparent agitation, not the specific facial/limb movements described.
  • Acute muscular dystonia presents as muscle spasms, torticollis and locked jaw, a different presentation from tardive dyskinesia.
  • 'Parkinsonian rigidity' describes a general extrapyramidal feature (rigidity, tremor, shuffling gait) rather than the specific purposeless movement pattern of tardive dyskinesia.
Know More
  • Antipsychotics can also cause blue pigmentation of exposed skin, corneal opacity and retinal degeneration.
  • Hypersensitivity reactions include rashes, urticaria, contact dermatitis, photosensitivity and agranulocytosis.
  • Anticholinergic adverse effects include dry mouth, constipation and urinary hesitancy.
  • Alpha-adrenergic blockade causes hypotension and inhibition of ejaculation.

posts.post_title: Definition of an autoreceptor
posts.post_content: An autoreceptor is best defined as a receptor that

_aimcq_options.text: Is located on a neuron and responds to the transmitter released by that same neuron
Responds only to hormones circulating in the blood
Is found exclusively on postsynaptic muscle membranes
Mediates only positive feedback amplification of transmitter release

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Is located on a neuron and responds to the transmitter released by that same neuron

An autoreceptor is located anywhere on a neuron and responds to the transmitter released by that same neuron.

Correct Option Explanation

It usually mediates a negative feedback response, and presynaptic receptors (like α2 receptors inhibiting further noradrenaline release) are classic examples of autoreceptors.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Autoreceptors respond to the neuron's own transmitter, not general circulating hormones.
  • Autoreceptors are not restricted to postsynaptic muscle membranes; they can occur presynaptically on the releasing neuron itself.
  • Autoreceptors typically mediate negative, not positive, feedback, limiting rather than amplifying transmitter release.
Know More
  • Presynaptic α2 receptors on adrenergic nerve terminals are a key example of autoreceptor-mediated feedback.
  • The blood-brain barrier is an important permeability boundary limiting passive diffusion of substances from blood into the CNS.
  • Autacoids are described as 'local' or 'tissue' hormones with a brief lifetime, acting near their site of synthesis.
  • An agonist possesses affinity for a receptor and causes a change producing an observable effect; an antagonist lacks intrinsic activity but blocks an agonist's action.

posts.post_title: Definition of an anodyne
posts.post_content: An 'anodyne' is defined as a

_aimcq_options.text: Smoothening agent that relieves pain, also known as antispasmodic-like soothing agent
Drug that stimulates the medullary respiratory center
Drug that lowers raised body temperature
Substance that binds plasma albumin without pharmacodynamic effect

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Smoothening agent that relieves pain, also known as antispasmodic-like soothing agent

An anodyne is a smoothening agent that relieves pain, exemplified by atropine.

Correct Option Explanation

This term overlaps conceptually with soothing, pain-relieving action distinct from classical narcotic or non-narcotic analgesics.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A drug stimulating the medullary respiratory center is an analeptic (e.g., doxapram), not an anodyne.
  • A drug lowering raised body temperature is an antipyretic (e.g., paracetamol), a different definition.
  • A substance binding plasma albumin without direct pharmacodynamic effect describes an acceptor site, an unrelated glossary term.
Know More
  • Antisialogues (e.g., atropine) reduce the flow and fluidity of saliva.
  • Antispasmodics (e.g., belladonna) relieve smooth muscle spasm of the intestine, bile duct and ureters.
  • Antitussives (e.g., codeine phosphate) relieve cough, usually via central depression of the cough centre.
  • Analgesics relieve pain by raising the pain threshold, classified as narcotic (morphine) or non-narcotic (aspirin).

posts.post_title: Definition of adrenergic neuron blocking dru…
posts.post_content: Adrenergic neuron blocking drugs, exemplified by reserpine, act by

_aimcq_options.text: Acting presynaptically to decrease release of the endogenous transmitter norepinephrine
Directly occupying and blocking postsynaptic adrenergic receptors
Mimicking the effects of epinephrine and norepinephrine
Stimulating the release of excess norepinephrine acutely

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Acting presynaptically to decrease release of the endogenous transmitter norepinephrine

Adrenergic neuron blocking drugs act presynaptically at the nerve terminal to decrease release of the endogenous transmitter norepinephrine, exemplified by reserpine.

Correct Option Explanation

This distinguishes them from adrenergic (receptor) blockers, which act postsynaptically by occupying the receptor itself, such as ergot-type agents described as adrenergic blockers.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Directly occupying postsynaptic receptors describes adrenergic (receptor) blockers like ergot, a distinct glossary category from neuron blockers.
  • Mimicking epinephrine/norepinephrine effects describes adrenergic drugs (agonists) like amphetamine, the opposite category.
  • Adrenergic neuron blockers decrease, rather than acutely stimulate, transmitter release as their defining action.
Know More
  • Adrenergic drugs (e.g., amphetamine) cause physiological responses similar to epinephrine/norepinephrine.
  • Adrenoceptors are macromolecular structures on cells innervated by adrenergic neurons, classed as α and β types.
  • An additive effect is when the combined effect of two agents equals the sum of each given alone (e.g., α-blocker plus thiazide diuretic for hypertension).
  • Alkaloids are plant-derived organic bases with heterocyclic nitrogen, normally insoluble in water though their salts are soluble (e.g., morphine).

posts.post_title: Biphasic blood pressure response to rapid IV…
posts.post_content: Rapid intravenous injection of a pharmacological dose of adrenaline (1-3 µg/kg) produces a characteristic biphasic blood pressure response consisting of

_aimcq_options.text: An initial rise due to alpha-1 activity followed by a fall due to beta-2 activity
An initial fall due to beta-2 activity followed by a sustained rise from alpha-1 activity
Two consecutive rises with no fall at any point
A single sustained fall throughout the observation period

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: An initial rise due to alpha-1 activity followed by a fall due to beta-2 activity

Rapid IV adrenaline produces a biphasic response: an initial rise in BP from α1-mediated vasoconstriction and myocardial stimulation, followed by a fall from β2-mediated vasodilatation.

Correct Option Explanation

This contrasts with slow IV infusion, SC injection, or very low doses (0.1 µg/kg), which produce only a fall in BP since the vasodilator β2 effect dominates at lower doses/rates.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • This option reverses the actual sequence — the rise comes first (α1), then the fall (β2), not the other way around.
  • The biphasic response is rise-then-fall, not two consecutive rises with no fall.
  • A rapid pharmacological IV dose does not produce a single sustained fall; that pattern is seen with slow/low-dose administration instead.
Know More
  • Adrenaline interacts with all subtypes (α1, α2, β1, β2, β3) of adrenergic receptors.
  • Adrenaline is a powerful cardiac stimulant via β1 receptors, increasing both heart rate and force of contraction.
  • The levo form of adrenaline is about 15 times more potent than the dextro isomer.
  • Large doses of adrenaline cause vasoconstriction even in skeletal muscle, since α-mediated action overrides β2-mediated relaxation.

posts.post_title: Structure-activity relationship: effect of r…
posts.post_content: According to the structure-activity relationship of catecholamines, removal of one or both ring hydroxyl (OH) groups results in

_aimcq_options.text: Selective loss of alpha activity only, with beta activity unaffected

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Reduced beta-adrenergic activity

Removal of one or both ring OH- groups reduces β activity according to the structure-activity relationship of catecholamines.

Correct Option Explanation

This is why non-catecholamines, which lack one or both hydroxyl groups, generally have poorer adrenoceptor affinity compared with true catecholamines.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Removing the hydroxyl groups reduces, not increases, β activity — the opposite direction of effect.
  • This structural change produces a measurable reduction in activity, not 'no change'.
  • The described effect is specifically on β activity, not a selective isolated effect sparing β while only removing α.
Know More
  • Maximum sympathomimetic activity occurs when two carbon atoms separate the aromatic ring from the amine group.
  • Increased bulkiness of N-atom substitution increases beta receptor activity.
  • Beta-carbon side chain substitution results in less active central actions.
  • Alpha-carbon substitution produces a compound not susceptible to MAO metabolism.

posts.post_title: Why noradrenaline decreases blood flow to sk…
posts.post_content: Unlike adrenaline, norepinephrine decreases blood flow to skeletal muscle because

_aimcq_options.text: It has little action on beta-2 receptors, leaving alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed
It selectively blocks beta-1 receptors in skeletal muscle
It has no effect on any adrenergic receptor in muscle
It preferentially binds muscarinic receptors in skeletal muscle vessels

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: It has little action on beta-2 receptors, leaving alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed

Norepinephrine has little action on β2 receptors, so the α-mediated vasoconstriction in skeletal muscle vessels is unopposed, decreasing blood flow.

Correct Option Explanation

This differs from adrenaline, which strongly activates β2 receptors in skeletal muscle vasculature, generally producing vasodilatation there except at very high doses.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Norepinephrine does not block β1 receptors; rather it has weak agonist action on β2 specifically, while remaining a potent agonist at β1 (cardiac) and α receptors.
  • Norepinephrine clearly does affect adrenergic receptors (α1, α2, β1) in skeletal muscle vasculature; it is not without effect.
  • Norepinephrine's action here is adrenergic, not muscarinic/cholinergic.
Know More
  • Norepinephrine and epinephrine are equipotent on β1 receptors but NE is 2-10 times less potent than epinephrine on α receptors.
  • Norepinephrine does not produce the biphasic BP response seen with rapid IV epinephrine; it simply raises BP dose-dependently.
  • In intact animals, norepinephrine causes reflex bradycardia via vagal stimulation through the baroreceptor mechanism.
  • Cardiac output with NE is unaffected or decreased due to reduced venous return from predominant vasoconstriction.

posts.post_title: Mechanism of adrenaline-induced hyperglycaem…
posts.post_content: Adrenaline's hyperglycaemic effect results from all of the following EXCEPT

_aimcq_options.text: Increased insulin release via beta-2 stimulation
Increased glycogenolysis in the liver via beta-2 action
Increased glucagon release via beta-2 action
Decreased insulin release via alpha-2 action

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Increased insulin release via beta-2 stimulation

Adrenaline's hyperglycaemic effect involves decreased, not increased, insulin release, mediated via α2 receptors.

Correct Option Explanation

This decreased insulin release, combined with increased hepatic glycogenolysis and glucagon release (both β2-mediated), together raise blood glucose significantly.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Increased hepatic glycogenolysis via β2 action IS a correctly documented contributor to adrenaline's hyperglycaemic effect.
  • Increased glucagon release via β2 action IS a correctly documented contributor.
  • Decreased insulin release via α2 action IS the correct, documented mechanism (the opposite of the false statement being asked about).

  • The order is clearly different between the two classes, not identical.
  • Neither class is described as paralyzing the diaphragm first; in both cases intercostal/trunk muscles are affected relatively late, with respiration stopping near the end.
  • Competitive blockers do eventually affect intercostal muscles, as shown in their listed order of paralysis, not sparing them entirely.
Know More
  • Recovery from non-depolarizing blockade occurs in the reverse order of paralysis onset.
  • Depolarizing blockers cause brief fasciculations before flaccid paralysis, unlike competitive blockers.
  • Apnoea with depolarizing blockers occurs within 45-90 seconds but lasts only 2-5 minutes with rapid recovery.
  • Dantrolene and quinine are centrally/directly acting muscle relaxant alternatives to peripheral neuromuscular blockers.

posts.post_title: Definition of a neuromodulator as distinct f…
posts.post_content: A 'neuromodulator', as distinct from a classical neurotransmitter, is defined as a substance that

_aimcq_options.text: Originates from cellular/nonsynaptic sites and influences excitability without altering membrane potential
Is stored exclusively in presynaptic vesicles and directly causes membrane depolarization
Is a hormone that arises specifically from a neuron
Only participates in second-messenger mediated responses to another transmitter

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Originates from cellular/nonsynaptic sites and influences excitability without altering membrane potential

A neuromodulator originates from cellular and nonsynaptic sites and influences the general level of excitability without altering the membrane potential directly.

Correct Option Explanation

Examples include ammonia, CO2, prostaglandins and steroid hormones — substances that adjust neuronal responsiveness rather than directly triggering an electrical signal.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Being stored in presynaptic vesicles and directly causing depolarization describes a classical neurotransmitter, not a neuromodulator.
  • A hormone arising from a neuron is the definition of a neurohormone (e.g., oxytocin, vasopressin), a distinct category.
  • Substances that participate in eliciting a response to a transmitter, like cAMP, cGMP and IP3, are defined as neuromediators, a different category from neuromodulators.
Know More
  • Neurotransmitters are substances stored in presynaptic vesicles that, on release, cause excitation or inhibition.
  • Fast neurotransmitters (glutamate, GABA) act via ligand-gated ion channels; slow transmitters/neuromodulators (dopamine, neuropeptides, prostanoids) act via G-protein coupled receptors.
  • Almost 100 neurotransmitters have been discovered so far.
  • Biogenic amine neurotransmitters include histamine, 5-HT, adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine and ACh.

posts.post_title: Classification of mivacurium among non-depol…
posts.post_content: Among non-depolarizing (competitive) neuromuscular blockers, mivacurium is classified as

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Short acting

Mivacurium is classified as a short-acting non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker.

Correct Option Explanation

This places it in a distinct duration category from long-acting agents like d-tubocurarine and pancuronium, and intermediate-acting agents like vecuronium and atracurium.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Long-acting non-depolarizing blockers include d-tubocurarine, gallamine triethiodide, pancuronium, doxacurium and pipecuronium — not mivacurium.
  • Intermediate-acting agents include vecuronium and atracurium, a different duration class from mivacurium.
  • 'Ultra-long acting' is not a category used in this classification scheme.
Know More
  • Depolarizing blockers (non-competitive) include succinylcholine and decamethonium.
  • Centrally acting muscle relaxant alternatives include dantrolene sodium and quinine.
  • d-Tubocurarine is an alkaloid obtained from Chondrodendron tomentosum, notable for prominent histamine release.
  • Non-depolarizing blockers act by occupying nicotinic (NM) receptors at the muscle end-plate without intrinsic activity, often via one or more quaternary N+ atoms.

posts.post_title: Anticonvulsant avoided due to photophobia re…
posts.post_content: Which anticonvulsant drug is not commonly used because its major side effect, photophobia, resembles a sign seen in canine distemper?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Trimethadione

Trimethadione's major side effect is photophobia, as observed in distemper, making it not commonly used.

Correct Option Explanation

This side effect could confuse the clinical picture with distemper-related neurological signs, complicating diagnosis and making this drug less favoured in veterinary practice.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Phenobarbitone is the preferred first-line anticonvulsant in dogs and cats, not associated with this photophobia issue.
  • Diazepam is the drug of choice for status epilepticus, with minimal cardiovascular/respiratory depression, not linked to photophobia.
  • Bromides (ammonium, potassium, sodium) are used to control convulsions without the described photophobia side effect.
Know More
  • Convulsions may result from hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, or poisoning by lead, strychnine or organophosphorus compounds, as well as infectious diseases like distemper.
  • The paroxysmal shift is a pathogenic mechanism where a damaged group of neurons suddenly depolarizes, generating a burst of action potentials.
  • Valproic acid is not used in dogs due to its short half-life in this species.
  • Carbamazepine's elimination is too rapid in dogs to be clinically useful.

posts.post_title: Traditional pharmacological classification o…
posts.post_content: Before the modern numerical classification (5-HT1, 5-HT2, etc.), serotonin receptors were classified pharmacologically into which two types?

_aimcq_options.text: Central type and peripheral type only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Musculotropic (D type) and neurotropic (M type)

Based on pharmacologic criteria, serotonin receptors were classified as musculotropic (D type) and neurotropic (M type).

Correct Option Explanation

This older classification predates the more recent numerical system (5-HT1, 5-HT2, 5-HT3, etc.) that is used to describe serotonin receptor subtypes today.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Ionotropic and metabotropic' is a general receptor mechanism classification, not the specific historical D-type/M-type terminology used for 5-HT receptors in this text.
  • 'Alpha type and beta type' is the classification used for adrenergic receptors, not serotonin receptors.
  • 'Central and peripheral type only' is not the described historical pharmacologic classification for 5-HT receptors.
Know More
  • Serotonin is a potent depolarizer of nerve endings, and tachyphylaxis with it is very common.
  • On the cardiovascular system, serotonin causes both arteriolar constriction (direct smooth muscle action) and dilatation (via EDRF release).
  • Serotonin also releases adrenaline from the adrenal medulla, making net cardiovascular reflexes complex.
  • 5-HT agonists include LSD, azapirones and cisapride; antagonists include methysergide, cyproheptadine and ondansetron.

posts.post_title: Hydromorphone's pupillary effect compared to…
posts.post_content: Unlike morphine, hydromorphone (a ketone-substituted morphine derivative) notably

_aimcq_options.text: Produces exaggerated miosis compared to morphine
Has no effect on the CNS at all

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Does not produce miosis

Hydromorphone notably does not produce miosis, unlike morphine.

Correct Option Explanation

Despite this difference, hydromorphone is a strong, highly potent agonist that is more sedative and less euphoric than morphine, with less constipation but more intense tolerance and physical dependence due to its high potency.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Hydromorphone specifically lacks the miosis effect seen with morphine, rather than exaggerating it.
  • Hydromorphone does not cause mydriasis at all doses; the documented finding is simply absence of miosis, not a reversed pupillary effect.
  • Hydromorphone clearly has significant CNS effects — it is a strong sedative-analgesic agonist, not devoid of CNS action.
Know More
  • Hydromorphone results from ketone substitution at the 6-hydroxyl position of morphine.
  • It causes more sedation and less euphoria than morphine.
  • It causes less constipation than morphine despite being a strong agonist.
  • Its high potency leads to more intense tolerance/dependence and significant respiratory depression.

posts.post_title: Definition of 'hallucinogens' (psychotomimet…
posts.post_content: Hallucinogens, also called psychotomimetics, are defined as drugs that

_aimcq_options.text: Alter mood, behaviour, thought and perception in a manner similar to psychosis
Selectively relieve pain without altering consciousness
Induce or maintain normal arousal sleep
Stabilize mood specifically in manic conditions

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Alter mood, behaviour, thought and perception in a manner similar to psychosis

Hallucinogens (psychotomimetics) are drugs that alter mood, behaviour, thought and perception in a manner similar to that seen in psychosis.

Correct Option Explanation

This distinguishes them from therapeutic psychiatric drugs, since hallucinogens mimic or induce psychosis-like states rather than treating them.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Selectively relieving pain without altering consciousness is the definition of an analgesic, not a hallucinogen.
  • Inducing or maintaining normal arousal sleep is the definition of a hypnotic, a different drug category.
  • Stabilizing mood in manic conditions is the definition of an antimanic drug, distinct from hallucinogens.
Know More
  • Anxiolytic drugs are mild CNS depressants producing a restful state of mind without interfering with normal mental or physical function.
  • Antidepressants elevate mood in depressive illness; antimanic drugs stabilize mood in manic conditions.
  • A sedative subdues excitement and calms without inducing sleep; a hypnotic induces or maintains sleep.
  • An antiepileptic drug is used to control seizures; an analeptic induces CNS stimulation.

posts.post_title: Route of absorption NOT available to opioids
posts.post_content: Opioids are readily absorbed from the GI tract, nasal mucosa, lung, and by subcutaneous, intramuscular and intravenous routes, but are notably NOT absorbed through

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Intact skin

Opioids are not absorbed through intact skin, despite being well absorbed from many other routes.

Correct Option Explanation

This is why transdermal opioid delivery (e.g., fentanyl patches) requires special formulation to enhance skin penetration rather than relying on simple diffusion through intact skin.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Opioids ARE absorbed from the stomach and small intestine, part of their GI absorption.
  • Opioids ARE absorbed from various mucous membranes (e.g., nasal mucosa).
  • Opioids ARE well absorbed after subcutaneous administration, one of their standard parenteral routes.
Know More
  • Opioids undergo glucuronide conjugation as their primary metabolic pathway.
  • Opioid toxicity decreases with maturity of the animal.
  • In dogs, opioid toxicity can cause convulsions similar to strychnine.
  • Addiction is rarely encountered in animals compared with humans.

posts.post_title: Location of AT2 angiotensin receptors
posts.post_content: AT2 angiotensin receptors, which do not mediate the classical actions of angiotensin II, have been identified mainly in the

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Adrenal medulla and CNS

AT2 receptors have been identified in the adrenal medulla and CNS, in contrast to AT1 receptors which mediate the classical peripheral actions of angiotensin II.

Correct Option Explanation

Since all the major, well-characterized effects of angiotensin II (vasoconstriction, aldosterone release, sympathetic outflow, etc.) are mediated through AT1, AT2's physiological role remains comparatively less defined.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Vascular smooth muscle vasoconstriction is mediated through AT1, not AT2, receptors.
  • Renal tubular effects of angiotensin II (indirect, via aldosterone) are attributed to AT1-mediated pathways, not a described AT2 renal tubule action.
  • Cardiac effects like increased inotropy are mediated through AT1 receptors, not AT2.
Know More
  • Losartan is the specific antagonist for the AT1 receptor.
  • AT1 is a G-protein coupled receptor using phospholipase C/IP3/DAG signalling in most tissues.
  • In liver and kidney, angiotensin II inhibits adenylyl cyclase via AT1 receptor signalling.
  • All the major effects of angiotensin II are mediated through AT1 receptors.

posts.post_title: Active narcotic metabolite of chloral hydrate
posts.post_content: Chloral hydrate exerts its hypnotic effect after being reduced in the body to

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 2,2,2-trichloroethanol

Chloral hydrate is reduced in the body to 2,2,2-trichloroethanol, which is the actual narcotic/hypnotic agent.

Correct Option Explanation

Chloral hydrate has a slow onset, making the depth of anaesthesia difficult to assess, and severe reactions can occur if it escapes perivascularly, contributing to its declining clinical use.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Pentobarbital is an unrelated barbiturate, not a metabolite of chloral hydrate.
  • Norketamine is the active hypnotic metabolite of ketamine, not chloral hydrate.
  • Succinic acid is a metabolite of succinylcholine breakdown, unrelated to chloral hydrate.
Know More
  • Chloral hydrate is used in large animals, sometimes combined as 12% chloral hydrate + 6% MgSO4 intravenously.
  • It has a low margin of safety and is not commonly used now that better agents are available.
  • Chloralose (glucose + chloral hydrate) produces long, shallow depth and slow recovery, and is also not used.
  • Urethane, another older agent, is carcinogenic and has been discontinued.

posts.post_title: Non-barbiturate imidazole intravenous anaest…
posts.post_content: Which non-barbiturate intravenous anaesthetic, an imidazole derivative, was developed as a hypnotic specifically in pigs and shows remarkable cardiovascular stability?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Metomidate

Metomidate, a non-barbiturate imidazole intravenous anaesthetic, was developed as a hypnotic in pigs, showing poor analgesia but strong muscle relaxation and remarkable CVS stability.

Correct Option Explanation

It is also used for restraint of birds in addition to pigs, reflecting its utility across multiple species where cardiovascular stability during sedation is valued.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Etomidate (hypnomidate) is a related but distinct imidazole compound with low CVS toxicity but known for suppressing adrenocortical function, and is expensive/unpopular — not the pig-specific hypnotic described.
  • Propofol is 2,6-diisopropylphenol, a completely different chemical class, not an imidazole.
  • Alphaxolone is a steroid anaesthetic component of Saffan, not an imidazole compound.
Know More
  • Etomidate releases histamine but generally causes low respiratory depression.
  • Etomidate suppresses adrenocortical function, an important adverse effect limiting its popularity.
  • Saffan (Althesin) combines alphaxolone and alphadolone, both steroids, with a high therapeutic index.
  • Saffan is contraindicated in dogs due to histamine release from its vehicle.

posts.post_title: Species with dopamine receptors mediating re…
posts.post_content: Dopamine's low-dose renal and mesenteric vasodilator effect, mediated by D1 receptors, is exploited clinically because dopamine, unlike norepinephrine, has

_aimcq_options.text: A unique dopaminergic receptor action in addition to direct alpha/beta and indirect actions
No effect whatsoever on the cardiovascular system
Purely indirect action with no direct receptor binding

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A unique dopaminergic receptor action in addition to direct alpha/beta and indirect actions

Dopamine is unique among catecholamines in having direct (α and β), indirect (norepinephrine release), and dopaminergic (D1/D2) actions.

Correct Option Explanation

This triple mechanism explains its distinctive dose-dependent effects — renal/mesenteric vasodilation at low doses (D1), cardiac stimulation at moderate doses (β1), and vasoconstriction at high doses (α1) — a profile not shared by norepinephrine or isoproterenol.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Dopamine clearly does have significant, well-characterized cardiovascular effects, not none at all.
  • Dopamine has both direct and indirect actions, not purely indirect action.
  • Dopamine's receptor selectivity is distinct from isoproterenol's, which lacks any dopaminergic receptor activity.
Know More
  • Dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier when given exogenously, so it has no central effects in this context.
  • Dopamine is the immediate metabolic precursor of norepinephrine in the catecholamine synthesis pathway.
  • At very high doses (≥10 µg/kg/min), dopamine's α1-mediated vasoconstriction predominates, potentially countering its beneficial renal effects.
  • Dopamine is used in cardiogenic or septic shock and severe congestive heart failure with oliguria.

posts.post_title: Term for drugs that potentiate antihypertens…
posts.post_content: When an alpha-adrenoceptor blocker and a thiazide diuretic are combined and their antihypertensive effect equals the simple sum of each drug's individual effect, this is termed

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: An additive effect

This is termed an additive effect — the combined effect of two chemicals equals the sum of the effect of each agent given alone.

Correct Option Explanation

The example of an α-adrenoceptor blocker combined with a thiazide diuretic producing an additive antihypertensive effect illustrates this precise pharmacological definition.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A 'synergistic effect' would imply the combined effect is greater than the simple sum, which is a distinct concept from the additive effect described here.
  • An 'antagonistic effect' describes interference of one chemical with the action of another, the opposite of an additive relationship.
  • An 'idiosyncratic effect' refers to an unusual individual reaction to a drug, unrelated to the concept of combined additive dosing effects.
Know More
  • Antagonism is defined as the interference of one chemical with the action of another.
  • An antagonist is devoid of intrinsic activity but inhibits the action of an agonist; a pure antagonist has no activating effect on the receptor at all.
  • An agonist possesses affinity for a receptor and can cause a change producing an observable effect.
  • Adverse effects are harmful or seriously unpleasant effects at therapeutic doses that call for dose reduction or drug withdrawal.

posts.post_title: Definition of an 'allergen' in pharmacologic…
posts.post_content: In pharmacological terminology, an 'allergen' is defined as a substance that

_aimcq_options.text: Refers only to synthetic drugs causing rash

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Causes formation of reaginic antibodies

An allergen is defined as a substance that causes reaginic antibody formation.

Correct Option Explanation

This antibody formation underlies the subsequent hypersensitivity/allergic reaction upon re-exposure to the same substance, triggering mediator release such as histamine from mast cells.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • An allergen triggers antibody formation; it does not itself function as a histamine receptor blocker — that describes antihistamines instead.
  • Allergens are not synonymous with autacoids; autacoids are locally-acting substances like histamine and serotonin, a distinct pharmacological category.
  • Allergens are not restricted to synthetic drugs; many natural substances (pollens, foods, venoms) can act as allergens.
Know More
  • Autacoids are local hormones with a brief lifetime, acting near their site of synthesis, and are usually vasoactive.
  • An alkaloid is a plant-derived organic base containing heterocyclic nitrogen, normally insoluble in water (e.g., morphine).
  • An antihypertensive drug lowers abnormally high blood pressure (e.g., guanethidine).
  • An anti-inflammatory drug relieves pain/discomfort by blocking inflammatory processes, grouped as steroidal (betamethasone) or non-steroidal (phenylbutazone).
